families.title: A multiplication fact
explanations: fact-slip (recall): A multiplication fact (12 × 12) is not yet reliable.
add-for-multiply (conceptual): 12 × 12 was added instead of multiplied.

teach.idea: a × b counts a groups of b: the same as b groups of a.
teach.method: Rebuild a fact from one you know: double, add or take away one group, or split a factor.

families.title: Area of a rectangle
explanations: perimeter-for-area (conceptual): The distance around (perimeter) was found instead of the space inside (area).
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (12 × 12) is not yet reliable.
add-sides (conceptual): The two sides were added; area multiplies them.

teach.idea: Area counts the unit squares that cover a shape.
teach.method: A rectangle has rows of equal squares: rows × squares in a row.

families.title: A missing part of an equivalent fraction
explanations: additive-scaling (conceptual): The same amount was added to the top as to the bottom; equal fractions multiply both by the same number.
scale-one-part (procedural): Only the bottom was changed; the top must be multiplied by the same number.
fact-slip (recall): A multiplication fact (9 × 10) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Equal fractions cover the same amount: cutting every piece into k smaller pieces multiplies top and bottom by k.
teach.method: Find what the bottom was multiplied by, and multiply the top by the same number.

families.title: Adding or subtracting like fractions
explanations: add-denominators (conceptual): The bottom numbers were added too; they name the size of the pieces, which does not change.
multiply-tops (procedural): The top numbers were multiplied; adding fractions adds the pieces.
subtract-reversed (procedural): The smaller top number was taken from the larger one the wrong way round.

teach.idea: Like fractions count the same size of piece: add or take away the pieces.
teach.method: Add or subtract the tops; the bottom (the size of the pieces) stays.

families.title: The definite integral of a constant
explanations: fencepost-width (procedural): The whole numbers from a to b were counted (one too many); the width is b − a.
add-width-height (conceptual): Width and height were added; the area multiplies them.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (12 × 4) is not yet reliable.
forget-height (conceptual): Only the width was found; the area is width × height.
ignore-lower-limit (conceptual): The width was taken as the upper limit only; the width is upper minus lower.

teach.idea: The integral of a constant c from a to b is the area of a rectangle: width b − a, height c.
teach.method: Width (upper minus lower) times height.

families.title: A quadratic equation with whole-number roots
explanations: root-signs (procedural): The numbers in the brackets were taken as the solutions; (x − 2) = 0 gives x = 2, so the signs flip.

teach.idea: If a product is zero, one of its factors is zero.
teach.method: Factorise x² + px + q = (x − r)(x − s), then each bracket gives a solution.

families.title: A value on a straight line
explanations: concatenate (conceptual): 9x with x = 9 was read as the digits 99; 9x means 9 × x.
add-for-multiply (conceptual): 9x was worked out as 9 + x; it means 9 × x.

teach.idea: y = mx + c gives y for any x: m × x, then add c.
teach.method: Multiply m by the value of x first, then add (or subtract) c.

families.title: Where a line meets y = x², by trying whole numbers
explanations: square-as-double (conceptual): x × x was worked out as x + x (doubling); x × x is x squared.

teach.idea: Where two graphs meet, their y values are equal.
teach.method: Try each whole number and compare x × x with the line's value.

families.title: Which graph is higher at a point

teach.idea: A graph is higher at x when its y value there is larger.
teach.method: Work out both y values at that x and compare.

families.title: The area between a parabola and a line
explanations: line-only (conceptual): The area under the line was found; the region is between the line and the parabola.
wrong-order (procedural): The parabola was taken as the top curve; here the line is above, so the answer was negative.

teach.idea: The area between two curves is the integral of (top − bottom) between where they meet.
teach.method: Find where they meet, check which is on top, integrate the difference.

families.title: A power of a whole number
explanations: one-factor-short (procedural): One factor too few was multiplied: 12 must appear 4 times.
multiply-for-power (conceptual): A power was worked out as a multiplication (12⁴ as 12 × 4); a power multiplies 12 by itself 4 times.
add-for-power (conceptual): The two numbers were added; a power is repeated multiplication.

teach.idea: aⁿ multiplies a by itself n times.
teach.method: Multiply step by step: 3, 9, 27, 81 for 3⁴.

families.title: Expanding a(x + b)
explanations: first-term-only (procedural): Only the x was multiplied by 12; the number outside multiplies every term in the bracket.
add-for-multiply (conceptual): 12 and 12 were added; the bracket means 12 × 12.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (12 × 12) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: The number outside a bracket multiplies every term inside.
teach.method: Multiply along an arrow to each term.

families.title: Expanding (x + a)(x + b)
explanations: product-for-sum (conceptual): The two numbers were multiplied for the x term; 8 × 9 is the number at the end, and the x term collects 8x and 9x.
one-cross-term (procedural): Only one of the two middle products was kept; both x × b and a × x give an x term.
sign-slip (prerequisite): -1 + 9 was worked out without the signs; adding numbers with different signs is a difference.

teach.idea: (x + a)(x + b) has four products; two of them are x terms.
teach.method: The x coefficient is a + b and the constant is ab.

families.title: The derivative of k xⁿ at a point
explanations: power-not-multiplied (procedural): The power was lowered but not brought down as a factor: the derivative of xⁿ is n xⁿ⁻¹.
value-not-slope (conceptual): The function's value was found, not its rate of change (the derivative).
power-not-lowered (procedural): The power was not lowered: the derivative of xⁿ is n xⁿ⁻¹.
multiply-for-power (prerequisite): A power was worked out as a multiplication (3⁴ as 3 × 4); a power multiplies 3 by itself 4 times.

teach.idea: The derivative of k xⁿ is k n xⁿ⁻¹.
teach.method: Multiply by the power, lower it by one, then substitute.

families.title: The definite integral of k xⁿ
explanations: no-divide (procedural): The power was raised but not divided by: ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1).
differentiated (conceptual): The function was differentiated instead of integrated: integrating raises the power.
power-not-raised (procedural): It was divided by the power without raising it: xⁿ becomes xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1).
multiply-for-power (prerequisite): A power was worked out as a multiplication (4⁴ as 4 × 4); a power multiplies 4 by itself 4 times.
ignore-lower-limit (conceptual): Only the upper limit was used; the answer is F(upper) − F(lower).

teach.idea: An antiderivative of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1).
teach.method: Raise the power, divide by the new power, then F(upper) − F(lower).

families.title: An integral by substitution
explanations: limits-not-changed (procedural): The old limits were used for u: when x goes from 2 to 3, u = x² + 4 goes from 8 to 13.
no-divide (procedural): The power was raised but not divided by: ∫ uⁿ du = uⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1).
extra-half (conceptual): It was divided by 2 for du = 2x dx, but the 2x is already in the integral: 2x dx is exactly du.
multiply-for-power (prerequisite): A power was worked out as a multiplication (12⁴ as 12 × 4); a power multiplies 12 by itself 4 times.

teach.idea: With u = x² + c, 2x dx becomes du.
teach.method: Change the limits to u, integrate uⁿ, and evaluate between the u limits.

families.title: How many real solutions a quadratic has
explanations: negative-square (prerequisite): b² was taken as negative for a negative b; a square is never negative.
minus-c-sign (prerequisite): The sign of −4ac was lost when c is negative: − 4 × (a negative number) adds.
forgot-four (procedural): The discriminant was taken as b² − c; it is b² − 4ac.

teach.idea: b² − 4ac decides how many real solutions there are.
teach.method: Positive: two; zero: one; negative: none.

families.title: The perimeter of a rectangle
explanations: area-for-perimeter (conceptual): The space inside (area) was found; the perimeter is the distance around the edge.
two-sides-only (procedural): Only two sides were added; a rectangle has four sides, two of each length.
three-sides (procedural): One side was left out; go all the way around: four sides.

teach.idea: The perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape: add the lengths of every side.
teach.method: A rectangle has two lengths and two widths: add one length and one width, then double.

families.title: Multiplying a two-digit number by a one-digit number
explanations: tens-as-ones (conceptual): The tens digit was multiplied as if it were 9, not 90: each digit's place value counts.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (9 × 9) is not yet reliable.
lost-carry (procedural): The tens carried from the ones were not added: they belong in the tens column.

teach.idea: Split the two-digit number into tens and ones, multiply each part, then add.
teach.method: 47 × 6 = 40 × 6 + 7 × 6 = 240 + 42 = 282. The 4 tens of 42 join the tens.

families.title: The remainder of a division
explanations: quotient-as-remainder (conceptual): The number of groups was given; the remainder is what is left over after the groups.
remainder-too-big (procedural): One group too few was taken: a remainder is always less than 8.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (12 × 8) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Dividing makes equal groups; the remainder is what is left when no more full groups fit.
teach.method: Find the biggest multiple of the divisor that fits, then subtract it from the number.

families.title: Dividing a number exactly
explanations: digits-reversed (procedural): The digits of the answer were written in the wrong order: the first step gives the tens.
one-group-off (recall): A multiplication fact with 9 slipped by one group.
dropped-zero (procedural): A zero in the answer was left out: when the divisor does not go into a step, write 0 there.

teach.idea: Dividing undoes multiplying: 84 ÷ 4 asks how many 4s make 84.
teach.method: Take away a large, easy chunk first (20 × 4 = 80), then divide what is left (4 ÷ 4 = 1): 20 + 1 = 21.

families.title: A fraction times a whole number
explanations: multiply-both (conceptual): Top and bottom were both multiplied by 9: that gives an equal fraction, not 9 lots of it.
multiply-bottom (procedural): The bottom was multiplied; 9 lots of 11/12 is 9 × 11 pieces of the same size.
add-whole (conceptual): 9 was added to the top; multiplying means 9 lots.

teach.idea: k × a/b means k lots of a/b: the pieces stay the same size, there are just more of them.
teach.method: Multiply the top by k and keep the bottom: 3 × 2/7 = 6/7.

families.title: Adding fractions with different denominators
explanations: add-tops-and-bottoms (conceptual): Tops and bottoms were added separately; fractions with different pieces must first be written with the same pieces.
same-bottom-not-scaled (procedural): A common denominator was chosen but the tops were not changed to match it.

teach.idea: Fractions can be added only when they count the same size of piece.
teach.method: Write both with a common denominator (an equivalent fraction for each), then add the tops.

families.title: A percentage of an amount
explanations: no-hundred (conceptual): Per cent means out of 100: the amount must be divided by 100 as well as multiplied.
percent-as-divisor (conceptual): It was divided by 95; 95% means 95 out of every 100.
subtracted (procedural): 95% of 400 is a part of 400, not 400 minus 95.

teach.idea: Per cent means out of 100: 30% of an amount is 30 parts of every 100.
teach.method: Find 1% (divide by 100) or 10% (divide by 10), then build up: 30% of 200 = 3 × 20 = 60.

families.title: The mean of four numbers
explanations: total-not-shared (procedural): The numbers were added but the total was not shared out among the four.
divide-by-three (procedural): The total was divided by the wrong count: there are four numbers.
middle-for-mean (conceptual): A middle value was chosen; the mean shares the total equally.

teach.idea: The mean shares the total out equally: it is the value every number would have if they were levelled out.
teach.method: Add all the numbers, then divide by how many numbers there are.

families.title: The square root of a perfect square
explanations: squared-instead (conceptual): The number was squared; the square root goes the other way.
near-square (recall): A square fact next to the right one was used.
half-for-root (conceptual): The number was halved; the square root is the number that multiplied by itself gives it.

teach.idea: A square root undoes squaring: √49 is the number that, multiplied by itself, makes 49.
teach.method: Think of the square facts: 7 × 7 = 49, so √49 = 7.

families.title: The volume of a cuboid in unit cubes
explanations: one-layer (conceptual): Only the bottom layer was counted; there are as many layers as the height.
added-sides (conceptual): The three lengths were added; volume multiplies them.
outside-only (conceptual): The squares on the outside faces were counted; volume counts the cubes inside too.

teach.idea: Volume counts the cubes that fill a shape: layers of cubes stacked up.
teach.method: Count one layer (length × width), then multiply by the number of layers (the height).

families.title: Solving ax + b = c
explanations: forgot-divide (procedural): 20 was taken away but the 9 was not divided out: 9x = 108 means x = 108 ÷ 9.
added-not-subtracted (procedural): 18 was added to both sides; to undo + 18, subtract 18.
divided-first (procedural): Only part of the left side was divided: undo the + 18 first, then the × 9.

teach.idea: An equation is a balance: do the same to both sides and it stays true.
teach.method: Undo the operations in reverse order: first take away the number added, then divide by the number multiplying x.

families.title: A direct proportion
explanations: additive (conceptual): The difference in pencils was added to the price; in a proportion every pencil costs the same, so the price is multiplied.
no-unit (procedural): The total for 8 was multiplied by 12; first find the price of one pencil.

teach.idea: In a direct proportion, twice as many costs twice as much: the price of one stays the same.
teach.method: Find the cost of one (divide), then multiply by how many you want.

families.title: Factorising x² + px + q
explanations: sum-minus-product (procedural): The number was found from the product alone, with the wrong sign: the two numbers must multiply to q AND add to p.
coefficient-as-number (conceptual): The x coefficient was copied into the bracket; the two numbers in the brackets add up to it.
constant-minus (procedural): The given number was taken away from the constant; the two numbers multiply to the constant.

teach.idea: (x + m)(x + n) = x² + (m + n)x + mn: the two numbers multiply to the constant and add to the x coefficient.
teach.method: List pairs that multiply to the constant; choose the pair that adds to the x coefficient. Watch the signs.

families.title: The nth term of an arithmetic progression
explanations: n-jumps (procedural): 20 jumps were counted; from term 1 to term 20 there are 19 jumps.
times-n (conceptual): The first term was multiplied; an arithmetic progression adds the same difference each time.
forgot-start (procedural): Only the jumps were counted; the sequence starts at the first term.

teach.idea: Each term of an arithmetic progression is the one before plus the common difference d.
teach.method: Term n = first term + (n − 1) × d: count the jumps, not the terms.

families.title: The distance between two points
explanations: added-sides (conceptual): The across and up distances were added; the straight distance is the hypotenuse: √(across² + up²).
no-root (procedural): The square root was not taken at the end.
sign-slip (prerequisite): A difference of coordinates lost a sign: from −2 to 3 is 5, not 1.

teach.idea: The distance between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose sides are the across and up distances.
teach.method: Find across and up (differences of coordinates), square them, add, and take the square root.

families.title: The highest common factor
explanations: lcm-for-hcf (conceptual): The lowest common multiple was found; the HCF is the largest number that divides both.
a-common-factor (conceptual): A common factor was found, but not the highest one.
difference (procedural): The difference was given; keep going: the HCF also divides the difference, so repeat with the smaller numbers.

teach.idea: The HCF is the largest number that divides both exactly. Euclid: it also divides their difference and the remainder.
teach.method: Divide the larger by the smaller and keep the remainder; repeat with the smaller number and the remainder until the remainder is 0.

families.title: A 2 × 2 determinant
explanations: added-diagonals (procedural): The two diagonal products were added; the determinant subtracts them: ad − bc.
reversed (procedural): The products were subtracted the wrong way round: ad − bc, not bc − ad.
wrong-pairs (procedural): The wrong entries were paired: multiply along the diagonals, a × d and b × c.

teach.idea: The determinant of [[a, b], [c, d]] is ad − bc: the product down one diagonal minus the product down the other.
teach.method: Multiply top-left by bottom-right, multiply top-right by bottom-left, and subtract the second from the first. Keep the signs.

families.title: A limit that needs factorising
explanations: zero-for-undefined (conceptual): 0 ⁄ 0 was taken as 0; it means the expression must be simplified first (factorise and cancel).
half-factor (procedural): Only one a was kept after cancelling (as if x² − a² were (x − a) × x, then x = a); it is (x − a)(x + a), which gives a + a = 2a.
top-only (conceptual): Only the top was worked out at x = a, as k × a²; the bottom is 0 there, so simplify first: cancel (x − a).

teach.idea: When substituting gives 0 ⁄ 0, the limit still exists: simplify first, then substitute.
teach.method: Factorise x² − a² = (x − a)(x + a), cancel (x − a), then put x = a.

families.title: A conditional probability from a table
explanations: whole-class (conceptual): The whole class was counted; given that a girl is chosen, only the girls count.
not-over-yes (procedural): Chess girls were compared with non-chess girls; a probability divides by all the girls.
reversed-condition (conceptual): The chess club was taken as the group; the question is among the girls.

teach.idea: P(A given B) counts only the cases where B happened: B becomes the whole.
teach.method: Find the group you are told about (the girls), then the fraction of that group with the property (in the chess club).

families.title: Counting objects in a picture
explanations: skip-one (procedural): One object was missed. Touch each one as you say its number.
count-twice (procedural): One object was counted twice. Move each one (or tick it) once you have counted it.
teen-reversal (conceptual): The number was said the wrong way round: 20 is 1 ten and 10 ones.

teach.idea: Each object gets exactly one number. The last number you say tells how many there are.
teach.method: Touch each object once as you count, starting from 1. Stop when every object has a number.

alternatives.title: Fill a ten frame
text: Put the objects in a ten frame: each square holds one.
A full frame is 10; count the extra squares after 10.

families.title: Adding two-digit numbers with regrouping
explanations: no-regroup (prerequisite): The ten made by the ones (9 + 9 = 18) was not carried to the tens: 18 ones are 1 ten and 8 ones.
write-both-digits (conceptual): All of 18 was written in the ones place; 18 is 1 ten and 8 ones.
fact-slip-add (recall): An addition fact (9 + 9) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Ten ones make one ten. When the ones add up to 10 or more, swap ten of them for a ten.
teach.method: Add the ones first. If there are 10 or more, carry 1 ten to the tens column. Then add the tens, including the carried ten.

alternatives.title: Make a ten first
text: Break the second number to make a ten with the first: 38 + 25 = 38 + 2 + 23 = 40 + 23.
A round number of tens is easy to add to.

families.title: Simplifying a square root
explanations: root-not-squared (conceptual): 100 came out of the root as 100; a square comes out as its square root (√100 = 10).
halve-instead (conceptual): The number was halved; a square root asks which number times itself gives it.

teach.idea: √(a × b) = √a × √b, so a perfect-square factor can come out of the root as its square root.
teach.method: Find the largest perfect square that divides the number, write the number as square × rest, and take the square root of the square outside.

alternatives.title: Pair the prime factors
text: Write the number as a product of primes, e.g. 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.
Each pair of equal primes comes out as one prime: (2)(3)√2 = 6√2.

families.title: Solving a linear inequality
explanations: keep-sign-negative (conceptual): Both sides were divided by −1, a negative number, but the inequality sign was not reversed.
add-instead (procedural): 15 was moved to the other side without changing its sign.
boundary-included (procedural): The boundary value was included; with < it is not part of the answer.

teach.idea: An inequality stays true when you add, subtract, or multiply and divide by a POSITIVE number; dividing by a negative number flips the order, so the sign reverses.
teach.method: Get the x term alone as for an equation. When you divide by the coefficient, reverse the sign if it is negative. Check with one number from your answer.

alternatives.title: Test numbers on a number line
text: Find the boundary by solving the equation ax + b = c.
Try one number on each side in the original inequality: the side where it is true is the answer.

families.title: Differentiating k xⁿ times sin(ax) or cos(ax)
explanations: product-of-derivatives (conceptual): The two derivatives were multiplied; the derivative of a product is u′v + uv′, not u′v′.
one-term-only (procedural): Only one part of the product rule was used; there are two terms, u′v and uv′.
chain-forgotten (procedural): The inner 3x was forgotten: the derivative of cos(3x) has a factor 3 (chain rule).
cos-derivative-sign (recall): The derivative of cos is −sin (with a minus sign).

teach.idea: When y = u × v, a small change in x changes both factors: y′ = u′v + uv′. The derivative of sin(ax) is a cos(ax), and of cos(ax) is −a sin(ax).
teach.method: Name u and v, differentiate each (remember the inner factor a), then write u′v + uv′.

alternatives.title: A u, v table
text: Write u and u′ in one row, v and v′ in the next.
Cross-multiply: u′ times v, plus u times v′.

families.title: What comes next in a repeating pattern
explanations: copy-last (procedural): The last card was copied. Find the part that repeats, then see what comes after the last card in that part.
skip-one (procedural): One place was skipped. Point to each card as you say the pattern, then say the next one.
start-again (conceptual): The pattern was started again from its first number, but the last repeating part is not finished yet.

teach.idea: A repeating pattern has one part that comes again and again, always in the same order.
teach.method: Find the part that repeats and say the pattern aloud part by part. See where the last part stops: the next number is the one that comes after it in the part.

alternatives.title: Put each repeat in its own row
text: Write the pattern in rows, one repeating part in each row.
The ? sits under a number in the row above: it is the same number.

alternatives.title: Clap and say it
text: Say the pattern aloud and clap on the first number of each repeat.
Keep going one more number after the last card.

families.title: How many shapes are in the part that repeats
explanations: count-all (conceptual): All the shapes in the row were counted. The repeating part is the group that comes again and again.
two-repeats (procedural): Two repeats were counted as one. Stop at the first place where the pattern starts again.
count-kinds (conceptual): The different kinds of shape were counted. A shape can come twice inside one repeating part (like ● ● ▲).

teach.idea: The repeating part is the smallest group of shapes that, put again and again, makes the whole pattern.
teach.method: Start at the first shape and look for the place where the same shapes start again in the same order. Count the shapes before that place.

alternatives.title: Cut the row into repeats
text: Draw a line after the first group and check that the next shapes are the same group.
If every group matches, you found the repeating part.

families.title: Places in a row: left and right
explanations: other-side (conceptual): The animals on the other side were counted. Right is the side marked right in the picture.
count-self (procedural): The animal itself was counted too. Count only the animals beside it, not the animal named.

teach.idea: A place in a row depends on where you start counting: first from the left can be last from the right.
teach.method: Put your finger on the side you are told (left or right). Count each animal once, moving along the row, until you reach the one asked about.

alternatives.title: Number the boxes
text: Write 1, 2, 3 … under the boxes, starting from the side you are told.
The number under the animal is its place. The animals before it are one fewer.

families.title: Above and below on shelves
explanations: same-shelf (procedural): The things on the toy cars shelf itself were counted. Move one shelf up first.
above-below (conceptual): Below means lower down: the shelf under the cups, not the one on the other side.

teach.idea: Above means higher up and below means lower down. 'Just above' is the very next shelf up.
teach.method: Put your finger on the shelf named. Move it one shelf up for 'above' or one shelf down for 'below', and read what is there.

alternatives.title: Use your body
text: Your head is above your shoulders; your feet are below your knees.
Point up for above and down for below, then move one shelf that way.

families.title: Things shaped like a sphere, cylinder, cube or cone
explanations: mix-up (conceptual): Things with a circle face were all counted as cones. A cone has one flat circle face and comes to a point; a cylinder has two circle faces.
missed-one (procedural): One thing was missed. Go through the list one by one and tick each thing of this shape.

teach.idea: Solid shapes are known by their faces: a sphere has no flat face, a cylinder two circle faces, a cone one circle face and a point, a cube six equal square faces.
teach.method: For each thing, picture it in your hand: does it have flat faces? What shape are they? Then match it to the solid.

alternatives.title: Stamp the faces
text: Press each flat face in clay or ink: a cube prints squares, a cylinder prints circles, a cone prints one circle.
A sphere prints only a dot, because it has no flat face.

alternatives.title: Roll, slide or both
text: A sphere rolls every way. A cylinder rolls one way and also slides on its flat face.
A cube only slides. A cone rolls round in a circle.

families.title: Finding triangles, squares and circles turned different ways
explanations: only-upright (conceptual): Only the triangles pointing up were counted. A triangle is still a triangle when it is turned: it has 3 sides and 3 corners.
missed-one (procedural): One shape was missed. Touch each shape in the row once as you look at it.
rectangles-too (conceptual): Long rectangles were counted as squares. A square has 4 sides that are all the same length.
only-filled (conceptual): Only the coloured circles were counted. An empty circle is still a circle: the colour does not change the shape.

teach.idea: A shape keeps its name when it is turned or coloured differently: a triangle always has 3 sides and 3 corners, a square 4 equal sides, a circle no corners.
teach.method: Look at each shape in turn and count its sides with your finger. Then count the shapes that match.

alternatives.title: Count sides and corners
text: Triangle: 3 sides, 3 corners. Square: 4 equal sides, 4 corners. Circle: no sides, no corners.
Turning a shape does not change how many sides it has.

families.title: The date of the first, second … Monday on a calendar
explanations: one-week-out (procedural): The Mondays were counted one too many. Say first, second, third … as you go down the column.
next-column (procedural): The date was read from the column next to Monday. Keep your finger in the Mon column.
blank-box (procedural): The empty box in the first row was counted as a Monday. Start from the first box in the Mon column that has a date.

teach.idea: On a calendar each column is one day of the week, and going down one row moves on 7 days.
teach.method: Find the column for the day. Go down it from the first date in that column, counting first, second, third … The date in the box is the answer.

alternatives.title: Add 7 for each week
text: Find the date of the first one.
Add 7 for each week after it: the third one is the first one + 7 + 7.

families.title: How many Mondays (or other days) are in a month
explanations: count-rows (procedural): The rows of the calendar were counted, but some rows have an empty box in this column. Count only boxes with a date.
always-four (conceptual): It was taken that every month has 4 of each day. A month is a little longer than 4 weeks, so some days come 5 times.

teach.idea: Each column of a calendar holds one day of the week; a month of 29 to 31 days has some days 5 times.
teach.method: Find the column for the day and count the boxes in it that have a date. Skip empty boxes.

alternatives.title: Four weeks and a few days
text: 4 weeks are 28 days, so every day comes at least 4 times.
The days left over after 28 (the 29th, 30th, 31st) are the days that come a 5th time.

families.title: Days from one date to another in the same month
explanations: count-both (procedural): Today was counted as well as the last day. Start counting with tomorrow: tomorrow is 1 day away.
count-between (procedural): Only the days in between were counted. The day itself must be reached too.

teach.idea: The number of days from one date to a later one is how many steps you take, one day at a time, from the first date to the second.
teach.method: Put your finger on today. Count 1 for tomorrow, 2 for the next day … and stop on the day itself. Or take the smaller date from the bigger one.

alternatives.title: Jumps on a number line
text: Mark both dates on a number line.
Count the jumps between them, not the marks.

families.title: Days from a date in one month to a date in the next
explanations: thirty-days (recall): It was taken that December has 30 days. December has 31 days: use the knuckle rhyme or the calendar.
count-both (procedural): Today was counted as well as the birthday. Start counting with tomorrow.
thirty-one-days (recall): It was taken that November has 31 days. November has 30 days: use the knuckle rhyme or the calendar.

teach.idea: Months have different numbers of days: April, June, September and November have 30, February has 28 (29 in a leap year), the rest have 31.
teach.method: Count the days left in this month (its last date minus today), then add the date in the next month.

alternatives.title: The knuckle way
text: Make two fists. Say the months along your knuckles and the gaps between them.
Months on a knuckle have 31 days; months in a gap have 30 (February 28 or 29).

families.title: Which is the longest or the shortest
explanations: opposite (conceptual): The shortest one was chosen. The tallest one reaches the furthest.
label-number (conceptual): The number written under it was taken as its length. The numbers only name them; look at how far each one reaches.

teach.idea: To compare lengths, start everything from the same line; then the one that reaches furthest is the longest.
teach.method: Check that all the ends start together. Look at the other ends: the one that goes furthest is longest, the one that stops first is shortest.

alternatives.title: Compare two at a time
text: Hold the first two side by side and keep the longer one.
Compare it with the next, and keep the longer again. The one you keep at the end is the longest.

families.title: Ordering three or four things by length
explanations: reversed (procedural): The order was turned round: it starts with the shortest. Read again which one comes first.
label-order (conceptual): The numbers were written in counting order. The numbers only name them; the order comes from how long each one is.

teach.idea: Putting things in order by length means each one is longer than the one before it (or shorter, if you start from the longest).
teach.method: Find the shortest and write its number. Then find the shortest of the ones left, and so on, until all are used.

alternatives.title: Make a staircase
text: Stand them up next to each other from shortest to longest: the tops make a staircase going up.
If a step goes down, two of them are in the wrong order: swap them.

families.title: Which is the heaviest or the lightest (a balance with cubes)
explanations: bigger-heavier (conceptual): The biggest one was chosen. Size does not tell weight: a big box of cotton can be lighter than a small stone. The balance tells.
opposite (conceptual): The lightest one was chosen. More cubes on the balance means heavier.

teach.idea: A balance goes down on the heavier side. The more cubes it takes to balance a thing, the heavier the thing is.
teach.method: Look at how many cubes balanced each one. The most cubes means heaviest; the fewest means lightest. Do not go by size.

alternatives.title: Hold one in each hand
text: Hold two things, one in each hand: the hand that is pulled down more holds the heavier one.
A balance does the same, but it is fair and exact.

families.title: Ordering three bags from lightest to heaviest using balance results
explanations: reversed (procedural): The order starts with the heaviest. The question asks for the lightest first.
order-told (conceptual): The numbers were written in the order the table names them. Use what each sentence says: which one is heavier, which one is lighter.

teach.idea: On a balance, the side that goes down is heavier. If A is heavier than B and B is heavier than C, then A is the heaviest and C the lightest.
teach.method: Find the one that never goes down: it is the lightest. Find the one that never goes up: it is the heaviest. The other one is in the middle.

alternatives.title: Put them on a line
text: Draw a line from light to heavy. Put the first two on it as the balance says.
Then fit the third one in, using the second result.

families.title: Knowing the value of Indian coins and notes
explanations: opposite (conceptual): The one worth the most was chosen. Compare the numbers printed on them.
most-coins (conceptual): The kind there are most of was chosen. How much a coin or note is worth is the number printed on it, not how many there are.
count-all (procedural): All the money was counted. Count only the ₹5 ones: read the number on each.

teach.idea: Every Indian coin and note has its value printed on it in rupees (₹): ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100.
teach.method: Read the number on each coin or note. To find the one worth the most, compare those numbers, not the sizes or how many there are.

alternatives.title: How many ₹1 coins?
text: Think of each coin or note as a pile of ₹1 coins: ₹5 is 5 one-rupee coins, ₹10 is 10.
The one that stands for the biggest pile is worth the most.

families.title: Adding up coins and notes
explanations: count-coins (conceptual): The coins and notes were counted, one each. Each one is worth the number printed on it.
missed-one (procedural): One coin was left out. Touch each coin as you add it.

teach.idea: The total is the sum of the values printed on the coins and notes, not the number of coins.
teach.method: Start with the coin or note worth the most and count on: for ₹10, ₹5, ₹2 say 10 … 15 … 17.

alternatives.title: Jumps on a number line
text: Start at 0 and jump the value of each coin.
Where you land is the total.

families.title: Making an amount with a note and coins
explanations: rupees-not-coins (conceptual): The rupees still needed were given instead of the number of coins. Each coin is worth ₹10, so count in 10s.
forgot-note (procedural): The ₹50 already given was forgotten. Only ₹50 more is needed after it.

teach.idea: To make an amount, the coins together must add up to exactly that many rupees.
teach.method: Start from what is already given and count on in steps of the coin: for ₹20 and ₹5 coins up to ₹35, say 20 … 25, 30, 35: that is 3 coins.

alternatives.title: Skip-count on a number line
text: Start at the amount given and jump by the coin's value.
Count the jumps until you land on the price.

families.title: Measuring a length with paper clips or matchsticks
explanations: count-marks (procedural): The dots or marks were counted instead of the erasers between them. There is one more mark than erasers.
read-end (conceptual): The number at the end was read, but the straw does not start at 0. Count the erasers it covers.

teach.idea: A length is how many equal units fit along it, end to end, with no gaps and no overlaps.
teach.method: Count the units (the jumps) from one end to the other. If it does not start at 0, count jumps, or take the start number from the end number.

alternatives.title: Hand spans
text: Put your hand flat at one end, then move it so your thumb starts where your little finger ended.
Count each hand you put down: that is the length in spans.

families.title: Which container holds the most cups
explanations: tallest-most (conceptual): The tallest one was chosen. A short, wide pot can hold more than a tall, thin bottle: count the cups.
opposite (conceptual): The one that holds the least was chosen. More cups means it holds more.

teach.idea: How much a container holds is how many cups of water fill it. Height alone does not tell: width matters too.
teach.method: Look at how many cups each one took. The most cups means it holds the most.

alternatives.title: Pour from one into another
text: Fill one container and pour it into another.
If it overflows, the first holds more; if it does not fill up, the second holds more.

families.title: Putting the day's events in order
explanations: reversed (procedural): The order starts with the last thing in the day. Start with what happens first, in the morning.
as-listed (conceptual): The numbers were kept in the order they are listed. Think about when each one happens in the day.

teach.idea: A day goes in order: morning (waking up, breakfast), then school, then afternoon, evening and night.
teach.method: Find what happens first in the morning and write its number. Then ask 'what comes next?' until every number is used.

alternatives.title: Match each to a time
text: Think of when each thing happens: waking up near 6 in the morning, school near 8, dinner near 8 at night.
Earlier times come first.

families.title: Which takes the longest or the shortest time
explanations: opposite (conceptual): The one that takes the longest time was chosen. Think: which one could you finish first?

teach.idea: Some things take minutes, some hours, some days or weeks. Minutes are short, hours longer, days and weeks longer still.
teach.method: For each one, think: does it take a few minutes, a few hours, or days? Then compare.

alternatives.title: A time ladder
text: Make a ladder: minutes at the bottom, then hours, then days, then weeks.
Put each activity on the ladder; the higher one takes longer.

families.title: Adding two numbers with a total up to 20
explanations: count-start (procedural): 19 was counted again as the first step. Start at 19 and say the NEXT number as 1.
one-extra (procedural): One number too many was counted. Count exactly as many steps as the number you add.
take-away (conceptual): The smaller number was taken away. The + sign means put the two groups together.

teach.idea: Adding puts two groups together; the total is how many there are in all.
teach.method: Start at the bigger number and count on the other number, one step at a time. Where you stop is the total.

alternatives.title: Fill ten frames
text: Put the first number of counters in a ten frame, then the second number.
A full frame is 10; count the rest after 10.

alternatives.title: Make a ten first
text: Break the second number to fill up to 10: 8 + 5 = 8 + 2 + 3 = 10 + 3.
10 and some more is a teen number: 13.

families.title: How many more to make 10 (or another number up to 20)
explanations: gave-total (conceptual): The total 20 was given. The question asks how many MORE are needed after the 19 already there.
gave-filled (procedural): The counters already there were counted. Count the empty boxes you still need to fill.
count-start (procedural): 19 was counted as one of the steps. Start counting at the next number after 19.

teach.idea: A number can be split into two parts: 10 is 7 and 3, 6 and 4, and so on. If you know one part, the other part is what is missing.
teach.method: Count the empty boxes, or count up from the number you have to the number you want.

alternatives.title: Count up on a number line
text: Put your finger on the number you have.
Jump one at a time to the number you want; count the jumps.

families.title: Which number is more (or less)
explanations: other-way (conceptual): The smaller number was chosen. On the number line, the number further right is more.
ones-first (conceptual): The ones digits were compared first. Compare the tens first: the number with more tens is more.

teach.idea: A number is more when it comes later when we count; on a number line it is further to the right.
teach.method: For two-digit numbers, compare the tens first. Only if the tens are the same, compare the ones.

alternatives.title: Build both with blocks
text: Build each number with tens and ones.
The one with more tens is more, whatever the ones.

families.title: The number just before, just after or between
explanations: before-after (conceptual): The number before was given. 'After' is the number we say next when counting.
next-of-last (procedural): The number after 99 was given. The number between 97 and 99 is the one we say in the middle.
decade (conceptual): After 99 comes a new ten: 99 + 1 = 100, not 910.

teach.idea: Counting goes up by 1 each time: the number after is 1 more, the number before is 1 less.
teach.method: Say the numbers in order up to the number. The one you said just before it comes before; the next one you say comes after. After 9 ones comes the next ten (39, 40).

alternatives.title: Add or take one cube
text: Build the number with tens and ones.
Add one cube for 'after', take one away for 'before'. Ten cubes make a new ten.

families.title: Putting numbers up to 99 in order
explanations: reversed (procedural): The order was turned round. Start with the biggest number.
ones-first (conceptual): The numbers were ordered by their ones digits. Look at the tens first: more tens means a bigger number.

teach.idea: Numbers further along the number line are bigger. For two-digit numbers, the tens tell you most.
teach.method: Look at the tens digits first and order by them. If two numbers have the same tens, order those two by their ones.

alternatives.title: Pick the smallest each time
text: Find the smallest number, write it and cross it out.
Do it again with the numbers left, until none are left.

families.title: Tens and ones: what number do the blocks show
explanations: count-blocks (conceptual): Each block was counted as one. A long block is a ten: it is worth 10 small cubes.
swap-digits (procedural): The tens and ones were written the wrong way round. The tens digit comes first: 9 tens.
join-digits (conceptual): 14 ones were written next to the tens. 14 ones are 1 ten and 4 ones, so there are 9 tens.

teach.idea: Ten ones make one ten. A two-digit number tells how many tens and how many ones: 47 is 4 tens and 7 ones.
teach.method: Count the tens in tens (10, 20, 30 …), then count on the ones. If there are 10 or more loose ones, make another ten first.

alternatives.title: Count in tens, then in ones
text: Touch each long block and say 10, 20, 30 …
Then touch each cube and keep counting by ones.

alternatives.title: Bundles of sticks
text: Tie ten loose sticks into a bundle: one bundle is one ten.
Write the bundles as the tens digit and the loose sticks as the ones digit.

families.title: The value of a digit in a two-digit number
explanations: face-value (conceptual): The digit itself was given. The 9 is in the tens place, so it stands for 9 tens, which is 90.
wrong-digit (procedural): The ones digit was read. The tens digit is the first digit.
value-not-count (conceptual): The value of the tens was given (90). The question asks how many tens: 9.

teach.idea: Where a digit stands tells what it is worth: in 47 the 4 is in the tens place, so it means 4 tens, which is 40.
teach.method: Find the digit. If it is the first of two digits, it counts tens: its value is that digit times 10.

alternatives.title: A tens and ones chart
text: Write the number in a chart with a Tens column and a Ones column.
The digit in the Tens column is how many tens; multiply by 10 for its value.

families.title: The greatest and smallest two-digit number from digit cards
explanations: wrong-order (conceptual): The two smallest digits were used but in the wrong places. The smaller digit (7) goes in the tens place.
first-two (procedural): The first two cards were used as they lie. Choose the cards: the smallest (not 0) in the tens place.
zero-first (conceptual): 0 was put in the tens place, but 08 is just 8, a one-digit number. The smallest tens digit that is not 0 goes first.

teach.idea: In a two-digit number the tens digit matters most: 71 is more than 17 because 7 tens is more than 1 ten.
teach.method: For the greatest, put the biggest digit in the tens place and the next biggest in the ones. For the smallest, put the smallest digit that is not 0 in the tens place.

alternatives.title: Make them all and compare
text: Write every two-digit number you can make with the cards.
Put them on a number line: the one furthest right is greatest, furthest left is smallest.

families.title: Writing a number name as a number
explanations: teen-ty (recall): "-ty" was read as "-teen". Ninety is 9 tens.
reversed (procedural): The digits were written the wrong way round. The tens come first.
write-parts (conceptual): "ninety-nine" was written part by part as 909. Ninety-nine is 9 tens and 9 ones: two digits, 99.

teach.idea: A number name tells the tens and the ones: sixty-three is 6 tens and 3 ones, written 63. The '-ty' words are tens; the '-teen' words are 1 ten and some ones.
teach.method: Find the tens word (twenty, thirty …) and write its digit first; then write the ones digit. A '-teen' number starts with 1.

alternatives.title: Fill a tens and ones chart
text: Write the tens in the Tens column and the ones in the Ones column.
Read the two digits together.

families.title: Taking away within 20
explanations: count-start (procedural): 20 was counted as the first step back. Start at 20 and say the number before it as 1.
added (conceptual): The two numbers were added. The − sign means take away.
one-extra (procedural): One too many was taken away. Take away exactly as many as the number says.

teach.idea: Taking away makes a group smaller; what is left is the difference.
teach.method: Start with all of them and take away one at a time, or count back on a number line. Check by adding back: what is left + what was taken = what you had.

alternatives.title: Cross out counters
text: Fill the ten frames with the first number.
Cross out as many as you take away. Count the counters left.

alternatives.title: Think of adding
text: 13 − 5: what goes with 5 to make 13?
5 + 5 = 10 and 3 more is 13, so 8.

families.title: How many more: comparing two groups in a picture
explanations: gave-bigger (conceptual): The bigger group's number was given. 'How many more' asks for the difference: the ones left after matching.
added (conceptual): The two groups were added. 'How many more' compares them; it does not put them together.
gave-smaller (conceptual): The smaller group's number was given. Match the two rows one to one and count the extra ones.

teach.idea: 'How many more' compares two groups: match them one to one, and the extra ones are the answer.
teach.method: Pair each picture in the shorter row with one in the longer row. Count the pictures with no partner, or subtract the smaller number from the bigger.

alternatives.title: Count up from the smaller
text: Start at the smaller number.
Count up to the bigger number; the number of steps is how many more.

families.title: Adding, taking away and multiplying with 0 (and times 1)
explanations: zero-makes-zero (conceptual): It was thought that anything with 0 gives 0. Taking away nothing leaves the number the same: 20.
nothing-taken (conceptual): Taking away all 20 leaves nothing: an empty group is 0.
times-zero-same (conceptual): × 0 was treated like + 0. 20 groups of 0 is nothing: 0.
times-one-plus (conceptual): × 1 was treated like + 1. 20 groups of 1 is 20.
times-one-one (conceptual): It was thought that × 1 gives 1. 20 groups of 1 thing are 20 things.

teach.idea: Zero means nothing: adding or taking away 0 leaves a number the same, and taking all away leaves 0. Groups of 0 make 0; groups of 1 make the number itself.
teach.method: Think of real things: 5 apples and no more apples is still 5. 4 empty plates hold 0 laddus.

alternatives.title: An empty box is zero
text: Show an empty ten frame: there are 0 counters.
Adding an empty box to a full one does not change how many there are.

families.title: Sorting buttons by colour and size
explanations: counted-the-rest (procedural): The buttons that do NOT belong were counted. Count only the ones that match.
missed-one (procedural): One matching button was missed. Tick each one as you count it.
one-attribute-only (conceptual): Only one thing was checked. Each button in the group must be blue and also small.
or-for-and (conceptual): Buttons that were blue OR small were counted. The group needs buttons that are both.

teach.idea: Things that share the same property (the same colour, or the same size) belong in the same group.
teach.method: Go down the list one button at a time. If it matches, put a tick next to it. Count the ticks.

alternatives.title: Sort twice
text: When you need two things to match, sort in two steps.
First take out all the buttons of the right colour. Then, from those, take out the ones of the right size.

families.title: Reading a picture record of toys
explanations: counted-all (conceptual): All the toys were counted. The question asks only about dolls.
missed-one (procedural): One picture was missed. Touch each picture as you count.
wrong-row (procedural): A different row was read. Find the word "Dolls" first, then count the pictures in that row.
fewest (conceptual): The row with the FEWEST pictures was chosen. The most means the longest row.
first-row (procedural): The first row was read without comparing the rows. Look for the longest row.

teach.idea: In a picture record each picture stands for one thing, so the number of pictures in a row is how many there are of that kind.
teach.method: Find the row with the name you want. Touch each picture in that row and count. For 'the most', find the longest row.

alternatives.title: Turn the rows into bars
text: Each row of pictures is like a bar: a longer row means more toys.
Put the rows side by side; the longest bar is the most.

families.title: How many more in a picture record
explanations: added (conceptual): The two rows were added. 'How many more' asks for the difference: match them up and count what is left.
gave-larger (conceptual): The number of dolls was given. The question asks how many MORE there are than cars.
gave-smaller (procedural): The shorter row was read instead of finding the difference.

teach.idea: To find how many more, match each picture in the short row with one in the long row; the pictures with no partner are the difference.
teach.method: Count both rows, then take the smaller number away from the bigger one (or count on from the smaller to the bigger).

alternatives.title: Count on
text: Start at the smaller number and count up to the bigger one.
The number of counts you make is how many more.

families.title: What comes next when skip counting
explanations: by-ones (conceptual): The count went on by ones. The numbers go down by 10 each time, so the next one must too.
skipped-one (procedural): One number was skipped: two jumps of 10 were made instead of one.
tens-habit (procedural): The jump was taken as 10. Check the gap between two numbers next to each other: it is 5.

teach.idea: In a skip-counting pattern the jump between neighbouring numbers is always the same.
teach.method: Find the jump from one number to the next. Make that same jump from the last number.

alternatives.title: Use a hundred chart
text: On a hundred chart, counting in tens moves straight down a column: only the tens digit changes.
Counting in 2s or 5s makes a pattern of coloured squares; follow the pattern to the next square.

families.title: The missing number in a counting pattern
explanations: by-ones (conceptual): The number one less than 177 was written. The pattern jumps by 10.
before-after (conceptual): The pattern was read the wrong way: the numbers go down, so the missing one is less than 177.
ones-for-tens (conceptual): The ones digit was changed. Counting in tens changes the tens digit and keeps the ones digit.

teach.idea: The numbers before and after the gap follow the same rule, so the gap is one jump from the number before it.
teach.method: Find the jump between two numbers next to each other. Make that jump from the number just before the gap; check it lands one jump before the number after.

alternatives.title: Halfway between
text: The missing number sits between its two neighbours.
It is the same jump up from the left neighbour as down from the right neighbour.

families.title: Letters made of straight or curved lines
explanations: mixed-as-straight (conceptual): Letters like B, D, P, R and U have straight lines AND a curve. A letter with any curve is not 'only straight'.
other-kind (procedural): The other kind of letter was counted. The question asks for letters with only straight lines.
repeats-once (procedural): A letter that appears twice was counted only once. Count every letter you see.

teach.idea: A straight line goes the same way all along; a curved line bends. Some letters use only straight lines, some have a curve.
teach.method: Trace each letter with your finger. If your finger ever goes round a bend, the letter has a curved line.

alternatives.title: The ruler test
text: Lay a ruler along each part of the letter.
If every part fits along the ruler, the letter has only straight lines; if a part does not fit, it is curved.

families.title: The shortest path along a grid
explanations: one-direction (procedural): Only the moves in one direction were counted. Count the moves across AND the moves up or down.
diagonal (conceptual): The path cut across a square diagonally. Moves must follow the grid lines.
counted-points (procedural): The points on the path were counted, including the start. Count the moves (the squares' sides) instead.

teach.idea: On a grid you can only move across or up and down, so the shortest way is the number of moves across plus the number of moves up or down.
teach.method: Count how many squares across S is from E, then how many up or down. Add the two numbers.

alternatives.title: Walk it with a finger
text: Put your finger on S. Move across one square at a time until you are in E's column, counting each move.
Then move up or down to E, still counting. The last number is the length of the path.

families.title: Where you end after moves on a grid
explanations: swapped (conceptual): The two numbers were written the wrong way round. The first number is how far across, the second is how far up.
one-move-only (procedural): Only the first move was made. Make the second move too.
down-as-up (procedural): Moving down was counted as moving up. Moving down makes the up number smaller.
left-as-right (procedural): Moving left was counted as moving right. Moving left makes the across number smaller.

teach.idea: A point on the grid is named by how far across it is and how far up it is. Moving right or up adds; moving left or down takes away.
teach.method: Change the across number for the left or right move, then change the up number for the up or down move.

alternatives.title: Trace the path
text: Put a finger on A and move one square at a time, saying each move.
When you stop, read the number below your finger, then the number beside it.

families.title: Counting sides and corners of flat shapes
explanations: one-of-each (procedural): Each kind of shape was counted only once. Every shape in the group has its own sides and corners.
circle-corner (conceptual): A circle was given a corner. A circle has one curved line all round and no corners.
counted-shapes (conceptual): The shapes were counted, not their corners.
missed-one (procedural): One corner was missed. Put a finger on one and go round, counting each once.

teach.idea: A side is a straight edge of a flat shape; a corner is where two sides meet. A shape with straight sides has as many corners as sides; a circle has none.
teach.method: Put a finger on one corner and go round the shape, counting each side (or corner) once. For several shapes, add the counts for every shape.

alternatives.title: Skip count for many shapes
text: Three triangles have 3 sides each: count 3, 6, 9.
Add the counts for each kind of shape.

families.title: Things that roll and things that slide
explanations: round-only (conceptual): Only the things that are round all over were counted. A tin or a pipe also rolls on its curved side.
counted-sliders (procedural): The things that slide were counted. Things with a curved surface roll.
flat-only (conceptual): Things with a curved side were left out. A tin standing on its flat end slides too.
counted-rollers (procedural): The things that roll were counted. Things with a flat face slide.
roll-for-both (conceptual): Everything that rolls was counted. A ball cannot slide: it has no flat face. Only things with a flat face AND a curved side do both.
or-for-and (conceptual): Things that roll OR slide were counted. 'Both' means a thing must do the two.

teach.idea: A curved surface lets a thing roll; a flat face lets it slide. A thing with both, like a tin, can do both.
teach.method: For each thing, ask: does it have a curved surface? Does it have a flat face? Then count the ones that fit the question.

alternatives.title: Try it on a slope
text: Put a ball, a box and a tin on a tilted book.
The ball rolls, the box slides, and the tin rolls on its side or slides on its end.

families.title: Faces, edges and corners of solids
explanations: only-visible (conceptual): Only the corners you can see in a drawing were counted. A box also has corners at the back and underneath.
one-of-each (procedural): Each kind of solid was counted once. Every solid has its own faces, edges and corners.
pyramid-as-box (conceptual): The pyramid was counted like a box. A square pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 corners.

teach.idea: A face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a corner is where edges meet. A cube and a cuboid have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 corners; a square pyramid has 5, 8 and 5.
teach.method: Hold the solid (or picture it) and count the top, the bottom and all round, marking each one as you go. For several solids, add the counts for each one.

alternatives.title: Count in layers
text: For a box: 4 corners on top and 4 on the bottom make 8.
Edges: 4 round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 standing up make 12.

families.title: Letters that fold onto themselves
explanations: other-kind (procedural): The other kind of letter was counted. The question asks for letters that are NOT symmetrical.
repeats-once (procedural): A letter that appears twice was counted only once. Count every letter you see.
standing-fold-only (conceptual): Only a standing fold (left onto right) was tried. Letters like B, C, D and E fold top onto bottom.

teach.idea: A shape is symmetrical when a fold line splits it into two halves that match exactly when folded. The fold can stand up (left onto right) or lie down (top onto bottom).
teach.method: For each letter, imagine a standing fold through the middle; if the halves do not match, try a lying fold. If either works, the letter is symmetrical.

alternatives.title: Use a mirror
text: Stand a small mirror on the middle line of the letter.
If the letter looks whole with its reflection, that line is a fold line.

families.title: Comparing how many cups containers hold
explanations: added (conceptual): The two amounts were added. 'How many more' asks for the difference.
gave-bigger (conceptual): The cups for the bucket were given. Take away the cups for the jug.
gave-smaller (procedural): The smaller amount was given instead of the difference.
wrong-bar (procedural): A different bar was read. Find "Bucket" under the chart first.
biggest (conceptual): The container that holds the most was read. Read the bar for the container asked about.

teach.idea: When every container is filled with the same cup, the one that takes more cups holds more water.
teach.method: Read the number of cups for each container. To find how many more, take the smaller number from the bigger one.

alternatives.title: Line up the cups
text: Picture the cups for each container standing in a row.
Match the rows cup by cup; the cups with no partner are how many more.

families.title: Reading millilitres on a measuring jug
explanations: mark-below (procedural): The number on the mark just below the level was read. The level is halfway between two marks, so add half of 200 mL.
steps-as-hundreds (conceptual): Each step of the scale was taken as 100 mL. Read the numbers on the scale: each step is 200 mL.
counted-steps (procedural): The steps of the scale were counted instead of reading the amount.
gave-level (conceptual): The water already in the jug was given. The question asks how much MORE is needed to reach the top.
stopped-at-hundred (procedural): Counting up stopped at the next hundred. Keep counting on from there all the way to 2000 mL and add the jumps.
top-as-litre (conceptual): The top was taken as 1000 mL. This jug holds 2000 mL: read the number at the top of the scale.

teach.idea: A measuring jug has a scale like a number line standing up; the water level points to how many millilitres are inside. 1 litre is 1000 mL.
teach.method: Read the numbers on the marks and find what one step is worth. Read the level; for 'how much more', count up from the level to the top.

alternatives.title: Count up to the top
text: Start at the water level and jump to the next hundred, then on to the top.
Add the jumps: that is how much more water is needed.

families.title: Reading the time on a clock
explanations: hands-swapped (conceptual): The long and short hands were mixed up. The short hand shows the hour; the long hand shows the minutes.
number-as-minutes (conceptual): The number the long hand points to was read as the minutes. Each number on the clock is 5 minutes for the long hand: it points to 11, so it is 55 minutes.
next-hour (procedural): The hour was read from the number the short hand is moving towards. After 12 o'clock it stays 12 until the short hand reaches the next number.

teach.idea: The short hand shows the hour; the long hand shows the minutes. When the long hand is at 12 it is o'clock; when it is at 6 it is half past.
teach.method: Read the hour from the short hand (the last number it has passed). Then count the long hand in fives from 12: 5, 10, 15 …

alternatives.title: Count the long hand in fives
text: Each number the long hand passes is 5 more minutes: 1 is 5, 2 is 10, 3 is 15, 6 is 30.
Skip count in fives from 12 to where the long hand points.

families.title: Finding the change
explanations: no-exchange (procedural): The smaller digit was taken from the bigger in each column. 100 − 99 needs a ten changed into ones; or count up from ₹99 to ₹100.
stopped-at-ten (procedural): Counting up stopped at the next ten (₹100). Keep counting on to ₹100 and add both jumps.
added (conceptual): The price and the money paid were added. Change is what is left after paying: take the price away.

teach.idea: Change is the money you get back: what you paid take away the price.
teach.method: Count up from the price to the money paid: first to the next ten, then in tens. Add the jumps. Or take the price away from the money paid.

alternatives.title: Count up like a shopkeeper
text: Start at the price and give coins until you reach the money paid: up to the next ten, then tens.
The coins you gave are the change.

families.title: How much more money is needed
explanations: coins-as-ones (conceptual): Each coin was counted as ₹1. Look at the number on each coin: a ₹10 coin is ten rupees.
gave-total (conceptual): The money Anu has was given. The question asks how much MORE she needs to reach the price.
added (conceptual): The price and the money were added. Take what she has away from the price.

teach.idea: First find how much money there is by adding the coins' values. If it is less than the price, the difference is how much more is needed.
teach.method: Add the coins, biggest first. Then count up from that amount to the price.

alternatives.title: Count on to the price
text: Start at the money you have.
Count on to the price; the number of rupees you count is how much more you need.

families.title: Measuring length with a ruler
explanations: read-end (conceptual): The number at the far end was read. The pencil does not start at 0: count the centimetres from 8 to 15.
counted-marks (procedural): The marks were counted, including the first one. Count the spaces between the marks: each space is 1 cm.
started-at-one (procedural): Counting started from 1 at the end of the ruler. Measuring starts at 0.

teach.idea: Length on a ruler is the number of 1 cm spaces the object covers, so it starts counting from where the object starts.
teach.method: Line one end up with 0 if you can. If it starts at another mark, take the start number from the end number (or count the spaces).

alternatives.title: Count the spaces
text: Put your finger at the start mark and hop to the next mark: that is 1 cm.
Count the hops until you reach the end.

families.title: Weighing on a balance in kilograms and grams
explanations: kg-as-100 (recall): 1 kg was taken as 100 g. 1 kg is 1000 g.
left-out-kg (procedural): The kilogram weight was left out because it is in kg. Change it to grams and add it too.
counted-weights (conceptual): The weights were counted, not added. Each weight has its own number of grams.

teach.idea: When a balance is level, both sides weigh the same, so the bag weighs as much as all the weights together. 1 kg = 1000 g.
teach.method: Change any kilograms to grams (1 kg = 1000 g). Add the grams of all the weights, biggest first.

alternatives.title: Build up to 1000
text: 500 g and 500 g make 1 kg; 200 g + 200 g + 100 g make 500 g.
Group the weights into easy amounts (hundreds), then add.

families.title: Equal groups: how many in all
explanations: one-group (conceptual): Only one group was counted. Count every group.
missed-group (procedural): One group was missed while skip counting. Touch each plate as you say the next number.
added-numbers (conceptual): 10 and 10 were added. There are 10 groups of 10: add 10 again and again, 10 times.

teach.idea: Equal groups can be added again and again: 4 groups of 3 is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3, which we also write 4 × 3.
teach.method: Skip count by the number in one group, once for each group: 3, 6, 9, 12. The last number is how many in all.

alternatives.title: Jumps on a number line
text: Make one jump for each group, each jump as long as one group.
Where you land after the last jump is the total.

families.title: Hundreds, tens and ones from blocks
explanations: missing-zero (conceptual): A place with nothing in it needs a 0.
counted-blocks (conceptual): The blocks were counted one each. A big square is 100 and a stick is 10.
tens-ones-swapped (procedural): The tens and the ones were written in each other's places. Tens come before ones.

teach.idea: Ten ones make a ten and ten tens make a hundred. A three-digit number tells how many hundreds, tens and ones, in that order.
teach.method: Count the hundreds, then the tens, then the ones. Write the three digits in order, putting 0 in any place that has nothing.

alternatives.title: A place-value table
text: Draw three boxes labelled H, T and O.
Write how many hundreds, tens and ones in the boxes; read the digits across.

families.title: Building a number from extra tens or ones
explanations: wrote-side-by-side (conceptual): The numbers were written next to each other. 15 tens is 1 hundred and 5 tens, so it must be exchanged.
dropped-extra (conceptual): Only the last digit of 15 was kept. The extra ten tens make a hundred: add it to the next place.

teach.idea: Ten tens make a hundred and ten ones make a ten, so a number can be built with more than 9 tens or ones; exchange them to write it.
teach.method: Change ten ones into a ten (or ten tens into a hundred). Then write the hundreds, tens and ones digits in order.

alternatives.title: Add the parts
text: Turn each part into a number: 2 hundreds is 200, 13 tens is 130, 4 ones is 4.

families.title: Adding and taking away tens or hundreds in your head
explanations: changed-ones (conceptual): 300 was treated as 3 ones. 300 is 3 hundreds, so the hundreds digit changes, not the ones.
wrong-place (procedural): The tens digit was changed instead of the hundreds digit.
no-carry (procedural): The tens went past 9 but the extra hundred was not carried on.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): There were not enough tens, so 4 was taken from 9 instead. Break one hundred into ten tens first.

teach.idea: Adding tens changes the tens digit; adding hundreds changes the hundreds digit. The ones stay the same.
teach.method: Say how many tens (or hundreds) you are adding, then count on (or back) that many tens (or hundreds) from the number.

alternatives.title: Jump along a number line
text: Start at the first number.
Make one jump of ten (or a hundred) for each ten (or hundred) you add, and say each new number.

families.title: Multiplying in your head by splitting into tens and ones
explanations: ones-not-multiplied (conceptual): Only the tens were multiplied (90 × 5); the 9 ones must be multiplied by 5 too.
tens-as-ones (conceptual): The tens digit 9 was multiplied as if it were 9 ones; it stands for 90.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (9 × 5) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Splitting a number into tens and ones lets you multiply each part separately and add: 23 × 4 = 20 × 4 + 3 × 4.
teach.method: Split the two-digit number into tens and ones. Multiply the tens, multiply the ones, then add the two answers.

alternatives.title: Double and double again
text: For × 2 double the number; for × 4 double it twice; for × 8 double it three times.
For × 5, multiply by 10 and halve.

families.title: Finding a number on a number line
explanations: count-by-ones (conceptual): Each gap was counted as 1, but the marks go up by 100 each time.
count-by-tens (conceptual): Each gap was counted as 10, but the marks go up by 100. Look at two labelled marks next to each other to find the step.

teach.idea: On a number line the marks are equally spaced, so every gap is worth the same amount.
teach.method: Find the step from two labelled marks next to each other, then count on in that step to the ?.

alternatives.title: Skip count aloud
text: Say the first number, then keep adding the step: for steps of 5, say 35, 40, 45 …
Touch one mark for each number you say until you reach the ?.

families.title: Counting on and back in jumps on a number line
explanations: count-start (procedural): The starting number was counted as the first jump. A jump starts at the number and ends at the next one.
extra-jump (procedural): One jump too many was made. Count the jumps as you make them.
wrong-way (procedural): The jumps went the wrong way: back means to smaller numbers.
jumps-of-one (conceptual): Each jump was taken as 1, but each jump is 10.

teach.idea: Each jump moves the same amount along the line: forward to bigger numbers, back to smaller numbers.
teach.method: Put your finger on the start. Make one jump at a time, saying the new number each time, and count the jumps.

alternatives.title: Find the total jump first
text: k jumps of s are k × s altogether.
Add (or take away) that total in one go, then check by jumping.

families.title: How many whole numbers lie between two numbers
explanations: difference (conceptual): 9815 − 9805 = 10 counts the jumps from 9805 to 9815, not the numbers in between. There is one fewer number between them than jumps.
both-ends (procedural): 9805 and 9815 were counted too; "between" leaves out both ends.

teach.idea: The numbers between two numbers leave out both end numbers.
teach.method: Find the difference (the number of jumps), then take away 1: that is how many numbers sit strictly between.

alternatives.title: Try a small case
text: Between 5 and 8 are 6 and 7: two numbers, although 8 − 5 = 3.
So the count between is always one less than the difference.

families.title: Sharing equally and making equal groups
explanations: gave-total (procedural): The answer given was the total number of objects; the total has to be split up.
took-away-once (conceptual): 5 was taken away once. Sharing keeps giving out until none are left: count how many each gets (or how many groups you make).
gave-divisor (conceptual): The answer given was the size of each group (5); the question asks how many groups.

teach.idea: Sharing equally means every share has the same number and nothing is left over.
teach.method: Deal the objects out one at a time to each share (or make groups of the given size) and count one share (or the groups).

alternatives.title: Use a times fact
text: Ask: what number times the number of shares gives the total?
For 15 shared among 3, 3 × 5 = 15, so each gets 5.

families.title: Subtracting two-digit numbers with regrouping
explanations: smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In the ones, 8 − 7 was worked out instead of 7 − 8. When the top digit is smaller, break a ten into 10 ones first.
tens-not-reduced (procedural): A ten was broken into ones, but the tens digit was not made one less.
fact-slip-sub (recall): A take-away fact (17 − 8) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: If there are not enough ones to take away, break one ten into 10 ones. The number stays the same; only how it is grouped changes.
teach.method: Start with the ones. If the top digit is smaller, take 1 ten and make it 10 ones, then subtract the ones and then the tens.

alternatives.title: Count up from the smaller number
text: Jump from the smaller number to the next ten, then on to the bigger number.
Add the jumps: that is the difference.

families.title: Subtracting three-digit numbers with regrouping
explanations: smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In a column where the top digit was smaller, the top was taken from the bottom. Break one from the next column into ten first.
next-not-reduced (procedural): A ten (or hundred) was broken up, but the column it came from was not made one less.

teach.idea: Breaking one hundred into ten tens, or one ten into ten ones, keeps the number the same, so you can always take away column by column.
teach.method: Work from the ones to the hundreds. When the top digit is smaller, break one from the next column on the left and make that column one less.

alternatives.title: Check by adding back
text: Add your answer to the number you took away.
If you get the first number back, your answer is right.

families.title: Naming the shaded part: a half, a quarter or three quarters
explanations: shaded-to-unshaded (conceptual): The shaded part was compared with the unshaded part. A fraction compares the shaded part with the whole shape.
count-only (conceptual): Only the shaded squares were counted (36); the fraction is shaded squares out of all 48 squares.
unshaded (procedural): The fraction of the shape that is NOT shaded was given.

teach.idea: A half is 1 of 2 equal parts; a quarter is 1 of 4 equal parts; three quarters is 3 of 4 equal parts.
teach.method: Count all the squares and the shaded squares. If the shaded squares are half of all, it is 1/2; a quarter of all, 1/4; three quarters, 3/4.

alternatives.title: Fold into equal parts
text: Fold the shape in half, then in half again: you get 4 equal parts.
Count how many of the 4 parts are shaded.

families.title: A half, a quarter or three quarters of a number of things
explanations: doubled (conceptual): The number was doubled. Half means splitting into 2 equal parts and taking one part.
take-two (conceptual): 2 was taken away. Half means 2 equal parts, not taking away 2.
quarter-as-half (conceptual): The things were split into 2 parts. A quarter is one of 4 equal parts.
take-four (conceptual): 4 was taken away. A quarter means one of 4 equal parts.
one-quarter (procedural): Only one quarter was found. Three quarters is 3 of the 4 equal parts.
take-three (conceptual): 3 was taken away. Three quarters means 3 out of 4 equal parts.

teach.idea: To find a half, share into 2 equal parts; a quarter, into 4 equal parts. Three quarters is 3 of those 4 parts.
teach.method: Deal the things out into 2 (or 4) equal piles. Count one pile for a half or a quarter; count three piles for three quarters.

alternatives.title: A quarter is half of a half
text: Halve the number, then halve it again: that is a quarter.
Three quarters is the whole minus one quarter.

families.title: Choosing whether to add, take away, multiply or share
explanations: took-away (conceptual): 6 was taken away from 48, but the story shares equally, so we divide.
added (conceptual): 6 and 7 were added, but the story has 6 equal groups of 7, so we multiply (or add 7 again and again).
multiplied (conceptual): 48 and 6 were multiplied, but sharing makes each share smaller than the total.

teach.idea: First picture what happens in the story: things put together (add), taken away (subtract), equal groups (multiply) or shared equally (divide).
teach.method: Ask: does the amount get bigger or smaller? Are the groups equal? Then choose the operation and work it out.

alternatives.title: Act it out with counters
text: Use beads or stones for the things in the story.
Do exactly what the story says with them, then count what you have.

families.title: Reading a pictograph with a key
explanations: wrong-row (procedural): The row for Cycle was read instead. Put a finger on the right label and follow its row.
no-key (conceptual): The pictures were counted, but each picture stands for 10 children, not 1.
