teach.idea: In a pictograph every picture stands for the same number of things: the number in the key.
teach.method: Count the pictures in the row, then count in the key's number once for each picture (or multiply).

alternatives.title: Turn it into a table
text: Write each label with its number of pictures.
Multiply each by the key and write the real number beside it.

families.title: Comparing two rows of a pictograph
explanations: added (conceptual): "How many more" asks for the difference, so take the smaller number from the bigger one; the two rows were added.
bigger-only (procedural): Only the bigger row was read. Compare it with the smaller row by taking away.
no-key (conceptual): The difference in pictures was found, but each picture stands for 10.

teach.idea: "How many more" compares two amounts: it is the bigger amount minus the smaller one.
teach.method: Read both rows using the key, then take the smaller number from the bigger one.

alternatives.title: Count the extra pictures
text: Line up the two rows. Count the pictures the longer row has that the shorter one does not.
Then count in the key's number once for each extra picture.

families.title: Making both sides of a number sentence equal
explanations: equals-gives-answer (conceptual): The answer to 20 − 17 was written in the box. The = sign means both sides have the same value.
add-all (conceptual): All the numbers were added together. Find what the box must be so that the right side has the same value as the left side.
took-away (procedural): 8 was taken away again; the box must be 8 MORE than 3, so that taking 8 from it leaves 3.

teach.idea: The = sign means "has the same value as", like a balance that is level: both sides must be worth the same.
teach.method: Work out the side you can finish. Then find the number in the box that makes the other side worth the same.

alternatives.title: Compare without adding up
text: In 9 + 7 = □ + 8, the 8 on the right is one less than the 9 on the left, so the box must be one more than 7: it is 8.
If one number goes up by some amount, the other must go down by the same amount for the sides to stay equal.

families.title: Finding the missing number in a number sentence
explanations: added-both (conceptual): The two numbers you can see were added. Taking the box away from 39 leaves 19, so the box is 39 − 19.
took-away-again (conceptual): 17 was taken away again. The box is the number we started with before 17 was taken away, so add 17 back.
took-away (conceptual): 9 was taken away from 81. The box is how many times 9 goes into 81: use the 9 times table.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (9 × 9) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Adding and taking away undo each other, and so do multiplying and dividing, so you can work backwards to the missing number.
teach.method: Read the sentence and ask what was done to the box. Do the opposite to the other number, then check by putting your answer in the box.

alternatives.title: Count on to find the gap
text: For □ + 7 = 15, start at 7 and count on to 15: 8, 9, … 15 is 8 counts.
The number of counts is the missing number.

families.title: Continuing a growing pattern
explanations: next-only (procedural): Only the next step (step 4) was found. Keep adding 6 until step 8.
one-too-many (procedural): 6 was added 8 times, but step 1 already has 10; from step 1 to step 8 there are 7 jumps.
times-step (conceptual): The step number was multiplied by 6, but the pattern started at 10, not at 6.

teach.idea: In a growing pattern the same amount is added each time; find that amount and keep adding it.
teach.method: Find how much the pattern grows from one step to the next. Keep adding that amount, step by step, until you reach the step you want.

alternatives.title: Extend the table
text: Write the step numbers 1, 2, 3, … in one row and the counts under them.
Fill each new box by adding the same amount as before.

families.title: Matchstick shapes in a row
explanations: no-sharing (conceptual): Each hexagon was given 6 sticks, but neighbours share a stick, so each new hexagon needs only 5 more.
forgot-first (procedural): Every hexagon was given 5 sticks, but the first one needs all 6.

teach.idea: The first shape needs all its sticks; every shape after it shares one stick with its neighbour, so it needs one stick fewer.
teach.method: Start with the sticks for one shape, then add (sides − 1) for each extra shape.

alternatives.title: Count all sides, then remove the shared ones
text: If the shapes were apart, n shapes need n × sides sticks.
Joining them in a row shares one stick between each pair of neighbours: take away one fewer than the number of shapes.

families.title: Counting line segments and lines through points
explanations: neighbours-only (conceptual): Only the short segments between neighbouring points were counted. Longer segments, such as from the first point to the third, count too.
counted-twice (procedural): Each segment was counted twice (AB and BA are the same).
counted-points (conceptual): The points were counted; a segment needs two points.

teach.idea: Every pair of points gives exactly one line segment (or one straight line), and AB is the same as BA.
teach.method: Start with the first point and join it to every point after it; then the second point to every point after it; and so on. Add up the counts.

alternatives.title: Make a list
text: Write the pairs in order: AB, AC, AD, then BC, BD, then CD.
Never write a pair you already have the other way round.

families.title: How many tiles cover a floor
explanations: counted-squares (conceptual): The squares were counted, but each tile covers 4 squares.
one-row (procedural): Only the tiles for the top two rows were counted. The same number fits in every pair of rows.
two-squares (conceptual): Each tile was taken to cover 2 squares, but it covers 4.

teach.idea: Tiles that fit with no gaps and no overlaps cover the floor exactly, so the floor splits into equal tile-sized pieces.
teach.method: Find how many tiles fit across one row of tiles and how many rows of tiles there are, then multiply (or add the rows).

alternatives.title: Share the squares among the tiles
text: Count all the squares on the floor.
Each tile covers the same number of squares, so share the squares into groups of that size.

families.title: How long something lasts, from the clock
explanations: hour-as-100 (conceptual): The times were taken away like ordinary numbers (1230 − 1145), but an hour has 60 minutes, not 100.
minutes-only (procedural): Only the minute numbers were compared and the hour that went past was forgotten. Count on to the next o'clock first.
hand-number (recall): The minute hand points to 10, which means 50 minutes (count in 5s), not 10 minutes.

teach.idea: Time is counted in hours of 60 minutes, so count on from the start to the next o'clock, then on to the end.
teach.method: Read the start time from the clock. Count on in 5s to the next o'clock, then count on to the end time, and add the two parts.

alternatives.title: Use a time line
text: Draw a line from the start time to the end time with a mark at the o'clock in between.
Write the minutes for each jump and add them.

families.title: Changing metres and centimetres
explanations: wrote-together (conceptual): 8 and 7 were written side by side (87); 8 m is 800 cm, so 7 cm goes in the ones place: 807.
added-numbers (conceptual): The numbers 9 and 95 were added, but metres and centimetres are different sizes: change the metres to centimetres first.
took-metres (conceptual): 9 was taken away, but 9 m is 900 cm.
ten-cm (recall): A metre was taken as 10 cm; 1 metre is 100 centimetres.

teach.idea: 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so each metre is a hundred in centimetres.
teach.method: Change the metres to centimetres by multiplying by 100, then add the extra centimetres (or take the metres away to find what is left).

alternatives.title: Metres are hundreds
text: In centimetres the metres go in the hundreds place.
3 m 7 cm is 3 hundreds, 0 tens and 7 ones: 307 cm.

families.title: Changing rupees and paise into paise
explanations: ten-paise (recall): ₹1 was taken as 10 paise; ₹1 is 100 paise.
added-numbers (conceptual): 20 and 60 were added, but a rupee and a paisa are different sizes: change the rupees to paise first.
paise-only (procedural): Only the paise after the dot (60) were given; the ₹20 before the dot are 2000 paise more.
wrote-together (conceptual): 20 and 5 were written side by side; ₹20 is 2000 paise, so the answer is 2000 + 5.

teach.idea: ₹1 is 100 paise, so each rupee is a hundred paise; in ₹3.45 the 3 is rupees and the 45 is paise.
teach.method: Multiply the rupees by 100 to get paise, then add the paise.

alternatives.title: Read the digits as paise
text: Write the amount with two digits after the dot: ₹3.05, ₹12.40.
Read all the digits without the dot: ₹3.05 is 305 paise, ₹12.40 is 1240 paise.

families.title: Adding and taking away rupees and paise
explanations: paise-over-100 (conceptual): The paise came to 115, which is more than 100: 100 paise make ₹1, so 115 paise is ₹1 and 15 paise.
no-carry (procedural): The rupee made from 100 paise was not carried to the rupees.
smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In the paise, 85 − 75 was worked out instead. Change ₹1 into 100 paise first.
rupee-not-reduced (procedural): ₹1 was changed into 100 paise, but the rupees were not made one less.

teach.idea: Rupees and paise work like hundreds: 100 paise make ₹1, so paise over 100 become a rupee, and a rupee can be broken into 100 paise.
teach.method: Write the amounts one under the other with the dots in line. Add (or take away) the paise first, carrying or breaking ₹1 when needed, then the rupees.

alternatives.title: Work in paise
text: Change both amounts to paise: ₹12.50 is 1250 paise.
Add or take away the whole numbers, then put the dot back two places from the right.

families.title: The perimeter of a shape from its side lengths
explanations: missed-side (procedural): One side was left out. Tick each side as you add it, and go all the way round.
side-twice (procedural): One side was added twice. Start at one corner and stop when you are back at it.
lost-ten (recall): A ten was lost while adding the lengths. Add the sides one at a time and check each step.
multiplied-sides (conceptual): Two sides were multiplied, as for the space inside. The perimeter is the distance around the edge: add all the sides.

teach.idea: The perimeter is the length of the boundary: the distance all the way around a shape.
teach.method: Start at one corner. Add the length of each side in turn, ticking it, until you are back where you started.

alternatives.title: Straighten the boundary
text: Imagine a string laid along every side of the shape, then pulled straight.
Its length is the perimeter: one jump on the number line for each side.

families.title: A missing side from the perimeter
explanations: added-perimeter (conceptual): The perimeter was added to the other sides. The perimeter is already the whole way round, so take the known sides away from it.
known-sum (procedural): The known sides were added, but the total was not taken away from the perimeter.
one-side-taken (procedural): Only one known side was taken away from the perimeter. Take away every side you know.

teach.idea: The perimeter is all the sides added together, so the missing side is what is left when the known sides are taken away.
teach.method: Add the sides you know. Take that total away from the perimeter. Check: all the sides together should make the perimeter.

alternatives.title: Count on to the perimeter
text: Jump along a number line by each known side.
The last jump, up to the perimeter, is the missing side.

families.title: Hours and minutes into minutes
explanations: hour-as-100 (conceptual): An hour was taken as 100 minutes, as if time were counted in hundreds. An hour has 60 minutes.
not-converted (conceptual): The hours and minutes were added as they are. Hours must first be changed to minutes: 1 hour = 60 minutes.
minutes-left-out (procedural): The hours were changed to minutes, but the extra 55 minutes were not added.

teach.idea: 1 hour is 60 minutes: the minute hand goes once all the way round the clock.
teach.method: Change the hours to minutes (60 for each hour), then add the extra minutes.

alternatives.title: Once round the clock
text: Each time the minute hand goes all the way round, 60 minutes pass and the hour hand moves to the next number.
Count 60, 120, 180 … for the hours, then count on the extra minutes.

families.title: Minutes into hours and minutes
explanations: minutes-as-hours (conceptual): The number of minutes was written as hours. Change minutes to hours by making groups of 60.
hour-as-100 (conceptual): The minutes were split into hundreds, as if an hour were 100 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes.
hour-left-in (procedural): Not every hour was taken out: 115 minutes is still more than an hour.

teach.idea: Every 60 minutes make 1 hour. The minutes left over, fewer than 60, stay as minutes.
teach.method: Take away 60 minutes as many times as you can. Count the 60s: that is the hours. What is left is the minutes.

alternatives.title: Use the 60 times table
text: Say 60, 120, 180, 240 … and stop before you pass the number of minutes.
The count of 60s is the hours; the difference to the total is the minutes.

families.title: Minutes and seconds into seconds
explanations: minute-as-100 (conceptual): A minute was taken as 100 seconds. A minute has 60 seconds.
not-converted (conceptual): The minutes and seconds were added as they are. Change the minutes to seconds first: 1 minute = 60 seconds.
seconds-left-out (procedural): The minutes were changed to seconds, but the extra 55 seconds were not added.

teach.idea: 1 minute is 60 seconds: the seconds hand goes once round the clock in a minute.
teach.method: Change the minutes to seconds (60 for each minute), then add the extra seconds.

alternatives.title: Just like hours and minutes
text: Minutes and seconds work the same way as hours and minutes: 60 of the small unit make one of the big unit.
So 2 minutes 10 seconds = 60 + 60 + 10 seconds.

families.title: Comparing two fractions with the same bottom or top number
explanations: more-parts-wrong-way (procedural): Both fractions count parts of the same size (a whole cut into 12 equal parts), so the one with more parts is greater. The smaller one was mixed up.
bigger-bottom-bigger (conceptual): The fraction with the smaller bottom number was chosen as smaller. A bigger bottom number means the whole is cut into more parts, so each part is smaller.

teach.idea: Same bottom number: the parts are the same size, so more parts is more. Same top number: the same number of parts, but a bigger bottom number cuts the whole into more, smaller parts.
teach.method: Look at which number is the same. If the bottoms match, compare the tops. If the tops match, the smaller bottom number gives the greater fraction.

alternatives.title: Shade both in the same whole
text: Draw two strips of the same length. Cut one into the first fraction's parts and the other into the second's, and shade.
The longer shaded part is the greater fraction.

alternatives.title: More sharers, smaller shares
text: Share one roti among 2 children, then another among 4.
With more children each piece is smaller: 1/4 is less than 1/2.

families.title: Ordering three fractions with the same bottom or top number
explanations: largest-first (procedural): The fractions were put from the largest to the smallest. The question asks for the smallest first.
as-given (procedural): The fractions were written in the order they were given. Compare them first, then write the smallest one first.
bigger-bottom-bigger (conceptual): The fractions were put in order of their bottom numbers. With the same top number, a bigger bottom number means smaller parts, so the order goes the other way.

teach.idea: With the same bottom number the parts are the same size, so order by the top numbers. With the same top number, a bigger bottom number means smaller parts.
teach.method: Find the smallest fraction and write it first, then the next, then the largest. Check each one is smaller than the next.

alternatives.title: Line up fraction strips
text: Shade each fraction on a strip of the same length, one under another.
Read the shaded lengths from the shortest to the longest.

families.title: Naming the shaded fraction of a shape
explanations: shaded-to-unshaded (conceptual): The shaded squares were put over the unshaded ones. The bottom number is ALL the equal parts of the whole.
count-only (conceptual): Only the shaded squares were counted. A fraction also says how many equal parts make the whole.
unshaded (procedural): The unshaded squares were counted. The question asks about the shaded part.

teach.idea: A fraction names equal parts of a whole: the bottom number is how many equal parts make the whole, the top number is how many we mean.
teach.method: Count all the equal parts for the bottom number. Count the shaded parts for the top number.

alternatives.title: The same fraction as a round cake
text: Cut a round cake into the same number of equal pieces and colour the same number.
The fraction is the same: it does not depend on the shape of the whole.

families.title: Building a fraction from unit fractions
explanations: add-bottoms (conceptual): The bottom numbers were added too. Every piece is still a 1/12 piece: the bottom number names the size of the piece and stays 12.
count-only (conceptual): Only the number of pieces was written. Say what size the pieces are too: that is the bottom number.
bottom-number (conceptual): The bottom number 12 was given. It says how many pieces make the WHOLE; the top number says how many pieces we have.
pieces-left (procedural): The pieces that are left over were counted. Count the pieces that make the fraction.

teach.idea: A unit fraction 1/n is one of n equal parts. Putting k of those parts together gives k/n: the top number counts the parts.
teach.method: Count how many pieces there are (the top number). The size of each piece (the bottom number) does not change.

alternatives.title: Count pieces like objects
text: Say the pieces like counting things: one eighth, two eighths, three eighths.
Three eighths is written 3/8: 3 pieces, each an eighth.

families.title: A fraction of a collection of objects
explanations: what-is-left (procedural): The part that is left was found (60 minus the fraction). The question asks for the fraction itself.
one-part-only (procedural): 60 was shared into 10 equal groups, but only one group was counted. 9/10 means 9 of those groups.
divide-by-top (conceptual): 40 was divided by the top number 8. Share into 10 equal groups first (the bottom number), then take 8 of them.

teach.idea: To find a fraction of a collection, share it into as many equal groups as the bottom number, and take as many groups as the top number.
teach.method: Divide by the bottom number to find one group. Multiply by the top number.

alternatives.title: Deal them out like cards
text: Make as many piles as the bottom number. Give one object to each pile in turn until none are left.
Count the objects in as many piles as the top number.

families.title: A fraction of an hour, a metre, a kilogram, a day or ₹100
explanations: hour-as-100 (conceptual): An hour was taken as 100 minutes. An hour has 60 minutes.
one-part-only (procedural): Only 1/12 was found. 11/12 is 11 of those parts.
divide-by-top (conceptual): The whole was divided by the top number 8. Divide by the bottom number 12 to find one part, then take 8 parts.
kg-as-100 (recall): A kilogram was taken as 100 grams. 1 kg = 1000 g.

teach.idea: First change the whole into small units (an hour is 60 minutes, a metre is 100 cm, a kilogram is 1000 g, a day is 24 hours). Then find the fraction of that number.
teach.method: Write the whole in the small unit, divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number.

alternatives.title: Fractions of an hour on a clock
text: Half past is the minute hand halfway round: 30 minutes. A quarter past is a quarter of the way round: 15 minutes.
Three quarters of an hour is three of those quarter turns: 45 minutes.

families.title: Adding and subtracting three-digit numbers with regrouping
explanations: no-carry (conceptual): A ten (or a hundred) made in one column was not carried to the next column.
first-carry-forgotten (procedural): The hundred was carried, but the ten carried from the ones was forgotten in the tens column. Add every carried 1 to the next column.
smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In each column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, take a ten from the next column first.
borrow-not-taken (procedural): A ten was borrowed, but the column it came from was not made one less.

teach.idea: Ten ones make a ten and ten tens make a hundred, so a column that gets too big passes a ten (or a hundred) on, and a column that is too small can break one from the next column.
teach.method: Write the numbers one under the other, ones under ones. Work from the ones to the hundreds, carrying or borrowing as you go. Check with an estimate.

alternatives.title: Jump by hundreds, tens and ones
text: Start at the first number. Jump by the hundreds of the second number, then its tens, then its ones (forwards to add, backwards to subtract).
Each jump is easy to do in your head.

families.title: Writing a number from its place-value parts
explanations: blocks-as-ones (conceptual): Every block was counted as 1. A flat is 100 and a long is 10.
tens-ones-swapped (procedural): The tens and the ones were written in each other's places.
parts-side-by-side (conceptual): The parts were written next to each other. Add them: each digit goes in its own place.
zero-left-out (conceptual): A place with nothing in it was left out. Write 0 to keep the other digits in their places.

teach.idea: Each place is worth ten of the place on its right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. A digit shows how many of that place there are.
teach.method: Write the thousands, hundreds, tens and ones digits in a place-value table. Write 0 for an empty place.

alternatives.title: Build it with blocks
text: Show the number with flats (100), longs (10) and cubes (1); a big cube is 1000.
Count each kind and write the counts in order: thousands, hundreds, tens, ones.

families.title: How much more makes 1000
explanations: made-999 (procedural): The number was made up to 999, one short of 1000.
ones-dropped (procedural): The ones were left out: only the tens and hundreds were made up.
each-digit-to-ten (conceptual): Each digit was made up to 10. Only the ones make 10; the tens and the hundreds each make 9, because the ten and the hundred carried over fill the rest.

teach.idea: Counting up in friendly jumps (to the next ten, then the next hundred, then 1000) finds the difference without regrouping.
teach.method: Jump from the number to the next ten, then to the next hundred, then to 1000. Add the jumps.

alternatives.title: Make 999, then one more
text: Each digit of the number and the missing number add up to 9: that makes 999.
One more makes 1000, so add 1 to what you found.

families.title: How many whole numbers lie between two numbers
explanations: difference-only (procedural): The difference 17 counts the steps from one number to the other, which includes the last number. The numbers between are one fewer.
both-ends (procedural): Both end numbers were counted. 'Between' leaves them out.

teach.idea: Subtracting counts the steps from one number to the other; the last step lands on the end number, so the numbers in between are one fewer than the steps.
teach.method: Subtract the smaller number from the larger, then take away 1.

alternatives.title: Try a small case
text: Between 3 and 7 are 4, 5 and 6: three numbers, and 7 − 3 = 4.
So the count between is always the difference minus one.

families.title: Estimating a sum or difference by rounding to tens
explanations: always-down (conceptual): Both numbers were rounded down. Round to the NEAREST ten: 5 or more in the ones goes up.
one-rounded (procedural): Only the first number was rounded. Round both numbers before working it out.
exact (procedural): The exact answer was worked out. An estimate uses the rounded numbers, so it is quick to find in your head.

teach.idea: A number rounded to the nearest ten is the ten it is closest to on the number line. Rounded numbers are easy to add or subtract in your head, and the estimate shows whether an exact answer is sensible.
teach.method: Look at the ones digit: 0 to 4 round down, 5 to 9 round up. Round both numbers, then work out the answer with the tens.

alternatives.title: Which ten is closer?
text: Put the number on a number line between two tens.
Count the steps to each ten: it rounds to the closer one (halfway goes up).

families.title: Reading a bar chart
explanations: next-bar (procedural): The bar next to the one asked about was read. Find the label first, then go straight up its bar.
counted-lines (conceptual): The lines on the scale were counted as 1 each. Each line on this scale stands for 5.
added (conceptual): The tallest and shortest bars were added. 'How many more' means the difference.
one-bar (procedural): Only the larger bar was read. Compare it with the other bar by subtracting.
missed-bar (procedural): One bar was left out of the total. Add every bar, ticking each one.
tallest-only (procedural): Only the tallest bar was read. Subtract the shortest bar from it.

teach.idea: In a bar chart the height of each bar shows a number. The scale on the side tells how much each line stands for.
teach.method: Find the label under the bar, go to the top of the bar and read across to the scale. For 'how many more', subtract; for 'in all', add.

alternatives.title: Turn the chart into a table
text: Write each label with the number its bar shows.
Then answer from the table: compare, add or subtract the numbers.

families.title: Reading tally marks in a table
explanations: wrong-row (procedural): The marks in another row were counted. Find the right row first.
missed-row (procedural): One row was left out of the total. Add every row.
bundle-as-one (conceptual): Each bundle 卌 was counted as 1 instead of 5.
added (conceptual): The two rows were added. 'How many more' asks for the difference.
one-row (procedural): Only one row was counted. Subtract the smaller count from the larger.
bundle-as-four (conceptual): Only the four upright marks of each bundle were counted. The line across is the fifth mark.

teach.idea: Tally marks record one mark for each thing counted; every fifth mark crosses the four before it, so the marks come in easy bundles of 5.
teach.method: Count the bundles in fives (5, 10, 15 …), then count on the single marks.

alternatives.title: Bundles as half ten frames
text: Each bundle of 5 fills half a ten frame; two bundles fill a whole frame.
Count the full frames as tens, then add the rest.

families.title: A missing number in a two-way table
explanations: added-to-total (conceptual): The total and the other number were added. The total is already both parts together, so take the other part away from it.
gave-total (procedural): The total of the row was given. The missing number is only one part of that total.
subtracted (conceptual): The two numbers were subtracted. A total puts the parts together: add them.
one-part (procedural): Only one of the numbers was given. The total includes both.
double-total (procedural): Both the row totals and the column totals were added, so every child was counted twice.
one-total (procedural): Only one group's total was given. Add the totals of both groups.

teach.idea: In a two-way table every row and every column adds up to its total, so any one missing number can be found from the others.
teach.method: Look along the row (or down the column) with the gap. If the gap is a total, add the parts; if it is a part, take the other part from the total.

alternatives.title: See the parts as bars
text: Draw the total as one long bar, split into the two parts.
The missing part is the piece of the bar that is not yet labelled.

families.title: Using a pattern rule to find a later number
explanations: n-jumps (conceptual): 12 jumps of 8 were added to the start, but the 1st number is the start itself: the 12th number is only 11 jumps along.
forgot-start (procedural): Only the jumps (12 × 8) were counted; the pattern starts at 30, not at 0.
next-only (procedural): Only the next number after those shown was found; keep using the rule until you reach the place asked for.

teach.idea: A rule like "add 5 each time" tells you how to get from one number to the next. The 1st number is the start, so the n-th number is n − 1 jumps after it.
teach.method: Count the jumps from the 1st number to the one asked for (one less than its place), multiply by the amount added each time, and add that to the start.

alternatives.title: Keep writing the pattern
text: Write the numbers in a row and keep adding the same amount.
Number each one with its place (1st, 2nd, 3rd …) and stop at the place asked for.

families.title: Moving on a 1–100 number grid
explanations: down-adds-one (conceptual): Moving down was counted as adding 1 and moving right as adding 10; on the grid one row down adds 10 and one square right adds 1.
down-is-up (procedural): The move went up instead of down: going up takes away 10 for each row.
one-row (procedural): Only one row was moved; each of the 3 rows down adds another 10.

teach.idea: Each row of the grid holds 10 numbers, so the number just below is always 10 more, and the number just to the right is 1 more.
teach.method: Add 10 for every row you move down, then add 1 for every square you move right.

alternatives.title: Watch the tens digit
text: Moving down one row changes only the tens digit: 34 → 44 → 54.
Moving right changes only the ones digit: 54 → 55 → 56 (until the end of a row).

families.title: Picking out an acute, right, obtuse or straight angle
explanations: acute-obtuse-swap (recall): The names were mixed up: an obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle; an acute angle is smaller.
right-as-acute (conceptual): An angle of exactly 90° is a right angle; an acute angle is less than 90°.
straight-as-right (conceptual): A straight angle (180°) was taken for a right angle; a right angle is a square corner, half of a straight angle.
straight-as-obtuse (conceptual): A straight angle (180°) is not obtuse; an obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°.
biggest-bent (conceptual): The biggest bent angle was chosen; a straight angle is exactly 180°, its arms make one straight line.
upright-as-straight (recall): A right angle (an arm standing straight up) was taken for a straight angle; a straight angle is a flat line, 180°.

teach.idea: A right angle (90°) is a square corner. Smaller than a right angle is acute, between a right angle and a straight line is obtuse, and a straight line is a straight angle (180°).
teach.method: Compare each angle with 90°: less is acute, equal is right; more than 90° but less than 180° is obtuse; exactly 180° is straight.

alternatives.title: Check with a folded-paper corner
text: Fold a paper twice to make a square corner: that is a right angle.
Hold the corner in the angle: if the angle fits inside the corner it is acute; if the corner fits inside the angle (and the arms are not one straight line) it is obtuse.

families.title: Angles as turns on a clock face
explanations: anticlockwise (procedural): The turn was counted the other way round (anticlockwise); clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move.
minutes-not-degrees (conceptual): The minutes were counted (5 for each number) instead of degrees; each number on the clock is 30° of turn.
count-start (procedural): The starting number was counted as a step too; count only the moves from one number to the next.

teach.idea: An angle is an amount of turn. A full turn is 360°, a half turn 180°, and a quarter turn is a right angle, 90°. On a clock, each number is one twelfth of a full turn: 30°.
teach.method: Count how many numbers the hand moves past clockwise, then multiply by 30°.

alternatives.title: Use quarter turns
text: 12 to 3 is a quarter turn (90°), 12 to 6 a half turn (180°), 12 to 9 three quarters (270°).
Each quarter turn is 3 numbers; find the nearest quarter and add or take away 30° for each number more or less.

families.title: Radius and diameter of a circle
explanations: same-length (conceptual): The diameter and the radius were taken as the same length; the radius goes only from the centre to the edge, half of the diameter.
halved (conceptual): The radius was halved; the radius is the shorter one (centre to edge), so the diameter is twice as long.
doubled (conceptual): The diameter was doubled; the diameter is the longer one, so the radius is half of it.

teach.idea: The radius goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre, so it is made of two radii.
teach.method: To find the diameter, double the radius. To find the radius, halve the diameter.

alternatives.title: Fold a paper circle
text: Cut out a circle and fold it in half: the fold is a diameter, and it passes through the centre.
Fold again: the two folds cross at the centre, and each half of the first fold is a radius.

families.title: Letters with a vertical or horizontal line of symmetry
explanations: axis-swap (conceptual): The letters were folded the other way (up and down); a horizontal line goes across, so the top half must match the bottom half.
turn-not-fold (conceptual): N, S or Z look the same when turned upside down, but folding them does not make the halves match: turning is not a line of symmetry.
any-line (procedural): Letters with any line of symmetry were counted; the question asks only for a horizontal one.

teach.idea: A line of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves of a shape match exactly, like a mirror image.
teach.method: Imagine folding each letter along the line (or stand a mirror on it): if the half you see in the mirror finishes the letter exactly, the letter has that line of symmetry.

alternatives.title: Use a mirror
text: Write the letter big and stand a small mirror on the line down its middle (or across its middle).
If the letter you see, half on paper and half in the mirror, looks just like the real letter, that line is a line of symmetry.

families.title: Reflecting a point in a mirror line on a grid
explanations: axis-not-line (conceptual): The point was reflected in the x-axis (the sign was just changed) instead of in the line y = 3.
wrong-coordinate (conceptual): The wrong coordinate was changed: a mirror line y = 3 goes across, so the point moves up or down and only y changes.
onto-line (procedural): The point was moved only as far as the mirror line; the image is as far beyond the line as P is in front of it.

teach.idea: A mirror image is as far behind the mirror line as the object is in front of it, straight across, at right angles to the line.
teach.method: Count how far P is from the mirror line, then count the same distance on the other side. Only the coordinate that crosses the line changes.

alternatives.title: Fold the grid paper
text: Draw the point on squared paper and fold the paper along the mirror line.
Press hard on the point: the mark it makes on the other side is the image.

families.title: Translating a point on a grid
explanations: wrong-way-across (procedural): The point was moved to the left instead of the right: moving right makes x bigger, moving left makes it smaller.
wrong-way-updown (procedural): The point was moved down instead of up: moving up makes y bigger, moving down makes it smaller.
swap-moves (conceptual): The across move was added to y and the up-down move to x; the first coordinate tells how far across, the second how far up.

teach.idea: A translation slides a shape without turning or flipping it: every point moves the same distance across and the same distance up or down.
teach.method: Add the move to the right to x (take away a move to the left), and add the move up to y (take away a move down).

alternatives.title: Walk it on the grid
text: Put a finger on P. Count the squares across first, one at a time, then the squares up or down.
Read the coordinates where your finger stops: across first, then up.

families.title: Writing a 12-hour time in 24-hour form
explanations: am-add (conceptual): 12 was added to a morning time; a.m. times keep the same hour in 24-hour time.
pm-no-add (conceptual): 12 was not added for a p.m. time; after noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting: 1 p.m. is 13, 2 p.m. is 14 …
add-ten (procedural): 10 was added instead of 12 to the hours.
midnight-12 (conceptual): 12 a.m. is just after midnight, the start of the day: in 24-hour time its hour is 00.
noon-plus-12 (conceptual): 12 was added to 12 noon; 12 noon is already 12:00 in 24-hour time (there is no 24:00 in the day's times).

teach.idea: The 24-hour clock counts the hours of the whole day from 00 at midnight to 23. Morning (a.m.) hours stay the same; afternoon and evening (p.m.) hours go on past 12: 1 p.m. is 13, 2 p.m. is 14, and so on.
teach.method: For a.m., keep the hour (but 12 a.m. becomes 00). For p.m., add 12 to the hour (but 12 noon stays 12). The minutes do not change.

alternatives.title: A line for the whole day
text: Draw a line from 0 (midnight) to 24 (the next midnight), with 12 (noon) in the middle.
Morning times are on the first half; for an afternoon time, count on past 12: 3 p.m. is 3 more than 12, which is 15.

families.title: Reading a 24-hour time on a 12-hour clock
explanations: midnight-zero (conceptual): 00 hours is midnight; a 12-hour clock shows it as 12 (12 a.m.), not 0.
noon-minus-12 (conceptual): 12 was taken away from 12; 12:00 in 24-hour time is 12 noon, so the clock shows 12.
minus-ten (procedural): 10 was taken away instead of 12; for times after 12 noon, take away 12 from the hours.
no-change (conceptual): The 24-hour number was kept; a 12-hour clock only goes up to 12, so 23 hours is 11 p.m.

teach.idea: After 12 noon the 24-hour clock keeps counting (13, 14, … 23), but a 12-hour clock starts again at 1. 00 hours is midnight, shown as 12.
teach.method: If the hours are more than 12, take away 12 (it is p.m.). 12 stays 12 (noon). 00 becomes 12 (midnight, a.m.). Keep the minutes.

alternatives.title: Two rings of numbers
text: Picture a clock face with an inner ring 1 to 12 and an outer ring 13 to 24 (13 beside 1, 14 beside 2 …).
The 24-hour number on the outer ring sits next to the 12-hour number on the inner ring.

families.title: Time between two 24-hour times
explanations: subtract-as-number (conceptual): The times were subtracted like ordinary numbers, borrowing 100 minutes; an hour has only 60 minutes.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): The smaller number of minutes was taken from the larger one; when the end minutes are fewer, change 1 hour into 60 minutes first.
hours-only (procedural): Only the hours were counted and the minutes were left out.

teach.idea: Time is counted in sixties: 60 minutes make 1 hour. So when you take away times you borrow 60 minutes, not 100.
teach.method: Count on from the start to the next full hour, then the full hours, then the minutes to the end time, and add them up.

alternatives.title: Count on in jumps
text: Jump from the start time to the next o'clock (for example 09:45 → 10:00 is 15 minutes).
Jump whole hours to the last o'clock before the end, then jump the leftover minutes. Add the jumps.

families.title: Area of a rectangle by counting unit squares
explanations: perimeter (conceptual): The edges round the outside were counted; that is the perimeter. Area counts the squares that cover the inside.
border-only (procedural): Only the squares along the border were counted; the squares in the middle are part of the area too.
add-sides (conceptual): The rows and the columns were added (10 + 12); there are 10 rows of 12 squares, so multiply.

teach.idea: Area is how much flat space a shape covers. We measure it by counting how many unit squares cover it with no gaps and no overlaps.
teach.method: Count the squares in one row, then count the rows. Equal rows can be counted by multiplying: rows × squares in each row.

alternatives.title: See the rows as an array
text: The squares sit in equal rows, like chairs in a hall.
Skip-count one row at a time: 6, 12, 18, … until every row is counted.

families.title: Choosing area or perimeter in a problem
explanations: perimeter-for-area (conceptual): The perimeter was found, but covering the inside needs the area (how many squares fit inside).
two-sides (procedural): Only one length and one width were added (14 + 16). Going round passes all four sides.
area-for-perimeter (conceptual): The area was found, but going round the edge needs the perimeter (the length all the way round).

teach.idea: Area is the space inside a shape (how many unit squares cover it). Perimeter is the distance all the way round its edge.
teach.method: Ask: am I covering the inside (area: multiply length × width) or going round the edge (perimeter: add all four sides)?

alternatives.title: Act it out
text: Covering a floor: you lay tiles all over it, so you count squares (area).
Fencing a garden: you walk round the edge, so you add lengths (perimeter).

families.title: Adding and subtracting measures in two units
explanations: no-regroup (conceptual): 1550 mL was left as it is; 1000 mL make 1 L, so change 1000 of them into 1 L.
carry-lost (procedural): 1000 mL were taken away, but the 1 L they make was not added to the L.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): 450 − 950 cannot be done, so 450 was taken from 950; instead, change 1 L into 1000 mL first.
borrow-not-taken (procedural): 1 L was changed into 1000 mL, but the L were not made 1 less.
borrow-100 (conceptual): 1 L was changed into 100 mL; 1 L = 1000 mL.

teach.idea: Measures in two units work like tens and ones, but the change-over is 100 cm = 1 m, 1000 g = 1 kg and 1000 mL = 1 L.
teach.method: Add or subtract the small units first. If the small units reach the change-over number, change them into 1 large unit; if there are too few to subtract, change 1 large unit into small units. Then do the large units.

alternatives.title: Change everything into the small unit
text: Write both measures in the small unit only (for example 2 m 45 cm = 245 cm).
Add or subtract these numbers, then change the answer back (310 cm = 3 m 10 cm).

families.title: Multiplying a measure in two units
explanations: no-regroup (conceptual): 5400 mL was left as it is; every 1000 mL make 1 L.
big-only (procedural): Only the L were multiplied; the mL must be multiplied by 6 too.
carry-lost (procedural): The extra mL were changed into L but those L were not added on.

teach.idea: Multiplying a measure is repeated adding: multiply the small units and the large units, then change extra small units into large ones.
teach.method: Multiply the small units; take out every full 100 cm (or 1000 g, 1000 mL) as a large unit. Multiply the large units and add the ones you took out.

alternatives.title: Work in the small unit
text: Change the measure into the small unit only (1 kg 250 g = 1250 g).
Multiply, then change back: 3 × 1250 g = 3750 g = 3 kg 750 g.

families.title: Changing a measure into the smaller unit
explanations: wrong-factor (recall): 1 km was taken as 100 m; 1 km = 1000 m.
added (conceptual): The two numbers were simply added; first change the large units into small units.
write-side-by-side (conceptual): The two numbers were written side by side; 75 m needs 3 places, so empty places are filled with zeros.

teach.idea: 1 m = 100 cm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 L = 1000 mL and 1 km = 1000 m. A measure in two units is the large part changed into small units, plus the small part.
teach.method: Multiply the large units by 100 or 1000, then add the small units. Check the small part fills its places: 3 kg 25 g = 3000 g + 25 g = 3025 g.

alternatives.title: Use a place-value chart
text: Write the large units in the thousands place (for g, mL, m) or hundreds place (for cm).
Write the small units ending in the ones place, and fill any empty places with 0.

families.title: How many parts make a kilogram or a litre
explanations: hundred (recall): 1 L was taken as 100 mL; 1 L = 1000 mL.
one-only (procedural): The parts in only 1 L were found; there are 9 of them.
times-n (conceptual): 9 and the number of parts in 1 L were added instead of multiplied.

teach.idea: 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 L = 1000 mL. Two 500 g packets make 1 kg, four 250 g packets make 1 kg, and so on.
teach.method: Find how many parts make 1 kg (or 1 L): 1000 ÷ the part. Then multiply by the number of kilograms (or litres).

alternatives.title: Skip-count to 1000
text: Count up in parts: 250, 500, 750, 1000 — that is 4 parts in 1 kg.
Each extra kilogram needs the same number of parts again.

families.title: Writing ones, tenths and hundredths as a decimal
explanations: places-swapped (conceptual): The tenths and hundredths were put in each other's places: the first place after the point is tenths, the second is hundredths.
cubes-as-tenths (conceptual): The small cubes were counted as tenths too; a small cube is ten times smaller than a rod.
whole-number (conceptual): All the pieces were counted as whole ones; only the flats are wholes.
zero-tenths-dropped (conceptual): The zero tenths were left out, so the hundredths moved into the tenths place; write 0 in the tenths place to keep it.

teach.idea: Splitting 1 whole into 10 equal parts gives tenths; splitting each tenth into 10 gives hundredths. After the decimal point, the first place is tenths and the second is hundredths.
teach.method: Write the wholes, then the point, then the number of tenths, then the number of hundredths. Use 0 for an empty place.

alternatives.title: Shade a hundred grid
text: A grid of 100 squares is 1 whole: one row (10 squares) is a tenth, one square is a hundredth.
Shade the rows for the tenths and single squares for the hundredths; 3 rows and 4 squares is 34 hundredths, 0.34.

families.title: Comparing a tenths decimal with a hundredths decimal
explanations: longer-is-larger (conceptual): 3.39 was taken as greater because 39 is more than 9; compare the tenths first: 9 tenths are more than 3 tenths.
shorter-is-larger (conceptual): 3.6 was taken as greater because hundredths are small pieces; but 3.89 has more tenths (8 against 6).

teach.idea: Decimals are compared place by place from the left, like whole numbers: first the wholes, then the tenths, then the hundredths. More digits does not mean bigger.
teach.method: Write both with the same number of places (0.7 = 0.70) and compare them as hundredths: 70 hundredths is more than 65 hundredths.

alternatives.title: Think of rupees
text: ₹0.70 is 70 paise and ₹0.65 is 65 paise.
70 paise is more, so 0.7 is greater than 0.65.

families.title: Picking out the even numbers
explanations: first-digit (conceptual): The first digit was looked at; whether a number is even depends only on its ones digit (the last digit).
zero-not-even (conceptual): Numbers ending in 0 were left out; 0 is even (0 things can be shared into pairs with none left over), so 10, 20, 30 … are even.
odd-for-even (recall): The odd numbers were picked; even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

teach.idea: An even number of things can be put into pairs with none left over; an odd number always leaves one. Tens and hundreds always pair up, so only the ones digit decides.
teach.method: Look at the last digit: 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 means even; 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9 means odd.

alternatives.title: Make pairs
text: Draw dots for the ones digit and join them in pairs.
If every dot has a partner the number is even; if one dot is left alone it is odd.

families.title: Writing a number in lakhs and thousands in figures
explanations: no-zeros (conceptual): The numbers heard were written one after another, without zeros for the empty places; each period has a fixed number of places (lakhs, then 2 for thousands, then 3 for hundreds, tens and ones).
lakh-as-ten-thousand (recall): A lakh was written like ten thousand; 1 lakh = 100 thousand = 1,00,000 (six digits).

teach.idea: In the Indian system the places are grouped as ones–tens–hundreds, then thousands–ten thousands, then lakhs–ten lakhs. Every place gets a digit, so empty places get 0.
teach.method: Draw a place-value chart (L, TTh, Th, H, T, O). Write each part in its own places, fill empty places with 0, then put commas: 4,07,052.

alternatives.title: Fill the periods
text: Write three boxes for hundreds-tens-ones, two boxes for thousands, and one or two for lakhs.
Fill each period from its right, and put 0 in any empty box.

families.title: Putting large numbers in ascending order
explanations: first-digit-only (conceptual): The numbers were compared by their first digits only; a number with fewer digits is always smaller, so count the digits first.
descending (procedural): The list was written from greatest to smallest; ascending means smallest first.

teach.idea: A number with more digits is bigger. When two numbers have the same number of digits, the first place where their digits differ decides.
teach.method: First sort by how many digits each number has. Then, for numbers with the same number of digits, compare ten thousands, then thousands, then hundreds … until the digits differ.

alternatives.title: Line them up in a place-value chart
text: Write each number in a place-value chart so the ones are in one column.
Read down the chart from the left: the first column where the digits differ shows which number is bigger.

families.title: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000
explanations: zeros-short (procedural): Too few zeros were taken off: ÷ 1000 takes 3 zeros off the end.
zeros-extra (procedural): Too many zeros were taken off: ÷ 1000 takes off only 3 zeros.
added (conceptual): 1000 was added instead of multiplied.
subtracted (conceptual): 1000 was subtracted instead of divided.

teach.idea: Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much, so each digit moves one place to the left and a 0 fills the ones place. Dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right.
teach.method: × 10, × 100, × 1000: write 1, 2 or 3 zeros on the end. ÷ 10, ÷ 100, ÷ 1000 (of a number ending in enough zeros): take 1, 2 or 3 zeros off the end.

alternatives.title: Swap each block for a bigger one
text: × 10 changes every one into a ten, every ten into a hundred, every hundred into a thousand.
So 34 (3 tens, 4 ones) × 10 is 3 hundreds and 4 tens: 340.

families.title: Multiplying by a multiple of 10 or 100
explanations: zeros-forgotten (procedural): 99 × 9 was found but the zeros of 900 were not put back on the end.
zeros-extra (procedural): One zero too many was put on the end; 900 has two zeros.
tens-only (procedural): Only the tens digit of 99 was multiplied; the ones digit must be multiplied too.

teach.idea: Multiplying by 40 is multiplying by 4 and then by 10, because 40 = 4 × 10.
teach.method: Multiply by the non-zero digit first, then put the zeros of the multiplier on the end of the answer.

alternatives.title: Split the two-digit number
text: Break the two-digit number into tens and ones: 23 × 40 = 20 × 40 + 3 × 40.

families.title: Rounding to the nearest ten, hundred or thousand
explanations: always-up (conceptual): The number was rounded up, but the next digit is less than 5, so it is nearer to 9,000.
always-down (conceptual): The digits after the thousands were just changed to zeros; when the next digit is 5 or more, round up.
wrong-place (procedural): The number was rounded to the wrong place (to the nearest hundred instead of the nearest thousand).

teach.idea: Rounding finds the nearest 'round' number: on a number line, which ten (hundred, thousand) is the number closer to? A number exactly halfway is rounded up.
teach.method: Look at the digit just to the right of the place you are rounding to. If it is 0–4, round down (keep the place, zeros after). If it is 5–9, round up (add 1 to the place, zeros after).

alternatives.title: The rounding hill
text: Picture the numbers from one ten to the next as a hill, with the halfway number at the top.
A number before the top rolls back down to the lower ten; at the top or after it, it rolls on to the higher ten.

families.title: Estimating a sum or difference by rounding
explanations: exact (procedural): The exact answer was worked out; an estimate rounds the numbers first so it can be done in your head.
round-down (conceptual): Both numbers were rounded down (digits just cut off); round up when the next digit is 5 or more.
round-answer (procedural): The exact answer was rounded at the end; the question asks you to round each number first.

teach.idea: An estimate is a quick, close answer. Rounding each number to a ten or hundred first makes the sum or difference easy to do in your head, and it tells you if an exact answer is sensible.
teach.method: Round each number to the place asked for, then add or subtract the rounded numbers.

alternatives.title: Use the estimate as a check
text: Work the exact answer, then compare it with the estimate.
If they are far apart, look again for a mistake in the exact working.

families.title: Shopping: total cost and change
explanations: no-multiply (procedural): The price of one of each item was used; the prices must be multiplied by how many were bought.
total-not-change (procedural): The total cost was given; the question asks for the change, so take the total away from the note.
one-item (procedural): Only the first item was paid for; add the cost of both kinds of item before finding the change.

teach.idea: A multi-step problem is a chain of small questions: what does each kind of item cost, what is the whole bill, and what is left from the note.
teach.method: Multiply to find the cost of each kind of item, add the costs to get the bill, then subtract the bill from the money paid.

alternatives.title: Count up like a shopkeeper
text: After finding the bill, count up from the bill to the note: ₹265 → ₹270 → ₹300 → ₹500.
Add the jumps: 5 + 30 + 200 = ₹235 change.

families.title: Water lost from a dripping tap
explanations: hours-as-minutes (conceptual): The hours were used as if they were minutes; 12 hours are 720 minutes.
hundred-minutes (recall): An hour was taken as 100 minutes; 1 hour = 60 minutes.
one-hour (procedural): Only the water for 1 hour was found; multiply by 12 for all the hours.

teach.idea: When something happens at the same rate every minute, the total is the amount each minute times the number of minutes. Hours must be changed into minutes first.
teach.method: Change the hours into minutes (× 60), then multiply by the millilitres lost each minute.

alternatives.title: One hour first
text: Find the water lost in one hour: 60 × the millilitres each minute.
Then add that amount once for every hour (or multiply by the number of hours).

families.title: Finding a missing digit in a sum or difference
explanations: carry-forgotten (procedural): The ten carried from the column on the right was forgotten. When a column adds up to 10 or more, 1 goes to the next column.
add-not-undo (conceptual): To find a missing part of an addition, take the other number away from the total; the digits were added instead.
borrow-forgotten (procedural): The ten borrowed by the column on the right was not taken off this column.
subtract-not-undo (conceptual): To find the first number of a subtraction, add the answer and the number taken away; the digits were subtracted instead.
smaller-from-larger (conceptual): In that column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, borrow a ten from the next column.

teach.idea: A sum or difference is a true sentence, so each column must work out, including any ten carried or borrowed from the column on its right.
teach.method: Start from the ones column and move left. In each column, note whether a ten is carried (addition) or borrowed (subtraction), then find the digit that makes the hidden column right. Check by doing the whole calculation.

alternatives.title: Try the digits and check
text: Put a digit in the box and work out the whole sum.
If it is not right, see whether the answer came out too big or too small and try a better digit. Only one digit works.

alternatives.title: Undo the operation
text: A missing part of an addition is total − other part.
A missing first number of a subtraction is answer + number taken away. Work out that calculation and read off the digit.

families.title: Winning move in a take-away game
explanations: groups-of-k (conceptual): The safe numbers to leave go up in steps of 6, not 5: whatever the other player takes (1 to 5), you can take enough to make 6.
take-most (conceptual): Taking as many as possible (3) does not always win. Look for the counts you want to leave for the other player.
wrong-goal (conceptual): This game was played as if taking the last counter wins. Here you want to leave the other player exactly 1 counter at the end.

teach.idea: Work backwards from the end. Some numbers of counters are "safe" to leave for the other player: from them, whatever they take, you can get back to the next safe number.
teach.method: If each turn takes 1 to k, the safe numbers go up in steps of k + 1 (0, k + 1, 2(k + 1) … when the last counter wins; 1 more than these when it loses). Take enough to leave a safe number.

alternatives.title: Play small games first
text: Play with 1, 2, 3 … counters and write W (the player to move wins) or L (loses) under each number.
A number is W if you can move to an L. The L numbers form a pattern; leave your partner an L number.

families.title: Counting every combination (one from each group)
explanations: add-choices (conceptual): The numbers of choices were added. Each choice from the first group goes with every choice from the next, so multiply.
add-last-group (procedural): The pairs were found (6 × 6), but then the sweets were added. Every pair goes with each of the 4 sweets, so multiply again.
forgot-group (procedural): One group was left out. A meal has one item from each of the three groups.

teach.idea: Every choice from one group can be matched with every choice from the next, so the number of combinations is the product of the numbers of choices.
teach.method: Fix the first choice and count how many ways the rest can go; that number is the same for every first choice, so multiply. With a third group, multiply again.

alternatives.title: Make an organised list
text: Take the first shirt and list it with every skirt, then the second shirt with every skirt, and so on.
Each row of the list has the same length, so the total is rows × length of a row.

alternatives.title: Draw a tree
text: Draw one branch for each first choice; from the end of each, draw one branch for each second choice.
Count the ends of the last branches.

families.title: How many numbers can be made from given digits
explanations: repeat-rule (procedural): A digit may be used again, so every place has all the choices; repeats were left out.
add-choices (conceptual): The choices for each place were added. Each first digit goes with every choice for the next place, so multiply.
zero-first (conceptual): Numbers starting with 0 were counted. A number does not start with 0 (07 is just 7), so 0 cannot be the first digit.

teach.idea: Fill the places one at a time from the left. The number of ways is the product of the choices for each place.
teach.method: Count the choices for the first place (0 is not allowed there), then for the next place (one fewer if digits cannot repeat), and so on; multiply.

alternatives.title: List by the first digit
text: Write all the numbers that start with the first digit, then those that start with the next digit, and so on.
Each starting digit gives the same number of numbers, so multiply.

families.title: Reading a pie chart
explanations: equal-parts (conceptual): The 5 parts were treated as equal. Look at the size of each part: they are not all the same.
the-rest (procedural): The number for all the other parts was found instead of this part.
denominator-only (procedural): Only the bottom of the fraction was used (240 ÷ 3). Then multiply by the top: that many of those pieces.

teach.idea: A pie chart shows the whole group as a full circle; each part's size is a fraction of the whole group.
teach.method: Find the fraction for the part (the whole circle is 1, so a missing part is 1 minus the others). Then find that fraction of the total: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top.

alternatives.title: Cut into equal pieces
text: Imagine the circle cut into equal pieces (for example 8 eighths). Share the total equally among the pieces.
Count how many pieces the part covers, and add up their shares.

families.title: Sector angles in a pie chart
explanations: count-as-degrees (conceptual): The number of students was used as the angle. The whole class is the full circle of 360°, so first find what fraction of the class this is.
percent-not-degrees (procedural): The angle was treated as a percentage (out of 100). Compare it with 360°, the whole circle.
half-circle (recall): A full turn is 360°, not 180°.
degrees-as-count (conceptual): The angle was given as the number of students. The angle is a fraction of 360°; the same fraction of the class chose cricket.

teach.idea: The whole group is the whole circle, 360°. Each part gets the same fraction of 360° as it is of the group.
teach.method: Angle = (part ÷ total) × 360°. Going back: part = (angle ÷ 360°) × total.

alternatives.title: Degrees for one person
text: Share 360° among everyone: each person gets 360 ÷ total degrees.
Multiply by the number in the part (or divide the angle by the degrees for one person).

families.title: Reading a bar chart with a scale
explanations: count-lines (conceptual): The lines were counted as 1 each. On this chart each line on the scale stands for 100.
assume-tens (procedural): Each line was taken as 10. Read the numbers on the scale: they tell how much each line stands for.
add-for-more (conceptual): "How many more" asks for the difference between the bars, not their total.
difference-for-total (procedural): "Together" asks for the total of the two bars; the difference was found instead.

teach.idea: On a scaled bar chart each line on the side stands for more than 1 (for example 5 or 50). The height of a bar is read off the scale, not by counting squares as ones.
teach.method: Find how much one line stands for (the difference between two numbers on the scale). Read each bar against the scale, then add or subtract as the question asks.

alternatives.title: Skip-count up the scale
text: Put a finger at the bottom of the bar and count up the lines in steps of the scale: 5, 10, 15 …
Stop at the top of the bar: that number is its value.

families.title: Writing a number rule with a letter
explanations: times-for-add (conceptual): 12m means 12 × m. Adding 12 is written m + 12.
reversed (conceptual): 12 − m takes m away from 12. Taking 12 away from m is written m − 12.
add-for-take (procedural): The rule takes away, so use −, not +.
add-for-times (conceptual): m + 12 adds 12. Multiplying by 12 is written 12 × m, or 12m.
brackets (procedural): 12(m + 9) adds 9 first and then multiplies. The machine multiplies first, then adds 9.
all-added (conceptual): Multiplying by 12 was written as adding 12.
joined-numbers (procedural): 9 was put with the 12 in front of m. 21m means 21 × m; the 9 is added on its own.

teach.idea: A letter stands for any number. A rule written with the letter works for every number at once.
teach.method: Do to the letter exactly what you would do to a number: 'add 5' gives n + 5; 'multiply by 4' gives 4n (4 × n). Test your rule with a small number.

alternatives.title: Try numbers first
text: Make a small table: put in 1, 2, 3 and write what comes out.
Look at what you did to each number every time, and write the same thing with the letter.

families.title: Writing the rule of a growing pattern with a letter
explanations: step-added (conceptual): n + 6 adds 6 once. The pattern adds 6 for every shape, so the rule has 6n (6 × n).
counted-from-zero (procedural): The shapes were numbered from 0. Check your rule with n = 1: it must give the first shape.
start-forgotten (procedural): 6n gives 6 for shape 1, but shape 1 has 11. Add the extra 5.
first-times-n (conceptual): 11n would add 11 each time, but the pattern grows by 6 each time.

teach.idea: If a pattern grows by the same amount each time, that amount is the number multiplied by n; a fixed extra makes the first shape right.
teach.method: Find how much the pattern grows each time (say 3): the rule starts 3n. Compare 3 × 1 with shape 1 to find what to add. Check with shape 4.

alternatives.title: See the groups in the shape
text: Look for the part that is added each time (for example a ⊓ of 3 matchsticks) and the part that is there from the start (one extra stick).
Shape n has n of the repeating parts plus the starting part.

families.title: Continuing square, triangular and other number patterns
explanations: same-gap (conceptual): The last gap (4) was added again and again. In this pattern the gap changes each time.
double-for-square (recall): A square number is n × n (25 × 25), not n × 2.
square-instead (conceptual): This picture has 20 rows and 21 columns, so 20 × 21; 20 × 20 would be a square.
times-three (recall): A cube number is n × n × n (10 × 10 × 10), not n × 3.
times-two (conceptual): Each number is double the one before; 2 × n adds 2 each time instead of doubling.
off-by-one (procedural): The 30th odd number is 2 × 30 − 1; 2 × 30 + 1 is the next one.

teach.idea: Square numbers come from square dot pictures (n rows of n), triangular numbers from triangles (1 + 2 + … + n), rectangular numbers from n rows of n + 1.
teach.method: Find the rule that makes each term from its position (for squares, n × n), test it on the terms you know, then use it for the term asked.

alternatives.title: Look at the gaps
text: Write the gaps between the terms: for square numbers they are 3, 5, 7, 9 … (the odd numbers); for triangular numbers 2, 3, 4, 5 ….
Keep adding the next gap until you reach the term you need.

families.title: Links between square, odd and triangular numbers
explanations: last-term (procedural): Only the last odd number was given; the question asks for the total of all of them.
count-terms (procedural): There are 25 odd numbers from 1 to 49, so the total is the 25th square number.
differ-by-one (conceptual): The two squares come next to each other in the list, but they are not next to each other as numbers: they differ by more than 1.
missed-one (procedural): Going from 30 × 30 to 31 × 31 adds a row of 30, a column of 30 and one corner dot.
doubled-one (procedural): The 20th triangular number was doubled; the question adds the 19th and the 20th.
wrong-square (procedural): The two triangles fit together into a square of side 20.
counted-one-end (procedural): One of the two squares was counted. "Between" leaves out both 625 and 676.
counted-both-ends (procedural): Both squares were counted; numbers between them do not include the ends.

teach.idea: Dot pictures show the links: odd numbers wrap round a square to make the next square; two neighbouring triangles fit together into a square.
teach.method: Draw (or imagine) the dot picture. Going from n × n to (n + 1) × (n + 1) adds n + n + 1 dots, an odd number; so adding the odd numbers from 1 gives the square numbers.

alternatives.title: Check small cases
text: Work the first few by hand: 1 = 1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 5 = 9 ….
Spot the pattern (here, square numbers), then use it for the case asked.

families.title: Reading an angle from a protractor
explanations: wrong-scale (procedural): The number was read from the wrong scale. Start from the 0 that one arm lies on and read the same scale up to the other arm.
one-reading (conceptual): The reading at one arm was given as the angle. Neither arm is on 0, so the angle is the difference between the two readings.
mixed-scales (procedural): One reading came from the inner scale and the other from the outer scale. Use the same scale for both arms.

teach.idea: A protractor has two scales running in opposite directions. Both arms must be read on the same scale; the angle is how far apart the readings are.
teach.method: Put the centre on the corner. Find the scale that reads 0 on one arm (or use either scale for both arms). Read the other arm on that same scale; if neither arm is on 0, subtract the smaller reading from the larger.

alternatives.title: Estimate first
text: Look at the angle: is it smaller than a right angle (less than 90°) or bigger?
If your reading says acute but the angle looks obtuse (or the other way round), you read the wrong scale.

families.title: Missing angle in a complementary or supplementary pair
explanations: wrong-total (recall): Supplementary angles make a straight angle, 180°. 90° is for complementary angles.
full-turn (recall): 360° is a full turn. Supplementary angles add up to 180°.

teach.idea: Complementary angles together make a right angle (90°); supplementary angles together make a straight angle (180°).
teach.method: Take the given angle away from 90° (complementary) or 180° (supplementary). Check: the two angles should add up to the total.

alternatives.title: Count on to the total
text: Start at the angle you know and count on to 90 (or 180), in tens and then ones.

families.title: Angles where two straight lines cross
explanations: opposite-as-linear (conceptual): Vertically opposite angles are equal; they do not add up to 180°. Angles next to each other on a straight line add to 180°.
full-turn (recall): Two angles on a straight line add up to 180°, not 360°.
neighbour-equal (conceptual): Angles next to each other are not equal (unless both are 90°); together they make a straight line, 180°.
straight-only (procedural): Only one neighbouring angle was found. All four angles together make a full turn, 360°.
all-equal (conceptual): The four angles are not all equal: only opposite angles are equal.

teach.idea: Where two straight lines cross, angles next to each other make a straight line (180°), so opposite angles are equal; all four make a full turn (360°).
teach.method: Opposite angle: the same. Angle next to it: 180° minus it. All the others together: 360° minus it.

alternatives.title: Go round the crossing
text: Start at the angle you know. The next angle round makes a straight line with it, so it is 180° minus it.
The next one makes a straight line with that one, so it is back to the first angle: opposite angles match.

families.title: Turns between compass directions as fractions of a full turn
explanations: other-way (conceptual): The turn was counted the other way round. Clockwise is the way the hands of a clock move: North → East → South → West.
quarters (procedural): Each step between neighbouring directions was counted as a quarter turn. With the in-between directions (North-East …) there are 8 steps in a full turn, so each is one eighth.
steps-not-fraction (procedural): The number of steps was given. A full turn has 8 steps, so write it as a fraction of 8.

teach.idea: A full turn brings you back to where you started. The four main directions split it into quarters; with the in-between directions (North-East and so on) it is split into eighths.
teach.method: Count the steps from the starting direction to the final one, going the way of the turn (clockwise is the way clock hands move). Each step is 1/8 of a turn; two steps make a quarter.

alternatives.title: Use a clock face
text: Imagine North at 12, East at 3, South at 6, West at 9.
North to East clockwise is like the minute hand going from 12 to 3: a quarter turn.

families.title: Degrees turned by the minute hand
explanations: six-per-number (procedural): Each number was counted as 6°. 6° is one minute mark; from one number to the next is 5 minutes, which is 30°.
minutes-not-degrees (conceptual): The minutes that passed were given, not the angle. A full turn of 60 minutes is 360°.
other-way (procedural): The angle the other way round the clock was found. The hand turned clockwise, the short way described.

teach.idea: The minute hand makes a full turn (360°) in an hour, passing 12 numbers, so it turns 30° from one number to the next.
teach.method: Count how many numbers the hand moves past (clockwise), then multiply by 30°. A quarter turn (3 numbers) is 90°; a half turn (6 numbers) is 180°.

alternatives.title: Fractions of a turn
text: Moving 3 numbers is a quarter turn (90°), 6 numbers a half turn (180°), 9 numbers three-quarters (270°).
For other moves, start from the nearest quarter and add or take away 30° for each number.

families.title: Counting the pieces at a stage of a repeating pattern
explanations: same-increase (conceptual): The pattern was taken to grow by the same number each stage (16). Every piece is replaced, so the number is multiplied by 5 each stage.
stage-off-by-one (procedural): Stage 0 is the start, so stage 3 has had 3 replacements; one stage too few was counted.
times-stage (conceptual): 4 × 5 × 3 multiplies by 5 only once. Multiply by 5 once for every stage: 3 times.

teach.idea: In a fractal pattern the same rule is used again and again on every piece, so the number of pieces is multiplied by the same number at every stage.
teach.method: Start with the pieces at stage 0 and multiply by the number of new pieces each piece becomes, once for every stage. A table of stages helps you keep count.

alternatives.title: A table of stages
text: Write the stages 0, 1, 2, … in a row.
Under each stage write the number of pieces: each is the one before times the number of new pieces per piece.

families.title: Faces, edges and vertices of prisms and pyramids
explanations: forgot-ends (conceptual): Only the 10 side faces were counted. A prism also has two ends (the top and the bottom decagon).
one-end (procedural): Only one end was counted; a prism has two.
euler-sign (procedural): Vertices = 2 + edges − faces; the 2 was taken away instead of added.
euler-forgot-2 (recall): The 2 in Euler's rule was left out.
forgot-side-edges (procedural): The edges round the top and bottom (10 + 10) were counted, but not the 10 edges joining them.
one-end-edges (procedural): The edges of only one end were counted.
one-end-vertices (procedural): Only the corners of one end were counted. The other end has 10 more.
forgot-base (conceptual): Only the 10 triangles were counted; the base (decagon) is a face too.
base-only (procedural): Only the 10 edges of the base were counted. There are also 10 edges going up to the top point.
extra-edge (procedural): An edge was counted twice: count the base edges, then the edges to the top point.
forgot-apex (procedural): The top point (apex) is a vertex too.

teach.idea: A prism has two equal ends joined by rectangles; a pyramid has one base joined to a top point by triangles. Counting part by part makes the counts easy.
teach.method: Prism on an n-sided base: faces n + 2, edges 3n, vertices 2n. Pyramid: faces n + 1, edges 2n, vertices n + 1. Check with Euler's rule: faces + vertices − edges = 2.

alternatives.title: Count part by part
text: Count the base, then the top (or the top point), then what joins them.
For edges: round the bottom, round the top, then the ones going up.

alternatives.title: Unfold it into a net
text: Imagine cutting the solid open and laying it flat: each face becomes one shape of the net.
Count the shapes in the net to get the faces.

families.title: Painted faces in a block of small cubes
explanations: kept-corners (procedural): The corner cubes were counted along each edge; corner cubes have paint on three faces, so leave them out (2 from each edge).
whole-faces (procedural): Every cube on a face was counted. Cubes on the edges of a face have paint on two or three faces; only the middle part of each face counts.
one-layer (procedural): Only one layer was taken off each length. The paint is on both sides, so take 2 from each length.
outside-cubes (conceptual): The question asks for the cubes with no paint: the hidden ones inside, not the ones on the outside.

teach.idea: Where a small cube sits decides its paint: corners get three faces, the rest of each edge two, the middle of each face one, and the hidden inside none.
teach.method: Take 2 off each length (the two outer layers). Edges: 4 × (sum of the shortened lengths). Faces: 2 × (sum of the products of pairs). Inside: the product of all three.

alternatives.title: Look layer by layer
text: Look at the top layer: count its corner, edge and middle cubes.
Then a middle layer: its outside ring has paint, its centre does not. Add up the layers.

families.title: Classifying quadrilaterals from their sides and angles
explanations: square-not-rectangle (conceptual): The squares were left out. A square has four right angles and opposite sides equal, so every square is also a rectangle.
opposite-sides-only (conceptual): Shapes with opposite sides equal were counted even without right angles. A rectangle needs all four angles to be 90°.
square-not-rhombus (conceptual): The squares were left out. A rhombus has four equal sides, so every square is also a rhombus.
rhombus-needs-right-angles (conceptual): Only the squares were counted. A rhombus needs four equal sides; its angles do not have to be 90°.
only-slanted (conceptual): Only the slanted shapes with unequal sides were counted. Squares, rectangles and rhombuses also have opposite sides equal and parallel, so they are parallelograms too.
right-angles-excluded (conceptual): Shapes with right angles were left out; rectangles and squares are parallelograms as well.
trapezium-included (conceptual): A trapezium was counted. Its opposite sides are not equal and only one pair is parallel, so it is not a parallelogram.

teach.idea: Shape names describe properties, so one shape can have several names: a square is a rectangle (four right angles), a rhombus (four equal sides) and a parallelogram (opposite sides equal and parallel).
teach.method: For each shape, check the property the name needs. Rectangle: all angles 90°. Rhombus: all sides equal. Parallelogram: opposite sides equal and opposite angles equal. Count every shape that has it.

alternatives.title: A family tree of shapes
text: Parallelograms are a big family. Rectangles and rhombuses are inside it, and squares are inside both rectangles and rhombuses.
When you count a family, count everyone inside it too.

families.title: Unknown angles in a parallelogram or rhombus
explanations: opposite-as-adjacent (conceptual): Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal; it is angles next to each other that add to 180°.
all-equal (conceptual): Only opposite angles are equal. Angles next to each other add up to 180°.
full-turn (recall): Neighbouring angles add to 180°; 360° is all four angles together.
no-split (conceptual): The diagonal of a rhombus cuts angle A into two equal halves; the whole angle was given.
wrong-angle-halved (procedural): Angle B was halved instead of angle A. The diagonal AC starts at A, so it splits angle A.

teach.idea: In a parallelogram (and so in a rhombus) opposite angles are equal, and angles next to each other add up to 180°. In a rhombus each diagonal also cuts its angles in half.
teach.method: Opposite angle: the same. Neighbouring angle: 180° minus it. Rhombus diagonal: half the angle it starts from.

alternatives.title: Think of parallel lines
text: Two sides of a parallelogram are parallel; a third side crosses them.
