The two angles between the parallel sides on the same side of that crossing line add to 180°.

families.title: Order and angle of rotational symmetry
explanations: missed-full-turn (procedural): The last position, back at the start after a full turn, was not counted. Count every time it looks the same, including the full turn.
doubled (procedural): Each matching position was counted twice (once for each direction of turning). Turn one way only.
half-turn-shared (conceptual): 180° was shared out instead of a full turn, 360°.
gave-order (procedural): The order (how many times) was given instead of the angle. Share 360° by the order.
upside-down (procedural): The fraction was written the wrong way up. The turn is 1 out of 8 equal parts of a full turn: 1/8.
angle-not-fraction (procedural): The angle in degrees was given. As a fraction of a full turn, divide by 360.
counted-start (procedural): The starting position was counted as the first time. The first time it looks the same is after the smallest turn.
first-angle (procedural): Only the smallest angle was given; the 7th time is 7 of those turns.
counted-corners (conceptual): The corners were counted. Turn the shape: it only fits onto itself after a half turn and a full turn.
mirror-only (conceptual): It has no mirror line, but it still looks the same after a half turn. Rotational symmetry is about turning, not folding.

teach.idea: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after a turn of less than a full turn. The order is how many times it fits onto itself in one full turn.
teach.method: Count the identical parts that go round the centre (sides of a regular shape, blades, petals): that is usually the order. The smallest turn is 360° ÷ order, which is 1/order of a full turn.

alternatives.title: Trace and turn
text: Trace the shape on thin paper, put a pin through the centre and turn the tracing slowly.
Count each time the tracing sits exactly on the shape before you get back to the start.

families.title: Classifying triangles by their angles
explanations: one-acute-enough (conceptual): A triangle was called acute-angled because it has an acute angle. Every triangle has at least two acute angles; an acute-angled triangle has all three less than 90°.
right-as-acute (recall): A 90° angle is a right angle, not an acute one. Acute means less than 90°.
big-as-right (recall): Triangles with an angle bigger than 90° were counted. A right angle is exactly 90°; bigger is obtuse.
right-as-obtuse (recall): A 90° angle was counted as obtuse. Obtuse means more than 90°.
biggest-first (procedural): Only the first angle of each triangle was checked. Look at all three angles: the largest one decides the type.

teach.idea: Every triangle has at least two acute angles, so the type is decided by its largest angle: less than 90° acute-angled, exactly 90° right-angled, more than 90° obtuse-angled.
teach.method: For each triangle find the largest angle and compare it with 90°. Then count the ones asked for.

alternatives.title: The square-corner test
text: Hold the corner of a sheet of paper (a right angle) against each angle.
If one angle fits exactly it is right-angled; if one is wider it is obtuse-angled; if all are narrower it is acute-angled.

families.title: Classifying triangles by their sides
explanations: not-equilateral (conceptual): Every triangle that is not equilateral was counted. A triangle with two equal sides is not scalene.
names-swapped (recall): Isosceles and scalene were mixed up. Isosceles: two sides equal. Scalene: all different.
two-equal-enough (conceptual): Triangles with only two equal sides were counted. Equilateral needs all three sides equal.
equilateral-included (procedural): The equilateral triangles were counted too; the question asks for exactly two equal sides.

teach.idea: Triangles are named by how many sides are equal: all three equal is equilateral, exactly two equal is isosceles (with two equal sides), none equal is scalene.
teach.method: For each triangle compare the three lengths in pairs (first and second, second and third, first and third). Count the equal pairs, name the triangle, then count the ones asked for.

alternatives.title: Sort the lengths first
text: Write the three lengths from smallest to largest.
Equal lengths are now next to each other, so they are easy to spot.

families.title: Rectangles with the same area or the same perimeter
explanations: same-perimeter (conceptual): Rectangles with the same area do not always have the same perimeter. Find the other side first, then go round the new rectangle.
half-perimeter (procedural): Only two sides were added. A rectangle has four sides: two of each length.
gave-area (procedural): The area was given; the question asks for the distance round the edge.
same-area (conceptual): Rectangles with the same perimeter do not always have the same area. Find the other side first, then multiply.
forgot-halve (procedural): The other side was found as perimeter − 23. The perimeter has two of each side: the other side is half the perimeter minus 23.
gave-perimeter (procedural): The perimeter was given; the question asks for the area (the squares inside).

teach.idea: Area counts the squares inside; perimeter is the distance round the edge. Rearranging the same squares can change the perimeter, and the same length of fence can enclose different areas.
teach.method: Same area: find the other side by dividing the area by the side you know, then add all four sides. Same perimeter: half the perimeter is one long side plus one short side, so take away the side you know, then multiply.

alternatives.title: Rearrange the squares
text: Imagine cutting the rectangle into its unit squares and laying them out in rows of the new length.
Count the rows to get the other side, then walk round the edge to get the perimeter.

families.title: Distance covered in one hour or one minute
explanations: multiply-not-divide (conceptual): The distance was multiplied by the time. In 1 minute the distance is less than the whole journey, so share it out: divide by 6.
whole-distance (conceptual): The whole distance was given. The question asks for the part covered in just 1 minute.
subtract-time (procedural): 6 was taken away from the distance. Sharing a distance equally over 6 minutes means dividing by 6.
division-slip (prerequisite): A slip in dividing 540 by 6. Check by multiplying back: the answer × 6 must give 540.

teach.idea: Speed tells how far something goes in ONE hour (or one minute). If the speed is steady, every hour covers the same part of the journey.
teach.method: Share the whole distance equally among the hours: distance ÷ time. Check by multiplying back.

alternatives.title: Build an hour-by-hour table
text: Make a table: after 1 hour, after 2 hours, and so on.
Guess the distance for 1 hour, keep adding it, and adjust the guess until the last row gives the whole distance.

families.title: Comparing two speeds from distance and time
explanations: farther-is-faster (conceptual): The child who went farther was taken as faster. Going farther may just mean cycling for longer: compare the distance in ONE minute.
bigger-distance (procedural): The longer distance was given instead of a speed. Speed is the distance in 1 minute: distance ÷ minutes.
less-time-is-faster (conceptual): The child with the shorter time was taken as faster, but they cycled different distances. Work out each child's metres in one minute.

teach.idea: To compare speeds fairly, compare the distance each covers in the SAME time: one minute (or one hour).
teach.method: For each one, divide distance by time to get the distance in 1 minute. The bigger result is the faster one.

alternatives.title: Stretch both to the same time
text: Find a time both can be scaled to, e.g. 12 minutes for 3 and 4 minutes.
Multiply each distance up to that time; the one that goes farther in the same time is faster.

families.title: Adding and subtracting decimals with different places
explanations: right-align (conceptual): The digits were lined up from the right, as for whole numbers, so tenths were added to hundredths. Line up the decimal points: write 19.8 as 19.80.
no-carry (procedural): A column added up to 10 or more, but the 1 was not carried to the next place on the left.
bring-down (procedural): The empty hundredths place in 19.9 was skipped and the 1 was brought down. Write 19.9 as 19.90: the empty place is a 0, and you take 1 away from it by exchanging.
smaller-from-larger (procedural): In each column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, exchange 1 from the next place first.

teach.idea: Each place has a value: ones, tenths, hundredths. Only digits of the same place can be added or taken away, so the decimal points must line up.
teach.method: Write the numbers one under the other with the decimal points in a line. Fill empty places with 0, then add or subtract from the right as with whole numbers, and keep the point in the answer.

alternatives.title: Think of rupees and paise
text: Read 4.5 as ₹4.50 and 2.37 as ₹2.37: 50 paise and 37 paise are both paise, so they go together.
Add the paise, then the rupees, exchanging 100 paise for ₹1 when needed.

families.title: Adding and subtracting money in rupees and paise
explanations: paise-over-100 (conceptual): The paise were added to 120 and all written after the point. 120 paise is ₹1 and 20 paise, so carry ₹1 to the rupees.
rupee-not-carried (procedural): 100 paise were taken away from the paise but the ₹1 they make was not added to the rupees.
smaller-paise-from-larger (procedural): 60 paise is less than 80 paise, so 60 was taken from 80 instead. Change ₹1 into 100 paise first: 160 − 80.
rupee-not-reduced (procedural): ₹1 was changed into paise, but the rupees were not made one less (₹80 becomes ₹79).

teach.idea: 100 paise make ₹1. Paise go with paise and rupees with rupees, and 100 paise can be swapped for ₹1 (or ₹1 for 100 paise).
teach.method: Line up the decimal points. Work on the paise first, exchanging ₹1 and 100 paise when needed, then the rupees.

alternatives.title: Change everything into paise
text: ₹45.50 is 4550 paise and ₹28.75 is 2875 paise.
Add or subtract the paise as whole numbers, then put the point back two places from the right: 7425 paise = ₹74.25.

families.title: Listing all the factors of a number
explanations: forget-1-and-n (conceptual): 1 and 100 were left out. Every number has 1 and itself as factors: 1 × 100 = 100.
half-the-pairs (procedural): Only the first number of each factor pair was written. Each factor comes with a partner: write both numbers of every pair.
multiples-for-factors (conceptual): Multiples of 100 were listed. Factors divide 100 exactly, so they are never bigger than 100.

teach.idea: A factor of a number divides it exactly. Factors come in pairs: if a × b = n, both a and b are factors of n.
teach.method: Try 1, 2, 3, … in order. Each time one divides exactly, write it and its partner. Stop when the numbers meet in the middle.

alternatives.title: Make rectangles of dots
text: Arrange the number as dots in a rectangle: rows × columns.
Every rectangle you can make gives a factor pair; a number with only one rectangle (1 row) is prime.

families.title: Common factors of two numbers
explanations: hcf-only (conceptual): Only the highest common factor was given. The question asks for every number that divides both.
forget-1 (conceptual): 1 was left out; 1 divides every number, so it is always a common factor.
factors-of-one (procedural): All the factors of 56 were listed. Check each one: does it also divide 60?

teach.idea: A common factor divides both numbers exactly. 1 is always one; the largest is the HCF.
teach.method: List the factors of the smaller number, then keep only the ones that also divide the larger number.

alternatives.title: Find the HCF first
text: Find the largest number that divides both (the HCF).
Every common factor is a factor of the HCF: list the factors of the HCF.

families.title: Common multiples from jumps on a number line
explanations: first-only (procedural): Only the first meeting point was given. After 24 they meet again every 24: keep going up to 60.
one-animal (conceptual): These are all the frog's landing places. A common multiple must be a landing place for the rabbit too.
product (conceptual): Only multiples of 8 × 12 were used. 8 and 12 share a factor, so they meet sooner, at 24.

teach.idea: A number where both animals land is in both times tables: a common multiple. After the first one, they meet again at regular steps of that same size.
teach.method: Write the multiples of the bigger jump and check each one: does the smaller jump also land there? Collect those up to the end of the line.

alternatives.title: Two lists side by side
text: Write the frog's landing places in one row and the rabbit's in the row below.
Circle the numbers that appear in both rows.

families.title: The lowest common multiple of two numbers
explanations: product (conceptual): 23 × 24 is a common multiple, but 23 and 24 share the factor 1, so a smaller one comes first.
hcf-for-lcm (conceptual): The highest common factor was found. The LCM is the smallest number that BOTH divide into: it is never smaller than the larger number.
larger-number (procedural): 24 was given, but 24 is not in the 23 times table. Keep going along the 24 times table.
common-not-lowest (procedural): A common multiple was found, but not the lowest one. Check the smaller multiples first.

teach.idea: A common multiple is in both times tables. The lowest one is the first time they meet.
teach.method: Go up the times table of the larger number and stop at the first one the smaller number divides exactly.

alternatives.title: Use prime factors
text: Write each number as a product of primes, e.g. 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 18 = 2 × 3 × 3.
Take each prime the greatest number of times it appears in either: 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 36.

alternatives.title: Divide both together
text: Divide both numbers by a common factor and write the quotients below; repeat until no common factor is left.
Multiply the divisors on the left by the numbers left at the bottom.

families.title: The highest common factor of three numbers
explanations: two-only (procedural): This is the HCF of 54 and 66 only. Check that it divides 70 too.
smallest-number (conceptual): The smallest number, 60, was given, but 60 does not divide all of them.
a-common-factor (conceptual): A common factor was found, but not the highest one. Look for a bigger number that divides all three.

teach.idea: The HCF is the biggest number that divides every one of the numbers exactly.
teach.method: Find the HCF of the first two numbers, then find the HCF of that result and the third number.

alternatives.title: List and compare factors
text: List the factors of the smallest number, biggest first.
The first one that divides the other two numbers exactly is the HCF.

alternatives.title: Common prime factors
text: Write each number as a product of primes.
Multiply the primes that appear in all three (as many times as they appear in every one).

families.title: Writing a mixed number as an improper fraction
explanations: add-whole-to-top (conceptual): 9 was added to the numerator. Each whole is 10/10, so 9 wholes are 90 pieces of size 1/10.
forget-numerator (procedural): Only the wholes were changed into pieces; the 9/10 was not added on.
fact-slip (prerequisite): The multiplication 9 × 10 is not yet reliable.
times-numerator (procedural): The whole number was multiplied by the numerator and the denominator was added. Multiply the whole number by the DENOMINATOR, then add the numerator.

teach.idea: A whole cut into d equal pieces is d/d. So w wholes are w × d pieces, and the fraction part adds a few more pieces of the same size.
teach.method: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and write the total over the same denominator.

alternatives.title: Cut every whole into pieces
text: Draw each whole as a bar cut into the same number of pieces as the denominator.
Count all the pieces, including the extra ones: that count goes on top.

families.title: Writing an improper fraction as a mixed number
explanations: swap (procedural): The quotient and the remainder swapped places. 99 ÷ 10 = 9 remainder 9: 9 wholes, and the 9 pieces left over go on top.
too-few-wholes (procedural): One whole was missed: 19/10 is more than 1, so another whole can be taken out.
remainder-as-denominator (conceptual): The pieces keep their size: the denominator stays 10.
division-slip (prerequisite): A slip in dividing 99 by 10. Check: 10 × whole number + numerator must give 99.

teach.idea: A whole is made of d pieces of size 1/d. Dividing the numerator by the denominator tells how many wholes there are; the remainder is the pieces left.
teach.method: Divide the numerator by the denominator. The quotient is the whole number, the remainder is the new numerator, and the denominator stays the same.

alternatives.title: Count out the wholes
text: Take away d/d (one whole) again and again, counting the wholes.
When less than a whole is left, that is the fraction part.

families.title: Order of operations with brackets
explanations: left-to-right (conceptual): The adding was done first. Division comes before addition: work out 12 ÷ 6 first.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (11 × 3) is not yet reliable.
ignore-brackets (conceptual): The brackets were ignored. Work out what is inside the brackets first.
add-before-subtract (conceptual): 11 + 8 was worked out first. Adding and taking away have equal rank: go from left to right, 39 − 11 first.

teach.idea: Everyone agrees on one order so an expression has only one value: brackets first, then × and ÷, then + and −; equal ranks go from left to right.
teach.method: Look for brackets and work them out. Next do every × and ÷, left to right. Last do + and −, left to right.

alternatives.title: Draw it as a tree
text: Put the last operation at the top of a tree, with its two parts as branches: 6 + 4 × 3 has + at the top, with 6 on one branch and 4 × 3 on the other.
Work from the bottom of the tree upwards: 4 × 3 = 12, then 6 + 12 = 18.

alternatives.title: Split into terms
text: Cut the expression at every + and − that is not inside brackets: each piece is a term.
Work out each term on its own, then add and take away the terms from left to right.

families.title: Writing a fraction or decimal as a percentage
explanations: numerator-as-percent (conceptual): The numerator was taken as the percentage. Per cent means out of 100: change 49/50 into hundredths first.
add-not-scale (procedural): The same number was added to the top and bottom to make the bottom 100. To keep the fraction the same size, MULTIPLY both by 2.
unit-fraction (procedural): 1/100 is 1%, but there are 99 of them: 99 × 1 = 99.
one-place (conceptual): The point moved only one place. Per cent means hundredths: 0.99 is 99 hundredths, so it is 99%.
zero-ignored (conceptual): The 0 straight after the point was ignored. 0.09 is 9 hundredths, not 9 tenths.

teach.idea: Per cent means 'out of 100'. A percentage is a number of hundredths: 37% = 37/100 = 0.37.
teach.method: Turn the fraction into hundredths by multiplying top and bottom by the same number; for a decimal, read how many hundredths it is. That number of hundredths is the percentage.

alternatives.title: Shade a hundred square
text: A 10 × 10 square has 100 small squares; each one is 1%.
Shade the part the fraction or decimal stands for and count the small squares.

families.title: Writing a percentage as a decimal
explanations: tenths (conceptual): 150% was written as 150 tenths. Per cent means hundredths: 150% = 150/100.
thousandths (procedural): The point moved three places. Dividing by 100 moves the point two places to the left.
drop-sign (conceptual): The % sign was just dropped. 150% is 150 out of 100, which is 1.5.

teach.idea: Per cent means hundredths, so x% is x/100. Dividing by 100 moves every digit two places to the right of where it was.
teach.method: Write the percentage over 100, then write it as a decimal: the last two digits of the number become the tenths and hundredths.

alternatives.title: Think of paise in a rupee
text: ₹1 has 100 paise, so 1% of a rupee is 1 paisa.
7% of a rupee is 7 paise = ₹0.07; 45% is 45 paise = ₹0.45.

families.title: Listing the prime numbers in a range
explanations: odd-is-prime (conceptual): Some odd numbers that are not prime were included (87, 91, 93). Being odd is not enough: test whether 3, 7 or another number divides it.
one-is-prime (conceptual): 1 was counted as prime. A prime has exactly two factors; 1 has only one factor.
two-not-prime (conceptual): 2 was left out because it is even. 2 has exactly two factors (1 and 2), so it is prime: the only even prime.

teach.idea: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. 1 is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime.
teach.method: For each number, try dividing by 2, 3, 5 and 7 (enough up to 100, unless the number is that prime). If none divides it exactly, it is prime.

alternatives.title: Use a sieve
text: Write the numbers in a grid. Cross out 1.
Keep 2 and cross out every other multiple of 2; keep 3 and cross out its multiples; do the same for 5 and 7. The numbers left are prime.

alternatives.title: Only one rectangle
text: Try to arrange the number as dots in a rectangle with more than one row.
If the only rectangle is a single row, the number is prime.

families.title: Finding a counterexample to a claim
explanations: confirming-example (conceptual): 21 agrees with the claim, so it does not show the claim is wrong. To show a claim is not always true, find ONE number where it fails.

teach.idea: A claim that says 'every' must work for ALL numbers. One number where it fails, a counterexample, is enough to show it is not always true; numbers where it works never prove it.
teach.method: Test each number: does it fit the first part of the claim? If yes, does the rest of the claim hold? The number that fits the first part but not the rest is the counterexample.

alternatives.title: Two ticks
text: Make two columns: 'is it one the claim talks about?' and 'does the claim hold?'.
The counterexample has a tick in the first column and a cross in the second.

families.title: Solving a one-step equation
explanations: same-operation (conceptual): 20 was divided by 10; x ÷ 10 = 20 is undone by multiplying by 10.
subtract-coefficient (conceptual): 10 was taken away from 190; 10x means 10 × x, so divide by 10.
add-for-multiply (procedural): 10 was added to 20; undoing ÷ 10 needs × 10.

teach.idea: An equation is a balance: both sides have the same value. Doing the opposite operation to both sides keeps it balanced and leaves x alone.
teach.method: Look at what is done to x (+, −, ×, ÷). Do the opposite to both sides. Then put your answer back into the equation to check it.

alternatives.title: Guess, check and improve
text: Ask: which number makes the equation true? Try one, work out the left side, and compare.
If the left side is too big, try a smaller number; too small, try a bigger one.

alternatives.title: Keep the balance level
text: Picture the two sides on a balance.
Whatever you take off or add on one side, do the same on the other, until x is alone.

families.title: Collecting like terms
explanations: unlike-combined (conceptual): x terms and y terms were added together into one term. Only like terms (the same letter) can be added: x terms with x terms, y terms with y terms.
squared-letters (conceptual): Adding x terms was written as a power (like x + x = x²). Adding like terms only adds the numbers in front: 2x + 3x = 5x.
sign-dropped (prerequisite): A minus sign in front of a term was lost. The sign belongs to the term that follows it.

teach.idea: Like terms have the same letter part: 3x and −5x are like terms, 3x and 2y are not. Like terms can be added because they count the same thing.
teach.method: Group the x terms and the y terms, keeping each sign with the term after it. Add the numbers in front of each group and write one term for each letter.

alternatives.title: Count things of the same kind
text: Read x as 'apples' and y as 'bananas': 3 apples + 2 bananas + 4 apples is 7 apples + 2 bananas.
You cannot add apples to bananas to get 'applebananas', just as 3x + 2y is not 5xy.

alternatives.title: Check with a number
text: Put x = 2 and y = 1 into the question and into your answer.
If the two values are different, a term has been combined wrongly.

families.title: Subtracting one expression from another
explanations: minus-first-term-only (procedural): The minus sign was used on 5x but not on −4. A minus in front of a bracket changes the sign of every term inside it.
added-instead (procedural): The two expressions were added. The question takes the second bracket away.
wrong-order (procedural): The first expression was taken away from the second. The order matters: (first) − (second).

teach.idea: Taking away a bracket takes away every term inside it, so each sign in the bracket changes: −(3x − 4) = −3x + 4.
teach.method: Remove the brackets, changing every sign in the second one. Then collect the x terms and the number terms.

alternatives.title: Add the opposite
text: Subtracting is adding the opposite: (5x + 2) − (2x − 3) = (5x + 2) + (−2x + 3).
Now add like terms as usual.

alternatives.title: Line up like terms
text: Write the first expression above the second, x terms under x terms and numbers under numbers.
Subtract each column, taking care with negative numbers.

families.title: Coefficients and the constant term
explanations: sign-dropped (conceptual): The sign was left out. The coefficient includes the sign in front of the term: in 5 − 3y the coefficient of y is −3.
invisible-one (conceptual): A term with no number in front was given coefficient 0. A term like xy means 1 × xy, so its coefficient is 1 (or −1 with a minus sign).
power-for-coefficient (conceptual): The power 2 in x² was taken as the coefficient. The coefficient is the number multiplying x², written in front of it.

teach.idea: An expression is a sum of terms. Each term is a number (the coefficient, with its sign) times letters; a term with no letter is the constant term.
teach.method: Split the expression at each + or −, keeping the sign with the term after it. The coefficient is the signed number in front of the letters; no number means 1.

alternatives.title: Make a table of terms
text: Write each term in its own column: for 4x² − xy + 3y − 9 the terms are 4x², −xy, 3y, −9.
Under each, write its number part: 4, −1, 3 and −9.

families.title: The top of a number pyramid
explanations: bottom-row-sum (conceptual): Only the bottom row was added up. Each block is used again in the rows above, so the middle blocks count more than once.
three-rows (procedural): The middle blocks were counted twice, as in a pyramid with three rows. With four rows, each middle block of the bottom row reaches the top 3 times.
x-counted-once (procedural): The x terms were not all collected: x appears in more than one block on the way up, and each one must be added.

teach.idea: In a four-row pyramid the corner blocks of the bottom row reach the top once and the two middle blocks reach it 3 times each, so the top is 1, 3, 3, 1 times the bottom blocks.
teach.method: Write the second row as sums, then the third row, then the top, collecting like terms at each step.

alternatives.title: Count the paths to the top
text: Each bottom block adds into the top once for every path upward.
A corner block has 1 path; a middle block has 3 paths. So top = first + 3 × second + 3 × third + fourth.

alternatives.title: Try a number for x
text: Put x = 0 and build the pyramid: that gives the number part of the answer.
Then put x = 1: the top grows by the coefficient of x.

families.title: An expression for a growing pattern
explanations: step-as-expression (conceptual): The rule 'add 9 each time' was written as n + 9. Figure n has 9 added n times, which is 9n, plus a fixed part.
first-term-as-coefficient (conceptual): The first figure's count, 18, was used as the number multiplying n. The number that multiplies n is how many are added each time (9).
first-term-as-constant (procedural): The first figure's count was added on as the fixed part. Check Figure 1: 9 × 1 + 18 is not 18.
constant-forgotten (procedural): Only the growing part 9n was written. Check with Figure 1: 9 × 1 = 9, but the figure has 18.

teach.idea: If a pattern grows by the same amount d each time, Figure n is d × n plus a fixed part. The fixed part is what makes Figure 1 come out right.
teach.method: Find how many are added each time: that number multiplies n. Then compare d × 1 with Figure 1 to find what to add or take away. Check with Figure 2.

alternatives.title: Go back to Figure 0
text: Step back once from Figure 1: Figure 0 would have (Figure 1) − d.
That is the fixed part; then add d for each figure: d n + (Figure 0).

alternatives.title: See the groups in the picture
text: In a row of squares made of matchsticks, each new square needs 3 more sticks and the first square needs one extra.
So n squares need 3n + 1 sticks: 3 for each square, plus the first stick.

families.title: Why a 'think of a number' trick works
explanations: bracket-not-multiplied (procedural): Only 9n was multiplied by 5, not the 9 added to it. Multiplying 'the result' multiplies the whole of 9n + 9.
number-not-multiplied (procedural): The 9 was multiplied by 5 but 9n was not. Every term in the bracket is multiplied by 5.

teach.idea: Using a letter for the number lets you follow the trick for every number at once. When the added numbers cancel, the answer depends only on n, which is why the trick always works.
teach.method: Write each step as an expression, using brackets when a whole result is multiplied. Expand the brackets and collect like terms.

alternatives.title: Try a few numbers first
text: Play the trick with n = 1, 2 and 3 and write the results.
Look for the pattern (each result is a fixed multiple of n), then show it with algebra.

alternatives.title: Bags and counters
text: Picture n as a closed bag of counters and the numbers as loose counters.
Follow the steps with bags and counters: the loose counters all leave at the end, so only the bags are left.

families.title: Terms from a recursive rule
explanations: started-late (procedural): The list started at t₂. The first term is t₁ = 9 itself; the rule makes the terms after it.
add-before-multiply (procedural): 9 was added before multiplying by 2. The rule multiplies the term first, then adds.
sign-dropped (prerequisite): The minus sign in the rule was lost: tₙ₊₁ = … − 1 takes 1 away.
multiplier-ignored (procedural): Only the addition was used. Each new term is 2 times the last one, then plus 9.

teach.idea: A recursive rule tells you how to get each term from the one before it; the first term starts the chain.
teach.method: Write t₁. Put it into the rule to get t₂, put t₂ in to get t₃, and so on. Do the operations in the order the rule gives.

alternatives.title: A table of n and tₙ
text: Make two columns: n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and tₙ.
Fill each row from the row above using the rule, showing the working.

alternatives.title: A number machine
text: Think of the rule as a machine: a term goes in, the next term comes out.
Feed each output back in as the next input.

families.title: From a recursive rule to a formula for tₙ
explanations: one-jump-too-many (procedural): t₁ = 20 was used as the fixed part. To reach tₙ from t₁ there are n − 1 jumps of −1, not n.
step-added-to-n (conceptual): The rule was copied with n in place of tₙ. Each step adds −1, so n steps add −1 × n.
swapped (procedural): The first term and the step were swapped. The number multiplying n is the step (what is added each time).

teach.idea: Adding d each time means tₙ is the first term plus (n − 1) steps of d: tₙ = t₁ + (n − 1)d.
teach.method: Write t₁ + (n − 1)d with the numbers, open the bracket and collect the numbers. Check that n = 1 gives t₁ and n = 2 gives t₂.

alternatives.title: Find term number 0
text: Step back once from t₁: t₀ = t₁ − d.
Then tₙ = dn + t₀, since n steps of d take you from t₀ to tₙ.

families.title: A Virahanka-Fibonacci style sequence
explanations: off-by-one (procedural): The terms were miscounted by one. Number each term as you write it: term 1 is the first number given.
arithmetic (conceptual): The sequence was treated as adding -2 each time. Here each term is the sum of the two before it, so the jumps grow.

teach.idea: Each new term is made from the two terms before it, so you must keep the last two terms in view as you go.
teach.method: Write the terms in a numbered row: add the last two to get the next, until you reach the term you need.

alternatives.title: Virahanka's rhythms
text: Virahanka counted rhythms made of short (1 beat) and long (2 beat) syllables: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 … rhythms for 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 beats.
A rhythm of n beats ends in a short syllable (after n − 1 beats) or a long one (after n − 2 beats), so the counts add.

alternatives.title: Number every term
text: Write 1, 2, 3 … above the terms as you go, so you stop at the right term.
Check each sum before moving on.

families.title: An inverse proportion
explanations: direct-for-inverse (conceptual): y was scaled the same way as x, as in a direct proportion. Here more of x means less of y: the product x × y stays 312.
not-divided (procedural): The product 12 × 29 = 348 is right, but it must then be shared by 6.
additive (conceptual): The change in x was taken off y. In an inverse proportion the product stays the same, not the sum.

teach.idea: In an inverse proportion, when one quantity is multiplied by some number the other is divided by it, so their product never changes (workers × days = the total work).
teach.method: Multiply the two given values to get the fixed product, then divide it by the new value.

alternatives.title: Go through one worker
text: If a workers take d days, 1 worker takes a × d days (one person does all the work).
Then b workers share it: (a × d) ÷ b days.

alternatives.title: Invert the ratio
text: If x becomes twice as big, y becomes half as big.
So y(new) = y(old) × x(old) ÷ x(new).

families.title: Time taken working together
explanations: add-times (conceptual): The two times were added. Working together is faster than either one alone, so the answer must be less than both times.
average (conceptual): The average of the two times was taken. Two people together finish sooner than either one alone.
rate-not-flipped (procedural): The work per day, 1/19 + 1/20, was given as the answer. That is the part of the job done in one day; the days needed is 1 divided by it.

teach.idea: Think of the work done in one day: a person who takes p days does 1/p of the job each day. Working together, the parts done per day add up.
teach.method: Add 1/p and 1/q to get the part of the job done in one day together; the number of days is 1 divided by that fraction.

alternatives.title: Count units of work
text: Pretend the job is p × q units of work (for example, bricks).
One person lays q units a day, the other p units a day; together p + q a day, so the job takes pq ÷ (p + q) days.

families.title: An equation with fractions of x
explanations: denominators-combined (conceptual): x/8 − x/9 was written as x/1, subtracting the bottom numbers. Fractions with different denominators are first written with a common denominator.
lcd-one-side (procedural): The left side was multiplied by 72 but the right side (2) was not. Multiply every term on both sides by the same number.
one-fraction-only (procedural): Only x/8 was used, as if x/8 = 2. Both fractions of x are part of the left side.

teach.idea: Multiplying every term on both sides by the same number keeps an equation true; choosing the least common multiple of the denominators clears all the fractions.
teach.method: Find the LCM of the denominators, multiply every term by it, collect the x terms, then divide.

alternatives.title: Combine the fractions first
text: Write both fractions over a common denominator: x/3 + x/4 = 4x/12 + 3x/12 = 7x/12.
Then 7x/12 = c gives x = 12c ÷ 7.

alternatives.title: Think in equal parts
text: If the whole is cut into (LCM) equal parts, x/a is LCM ÷ a of them and x/b is LCM ÷ b of them.
Find how many parts the right side is, and how big one part is.

families.title: An equation with x on both sides
explanations: x-sign-kept (procedural): 5x was moved to the left side without changing its sign. Taking 5x from both sides leaves 4x on the left.
number-sign-kept (procedural): 15 was moved to the right side without changing its sign. To remove + 15 from the left, take away 15 on both sides.
wrong-way-round (procedural): The numbers were subtracted the wrong way round, giving the right size with the wrong sign. Check by putting the answer back into both sides.

teach.idea: An equation stays balanced when the same thing is added to or taken from both sides, including a number of x's.
teach.method: Take the smaller x term from both sides so x is on one side only, move the numbers to the other side, then divide by the coefficient of x. Check by substituting.

alternatives.title: Remove x's from both pans
text: Picture x-bags and counters on a balance.
Take the same number of bags off both pans, then the same number of counters, until one bag is balanced by counters.

families.title: Reading the coordinates of a point
explanations: sign-dropped (conceptual): A coordinate left of the y-axis or below the x-axis is negative; the minus sign was left out.
swapped (conceptual): The coordinates were written the wrong way round. The x-coordinate (across) comes first, then the y-coordinate (up or down).

teach.idea: A point's coordinates say how to reach it from the origin: first across (x), then up or down (y). Left and down are negative.
teach.method: Start at the origin. Count squares across to the point's line: that is x (negative if left). Then count up or down: that is y. Write (x, y).

alternatives.title: Along the corridor, then up the stairs
text: You walk along the corridor (x) before you climb the stairs (y).
So the across number always comes first.

alternatives.title: Drop lines to the axes
text: From the point, imagine a line straight down (or up) to the x-axis: where it meets is x.
And a line straight across to the y-axis: where it meets is y.

families.title: Which quadrant a point is in
explanations: clockwise (recall): The quadrants were numbered clockwise. They go anticlockwise from the top right: I (+, +), II (−, +), III (−, −), IV (+, −).

teach.idea: The two axes cut the plane into four quadrants, numbered anticlockwise from the top right. The signs of x and y tell which one a point is in.
teach.method: Look at the sign of x (right +, left −) and of y (up +, down −). (+, +) is I, (−, +) is II, (−, −) is III, (+, −) is IV.

alternatives.title: Sketch it
text: Draw two crossing lines and mark I, II, III, IV anticlockwise starting top right.
Move right or left for x, up or down for y, and see where you land.

families.title: Moving on a grid
explanations: axes-swapped (conceptual): The left–right move was added to y and the up–down move to x. Moving right or left changes x; moving up or down changes y.
direction-ignored (prerequisite): A move left or down was added. Moving left or down makes the coordinate smaller.

teach.idea: Moving right or left changes only the x-coordinate; moving up or down changes only the y-coordinate. Right and up add; left and down take away.
teach.method: Add the across move to x (subtract for left). Add the up move to y (subtract for down). Write the new (x, y).

alternatives.title: Plot the start and walk
text: Mark the starting point on a grid.
Count the squares across, then up or down, and read off the point where you stop.

families.title: The third angle of a triangle
explanations: used-360 (recall): The angles were taken from 360°. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°; 360° is the sum around a point or in a quadrilateral.
added (procedural): The two angles were added, but the third angle is what is left over from 180° after them.
one-angle-only (procedural): Only one of the two angles was taken from 180°. Both known angles must be taken away.

teach.idea: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°: tear off the corners and they fit together on a straight line.
teach.method: Add the two angles you know, then take the sum from 180°.

alternatives.title: Tear off the corners
text: Cut out a paper triangle, tear off its three corners and place them side by side.
They make a straight line, which is 180°.

alternatives.title: Count on to 180
text: Start from the sum of the two angles and count up to 180 in easy jumps (to the next ten, then tens).
The total of the jumps is the third angle.

families.title: The exterior angle of a triangle
explanations: third-interior (conceptual): The third interior angle was found instead. The exterior angle sits outside, next to that angle, on the straight line.
one-angle (procedural): Only one of the opposite angles was used. The exterior angle equals the sum of both interior opposite angles.
exterior-as-interior (conceptual): The exterior angle was used as if it were inside the triangle (180° − 101° − 78°). The exterior angle equals the two opposite interior angles together.
added (procedural): The two angles were added. The exterior angle is the sum, so the missing part is the difference.
adjacent-interior (conceptual): The interior angle next to the exterior angle was found (180° − exterior). The question asks for the other opposite angle.

teach.idea: An exterior angle and the interior angle next to it make a straight line (180°), and the three interior angles also make 180°, so the exterior angle equals the two far interior angles together.
teach.method: To find the exterior angle, add the two interior opposite angles. To find one of those, subtract the other from the exterior angle.

alternatives.title: Go through the third angle
text: Find the third interior angle with the angle sum (180° minus the other two).
The exterior angle is 180° minus that third angle, because they lie on a straight line.

families.title: Angles of an isosceles triangle
explanations: not-halved (procedural): 180° − 160° = 20° is shared by the two equal angles, so each one is half of it.
all-equal (conceptual): All three angles were taken to be equal. In an isosceles triangle only the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
one-base-angle (procedural): Only one 85° angle was taken from 180°. There are two equal angles of 85°.
halved (procedural): The remaining angle was halved, but here only one angle (the third) is missing.

teach.idea: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the two equal sides are equal; with the angle sum of 180°, one angle tells you the other two.
teach.method: Vertex angle known: take it from 180° and halve. Base angle known: double it and take that from 180°.

alternatives.title: Fold it in half
text: Fold an isosceles triangle along the line from the top to the middle of the base: the two halves match.
So the two base angles are the same size.

families.title: How long can the third side be?
explanations: equal-allowed (conceptual): A third side of 40 cm was allowed. If it equals 20 + 20, the two sides lie flat along it and there is no triangle: it must be shorter.
longest-given (conceptual): The third side was thought not to be longer than 20 cm. It can be longer, as long as it is less than 19 + 20.
any-length (conceptual): It was thought any length will do. The two shorter sides together must be longer than the longest side, so the third side must be more than 20 − 19.

teach.idea: In a triangle, any two sides together are longer than the third. So the third side is less than the sum of the other two and more than their difference.
teach.method: Longest: one less than the sum of the two sides. Shortest: one more than their difference (for whole numbers).

alternatives.title: Try it with sticks
text: Hold two sticks at a hinge. Open them wide: the gap grows but never reaches their total length.
Close them up: the gap shrinks but never reaches their difference.

families.title: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles
explanations: alphabetical-match (conceptual): P, Q, R were matched with A, B, C in alphabetical order. The order of the letters in the congruence statement shows the matching: the first letters match, the second letters match, and the third letters match.

teach.idea: When ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, the letters are written in matching order: A goes with X, B with Y, C with Z. Matching parts are equal.
teach.method: Write the two names one above the other. Find the asked letters in the second name, read the letters above them in the first name, and use that side or angle.

alternatives.title: Stack the names
text: Write A B C on one line and the second triangle's name under it.
Each column is a matching pair of vertices; a side is two columns.

alternatives.title: Trace and place
text: Imagine tracing triangle ABC and placing the tracing exactly on the other triangle.
Each vertex lands on its matching vertex, so matching sides lie on top of each other.

families.title: Angles made by a transversal with parallel lines
explanations: supplementary-for-equal (conceptual): The vertically opposite angle was taken from 180°. With parallel lines, vertically opposite angles are equal.
equal-for-supplementary (conceptual): The linear pair angle was taken to be equal. Angles in a linear pair add up to 180°.

teach.idea: A transversal crosses parallel lines at the same slant, so the angles at the two crossings repeat: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, and co-interior angles add to 180°.
teach.method: Decide whether the two angles are the same 'shape' (equal: corresponding, alternate, vertically opposite) or together make a straight line (add to 180°: co-interior, linear pair).

alternatives.title: F, Z and C shapes
text: Corresponding angles sit in an F shape, alternate angles in a Z shape: they are equal.
Co-interior angles sit inside a C (or U) shape: they add up to 180°.

alternatives.title: Slide one crossing onto the other
text: Slide the upper crossing along the transversal until it lies on the lower one.
Because the lines are parallel the angles match exactly: that is why corresponding angles are equal.

families.title: Finding x from angles at parallel lines
explanations: gave-angle (procedural): The size of an angle was given instead of x. Once x is found, the angle is 5x + 30 worked out, but the question asks for x.
supplementary-for-equal (conceptual): The two angles were added to make 180°. Alternate angles at parallel lines are equal.
equal-for-supplementary (conceptual): The two angles were set equal. Co-interior angles at parallel lines add up to 180°.

teach.idea: The angle facts become equations: alternate angles give 'angle = angle', co-interior angles give 'angle + angle = 180'.
teach.method: Write the equation from the angle fact, collect the x terms and the numbers, and divide. Then check both angles with your x.

alternatives.title: Check the angles
text: Put your x into both expressions to get the two angles.
Alternate angles must come out equal; co-interior angles must add to 180°.

families.title: A missing side of a right triangle
explanations: added-sides (conceptual): The two sides were added. The theorem adds the squares of the sides, then takes the square root.
no-square-root (procedural): 9409 − 4225 = 5184 is the square of the side; its square root is the length.
subtracted-sides (conceptual): The sides were subtracted. Subtract the squares, then take the square root.

teach.idea: In a right-angled triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides (Baudhayana's rule for the diagonal of a rectangle).
teach.method: Hypotenuse: add the squares of the two shorter sides and take the square root. Shorter side: subtract the square of the known shorter side from the square of the hypotenuse, then take the square root.

alternatives.title: Squares on the sides
text: Draw a square on each side of the triangle. The two smaller squares together have the same area as the big one.
So the area of the big square is a² + b², and its side is the square root.

alternatives.title: Spot a triple
text: Many whole-number right triangles are multiples of 3-4-5, 5-12-13 or 8-15-17.
Divide the sides by a common factor, recognise the triple, then scale back.

families.title: The missing angle at a point of a tiling
explanations: exterior-for-interior (prerequisite): The angle of each polygon was taken as 360° ÷ (number of sides), which is its exterior angle. A tile's corner is the interior angle, 180° − 360° ÷ n.
straight-line (recall): The corners were made to add up to 180°. Angles all the way round a point add up to 360°.
not-shared (procedural): The whole gap was given as one corner. Two equal tiles share the gap, so each corner is half of it.

teach.idea: Tiles fit around a point with no gaps or overlaps only when their corner angles add up to exactly 360°.
teach.method: Find each regular polygon's interior angle (180° − 360° ÷ number of sides), add the angles already at the point, and take the total from 360°; share the gap if more than one tile fills it.

alternatives.title: Know the polygon angles
text: Triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°, octagon 135°, decagon 144°, dodecagon 150°.
Squares (4 × 90°), triangles (6 × 60°) and hexagons (3 × 120°) tile on their own; pentagons do not, since 360 ÷ 108 is not whole.

alternatives.title: Split into triangles
text: A polygon with n sides splits into n − 2 triangles from one corner, so its angles add up to (n − 2) × 180°.
In a regular polygon all n corners are equal: divide by n.

families.title: The missing angle of a polygon
explanations: n-triangles (conceptual): The angle sum was taken as 8 × 180°. An octagon splits into 6 triangles from one corner, so its angles add to 1080°.
assumed-regular (conceptual): The angle sum was shared equally, as if the octagon were regular; its angles are not all equal, so take the given angles away from 1080°.
sum-not-subtracted (procedural): The angle sum 1080° was found, but the given angles were not taken away from it.

teach.idea: From one corner, the diagonals cut a polygon with n sides into n − 2 triangles, and each triangle's angles add to 180°. So the angles of the polygon add to (n − 2) × 180°.
teach.method: Find the angle sum (n − 2) × 180°, add the angles you know, and take that total from the angle sum.

alternatives.title: Walk around the edge
text: Walk around the polygon: at each corner you turn through 180° minus the angle there.
One full walk turns you once round, 360°. Add the turns you know; the last turn is what is left of 360°, and the last angle is 180° minus that turn.

families.title: Angle sums and regular polygons
explanations: n-triangles (conceptual): 36 triangles were counted; from one corner a polygon with 36 sides splits into 34 triangles.
always-360 (conceptual): The angle sum was taken as 360° for every polygon; that is only true for quadrilaterals.
forgot-add-two (procedural): 6120 ÷ 180 = 34 gives the number of triangles; the polygon has 2 more sides than that.
add-one (procedural): One was added instead of two: sides = triangles + 2.
exterior-for-interior (conceptual): 360° ÷ 36 is each exterior angle (the turn at a corner); the interior angle is 180° minus it.
sum-not-shared (procedural): The angle sum was found but not shared among the 36 equal angles.
half-turn (conceptual): 180° was divided; walking once round a polygon turns through 360°.
exterior-as-interior (conceptual): 10° was treated as the inside angle; it is the exterior angle, the turn at each corner.

teach.idea: A polygon with n sides splits into n − 2 triangles from one corner, so its angles add to (n − 2) × 180°. In a regular polygon all the angles are equal, and the turns at the corners (exterior angles) add to 360°.
teach.method: For the sum, work out (n − 2) × 180°. For one angle of a regular polygon, divide the sum by n (or take 360° ÷ n from 180°). For the number of sides, divide 360° by the exterior angle.

alternatives.title: Build a table
text: Triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°, pentagon 540°: each new side adds one more triangle, 180° more.
Continue the pattern to the number of sides you need.

families.title: Euler's formula F + V − E = 2
explanations: forgot-two (procedural): The 2 in F + V − E = 2 was forgotten: V = E − F + 2.
two-wrong-way (procedural): The 2 was added instead of taken away: from F + V − E = 2, E = F + V − 2.
added-all (procedural): The faces were added to the edges; V = 2 + E − F.

teach.idea: For every polyhedron without holes, faces + vertices − edges = 2. Knowing any two of the counts gives the third.
teach.method: Write F + V − E = 2, put in the two numbers you know, and solve for the third.

alternatives.title: Check it on a cube first
text: A cube has 6 faces, 8 vertices and 12 edges: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.
Use the same pattern with the numbers in the question: the answer must make F + V − E come to 2.

families.title: Faces, edges and vertices of prisms and pyramids, from a name or a net
explanations: ends-forgotten (conceptual): Only the side faces were counted; a prism also has two end faces.
side-edges-forgotten (conceptual): Only the edges round the two ends were counted; there are also 10 edges joining the ends.
net-sides-counted (conceptual): Every corner of every piece of the net was counted; when the net folds up, several corners meet at each vertex.
one-end-only (conceptual): Only the corners of one end were counted; the other end has just as many.
base-forgotten (conceptual): Only the triangular faces were counted; the base is a face too.
base-edges-only (conceptual): Only the edges round the base were counted; 10 more edges go up to the top point.
apex-forgotten (conceptual): The top point (apex) was forgotten; it is a vertex too.

teach.idea: A prism has two equal ends joined by rectangles; a pyramid has one base and triangles meeting at a top point. The shape of the end or base tells you all the counts.
teach.method: For a prism on an n-sided end: n + 2 faces, 3n edges (n round each end and n joining them), 2n vertices. For a pyramid on an n-sided base: n + 1 faces, 2n edges, n + 1 vertices.

alternatives.title: Fold the net in your mind
text: Each piece of the net becomes one face.
When the net folds, sides of two pieces meet to make one edge, so the solid has half as many edges as the pieces have sides.

families.title: The fourth angle of a quadrilateral
explanations: angle-left-out (procedural): Only two of the three given angles were taken from 360°; all three (170°, 85° and 40°) must be taken away.
total-given (procedural): The three angles were added, but the total was not taken from 360°.

teach.idea: A diagonal cuts a quadrilateral into two triangles, so its four angles add to 2 × 180° = 360°.
teach.method: Add the three angles you know and take the total from 360°.

alternatives.title: Tear off the corners
text: Cut out a four-sided shape and tear off its four corners.
Put the corners together point to point: they make a full turn, 360°.

families.title: Angles of a parallelogram or rhombus
explanations: all-equal (conceptual): All the angles were taken to be equal; only opposite angles are equal. Neighbouring angles add to 180° because AB is parallel to DC.
neighbours-360 (conceptual): Neighbouring angles were taken to add to 360°; it is all four angles that add to 360°, and two neighbours add to 180°.
rhombus-square (conceptual): A rhombus was treated as a square; its sides are equal but its angles need not be right angles.
opposite-supplementary (conceptual): Opposite angles were taken to add to 180°; in a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and neighbouring angles add to 180°.

teach.idea: In a parallelogram (a rhombus is one), opposite sides are parallel, so neighbouring angles add to 180° and opposite angles are equal.
teach.method: Decide whether the angle you want is opposite ∠A (then it equals ∠A) or next to ∠A (then it is 180° − ∠A).

alternatives.title: See the parallel lines
text: AD and BC are parallel, and AB crosses them.
∠A and ∠B are co-interior angles between parallel lines, so they add to 180°. Going round, ∠C comes back to the same size as ∠A.

families.title: Diagonals of rectangles and parallelograms
explanations: whole-diagonal (procedural): The whole diagonal was given; the diagonals of a rectangle are equal and cut each other in half, so OB is half of BD.
side-for-half-diagonal (conceptual): The side AB was used; OB is half of the diagonal BD, not a side.
diagonals-equal (conceptual): The diagonals of a parallelogram were taken to be equal; they cut each other in half but need not be equal (that is only true in a rectangle).
not-doubled (procedural): OA is only half of AC; O is the midpoint of AC.
added-halves (procedural): OA and OB were added; they lie on different diagonals. AC = OA + OC = 2 × OA.

teach.idea: The diagonals of every parallelogram cut each other in half. In a rectangle they are also equal in length.
teach.method: Mark O as the midpoint of each diagonal. For a rectangle, BD = AC, so OB = AC ÷ 2. For a parallelogram, AC = 2 × OA.

alternatives.title: Fold and measure
text: Draw a rectangle and both diagonals, then fold the paper so A lands on C: the crease passes through O, the middle of AC.
Measure OA, OB, OC and OD: in a rectangle all four are equal.

families.title: Map scale: 1 cm stands for k km
explanations: divided (conceptual): The map distance was divided by 50; every 1 cm on the map is 50 km, so multiply.
multiplied (conceptual): The real distance was multiplied by 50; the map is smaller, so divide by 50.
added (conceptual): 50 was added; each of the 15 centimetres stands for 50 km.
subtracted (conceptual): 50 was taken away; find how many lots of 50 km make the distance.

teach.idea: A map scale says how much real distance each centimetre on the map stands for; distances on the map and on the ground are in the same proportion.
teach.method: Map to real: multiply the map length by the scale. Real to map: divide the real distance by the scale.

alternatives.title: A ratio table
text: Write 1 cm → k km in the first column.
Scale both sides by the same number to reach the length you know, then read the other side.

families.title: Ratio scales 1 : n with unit conversion
explanations: not-converted (procedural): The length was found in centimetres but not changed to kilometres (100 000 cm = 1 km).
thousand-for-hundred (recall): It was divided by 1000; 100 cm make 1 m.
thousand-for-km (recall): It was divided by 1000; 1 km = 1000 m = 100 000 cm.
metres-only (procedural): The centimetres were changed to metres but not on to kilometres.

teach.idea: A scale 1 : n means every length in the real world is n times the length on the drawing, in the same unit.
teach.method: Multiply the drawing length by n to get centimetres, then change units: ÷ 100 for metres, ÷ 100 000 for kilometres.

alternatives.title: What does 1 cm stand for?
text: Change the scale first: 1 : 50 000 means 1 cm stands for 50 000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km.
Then multiply by the number of centimetres on the drawing.

families.title: Volume of a cuboid or cube from its edges
explanations: added-edges (conceptual): The edges were added; volume multiplies length, width and height.
one-layer (conceptual): Only the base (length × width) was found; there are as many layers as the height.
surface-for-volume (conceptual): The area of the outside faces was found; volume measures the space inside.

teach.idea: Volume counts how many 1 cm cubes fill a solid. One layer on the base holds length × width cubes, and there are as many layers as the height.
teach.method: Volume = length × width × height. For a cube with edge a, volume = a × a × a = a³.

alternatives.title: Count in layers
text: Imagine filling the box with 1 cm cubes: the bottom layer is a rectangle of cubes, length × width.
Stack the same layer once for every centimetre of height.

families.title: Capacity of a tank in litres
explanations: cm3-not-litres (procedural): The volume in cm³ was given; 1000 cm³ make 1 litre, so divide by 1000.
hundred-for-thousand (recall): It was divided by 100; 1 litre is 1000 cm³.
m3-not-litres (procedural): The volume in m³ was given; each m³ holds 1000 litres.

teach.idea: Capacity is volume measured in litres. A 10 cm cube holds exactly 1 litre (1000 cm³), and a 1 m cube holds 1000 litres.
teach.method: Find the volume (length × width × height), then change units: cm³ ÷ 1000 = litres; m³ × 1000 = litres.

alternatives.title: Count litre cubes
text: A 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm cube holds 1 litre.
Count how many such cubes fit along each edge, and multiply the three counts.

families.title: Packing cubes into a box
explanations: volume-divided (conceptual): The box's volume was divided by a cube's volume; that counts cut pieces of cubes too. Count how many whole cubes fit along each edge instead.
rounded-up (procedural): A part of a cube was counted as a whole one; only whole cubes fit, so round each count down.

teach.idea: Only whole cubes fit, so a gap smaller than a cube is wasted. Count whole cubes along each edge first.
teach.method: Divide each edge of the box by the cube's edge and drop any remainder; multiply the three whole numbers.

alternatives.title: Build one layer
text: Fill the floor of the box: (cubes along) × (cubes across).
Then see how many such layers fit in the height, rounding down.

families.title: Area of a triangle from base and height
explanations: no-half (conceptual): Base × height gives the rectangle around the triangle; the triangle is half of it.
added (conceptual): Base and height were added; area multiplies them and then halves.

teach.idea: A triangle is exactly half of a rectangle (or parallelogram) with the same base and height.
teach.method: Area = ½ × base × height. Multiply the base by the height and halve the result.

alternatives.title: Half a rectangle
text: Draw the rectangle with the same base and height around the triangle.
The diagonal cuts it into two equal triangles, so each is half the rectangle's area.

families.title: A missing base or height of a triangle
explanations: not-doubled (conceptual): The area was divided by 20 without doubling it first; area = ½ × base × height, so the other length is 2 × area ÷ 20.
subtracted (conceptual): The known length was taken from the area; area and length are linked by multiplying, so undo it by dividing.

teach.idea: Area = ½ × base × height, so twice the area is base × height: the area of the matching rectangle.
teach.method: Double the area, then divide by the length you know.

alternatives.title: Write an equation
text: Write ½ × base × height = area with a letter for the missing length.
Multiply both sides by 2, then divide by the known length.

families.title: Circumference of a circle
explanations: radius-as-diameter (procedural): π × radius was found; the circumference is π × diameter = 2πr.
area-for-circumference (conceptual): πr² is the area (the space inside); the circumference is the distance around, 2πr.
doubled-diameter (procedural): The diameter was doubled again; C = π × diameter, or 2 × π × radius.

teach.idea: In every circle, the distance around (the circumference) divided by the diameter is the same number, π (about 22/7 or 3.14).
teach.method: C = π × diameter = 2 × π × radius. Double the radius first if you are given the radius.

alternatives.title: Measure with a string
text: Wrap a string around a bangle or a lid and lay it flat against a ruler.
It is a little more than 3 diameters long: that number is π.

families.title: Area of a circle
explanations: circumference-for-area (conceptual): 2πr is the circumference (the distance around); the area is πr².
diameter-squared (procedural): The diameter was squared; the formula uses the radius, half the diameter.
not-squared (procedural): π × r was found; the radius must be squared (r × r).

teach.idea: Cut a circle into many thin slices and lay them head to tail: they make a shape close to a rectangle, half the circumference (πr) long and r high. So the area is πr × r = πr².
teach.method: Find the radius (half the diameter), square it, and multiply by π.

alternatives.title: Compare with squares
text: Draw the square on the radius: its area is r².
The circle covers a little more than 3 of these squares — exactly π of them.

families.title: Distance travelled by a wheel
explanations: cm-not-m (procedural): The distance was left in centimetres; 100 cm = 1 m.
radius-for-diameter (procedural): The diameter was used as if it were the radius (2 × π × diameter); one turn rolls π × diameter.
one-turn (conceptual): Only one turn was counted; each turn rolls one circumference.
m-not-cm (procedural): Metres were divided by centimetres; change the distance to centimetres first.
diameter-for-circumference (conceptual): The distance was divided by the diameter; each turn rolls the circumference, π × diameter.

teach.idea: In one full turn, a wheel rolls a distance equal to its circumference, π × diameter.
teach.method: Distance = circumference × number of turns; turns = distance ÷ circumference. Keep the units the same (change m to cm or cm to m).

alternatives.title: Mark and roll
text: Put a chalk mark on a wheel and roll it until the mark touches the ground again.
The gap between the two marks on the ground is the circumference.

families.title: Arc length, area and perimeter of a sector
explanations: area-for-arc (conceptual): The area formula (πr²) was used; the arc is part of the circumference, 2πr.
whole-circle (conceptual): The whole circle's area was given; the sector is only 300/360 of it.
over-180 (procedural): The angle was divided by 180; a full circle is 360°.
arc-for-area (conceptual): The arc-length formula (2πr) was used; area uses πr².
radii-forgotten (procedural): Only the arc was found; the perimeter of a sector also has the two straight radii.
one-radius (procedural): Only one radius was added; a sector has two straight edges.

teach.idea: A sector with angle θ is θ/360 of the whole circle, so its arc is θ/360 of the circumference and its area is θ/360 of the circle's area.
teach.method: Arc = θ/360 × 2πr; area = θ/360 × πr²; perimeter = arc + 2r.

alternatives.title: Think of a clock face
text: 90° is a quarter of a full turn, so a 90° sector is a quarter of the circle; 60° is a sixth.
Find the whole circle's circumference or area, then take that fraction of it.

families.title: Area of a circular path (a ring)
explanations: width-squared (conceptual): π × width² (or π(R − r)²) was found; the path is the big circle minus the small one, π(R² − r²): square each radius first.
outer-only (procedural): The area of the big circle was found but the garden was not taken away.

teach.idea: A ring is a big circle with a small circle taken out of the middle.
teach.method: Outer radius R = inner radius + width. Area of the path = πR² − πr² = π(R² − r²).

alternatives.title: Two circles
text: Work out the area of the whole circle including the path.
Work out the area of the garden alone, then subtract.

families.title: Area and perimeter of a parallelogram
explanations: slant-for-height (conceptual): The slanting side was used; the height is the straight-up distance between the parallel sides.
halved (conceptual): The answer was halved as for a triangle; for a parallelogram area = base × height, so height = area ÷ base.
subtracted (conceptual): The base was taken from the area; divide the area by the base.
two-sides (procedural): Only two sides were added; a parallelogram has four sides, two of each length.
height-for-side (conceptual): The height was used for the slanting sides; the perimeter goes along the sides.
area-for-perimeter (conceptual): The area was found; the perimeter is the distance around.

teach.idea: Cut a triangle off one end of a parallelogram and slide it to the other end: it becomes a rectangle with the same base and height.
teach.method: Area = base × height (the height is at right angles to the base, not the slanting side). Perimeter = 2 × (base + slanting side).

alternatives.title: Cut and slide
text: Draw the parallelogram on squared paper and draw its height from one top corner.
Cut off the triangle and move it to the other side: count the squares of the rectangle you made.

families.title: Area of a rhombus from its diagonals
explanations: not-doubled (conceptual): The area was divided by 30 without doubling it first; area = ½ × d₁ × d₂.
subtracted (conceptual): The diagonal was taken from the area; undo the multiplying by dividing.
no-half (conceptual): The diagonals were multiplied but not halved; the rhombus fills half of the rectangle drawn round it.
added (conceptual): The diagonals were added; the area is half their product.

teach.idea: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at right angles and cut it into four equal right triangles; together they fill half of the rectangle d₁ by d₂.
teach.method: Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂. To find a missing diagonal, double the area and divide by the diagonal you know.

alternatives.title: Four triangles
text: Each of the four triangles has sides d₁/2 and d₂/2 at the right angle.
Each has area ½ × d₁/2 × d₂/2; four of them make ½ × d₁ × d₂.

families.title: Total surface area of a cuboid or cube
explanations: three-faces (procedural): Only three faces were added; each face has an equal face opposite it, so double the total.
volume (conceptual): The volume was found; surface area is the total area of the six faces.
walls-only (procedural): Only the four side faces were added; the top and bottom count too.

teach.idea: A cuboid has six rectangular faces in three matching pairs: top and bottom, front and back, two ends.
teach.method: Total surface area = 2(lw + wh + hl). For a cube with edge a, it is 6a².

alternatives.title: Unfold into a net
text: Unfold the box flat: it makes six rectangles.
Find each rectangle's area and add all six.

families.title: Area of the four walls of a room (lateral surface area)
explanations: two-walls (procedural): Only two walls were counted; a room has four walls, two of each size.
with-floor (procedural): The floor was added; the question asks for the four walls only.
total-surface (conceptual): Floor and ceiling were included; the walls are only the four sides.

teach.idea: Unrolled, the four walls of a room make one long rectangle: as long as the distance round the floor and as tall as the room.
teach.method: Lateral surface area = 2(l + w) × h.

alternatives.title: Wall by wall
text: Two walls are length × height; two walls are width × height.
Add all four.

families.title: Volume of a cylinder
explanations: curved-area (conceptual): 2πrh is the curved surface area; the volume is base area × height, πr²h.
not-squared (procedural): The radius was not squared: the base is a circle of area πr².
diameter-squared (procedural): The diameter was squared; use the radius, half the diameter.

teach.idea: A cylinder is a stack of equal circles, like a pile of coins: the volume is the area of one circle times the height.
teach.method: Volume = πr²h. Halve the diameter first if you are given it.

alternatives.title: Like a prism
text: For a cuboid, volume = base area × height.
A cylinder works the same way; only the base is a circle (πr²).

families.title: Curved and total surface area of a cylinder
explanations: forgot-two (procedural): πrh was found; the curved surface unrolls to a rectangle as long as the circumference, 2πr.
volume (conceptual): The volume (πr²h) was found; the curved surface is an area, 2πrh.
no-ends (procedural): Only the curved surface was found; a closed cylinder also has a top and a bottom circle.
one-end (procedural): Only one circle was added; a closed cylinder has two, top and bottom.

teach.idea: Cut the curved surface of a cylinder straight down and unroll it: it is a rectangle, as long as the circumference (2πr) and as tall as the cylinder.
teach.method: Curved surface area = 2πrh. Total surface area = 2πrh + 2πr² = 2πr(h + r).

alternatives.title: Peel the label
text: Peel the paper label off a can and lay it flat: it is a rectangle.
Its length went once round the can, so it equals the circumference.

families.title: Area of a trapezium
explanations: no-half (conceptual): The sum of the parallel sides × height was not halved; two copies of the trapezium make that parallelogram.
long-side-only (conceptual): Only the longer parallel side was used, as for a rectangle; the trapezium is narrower at the top, so use the average of the two sides.

teach.idea: Two copies of a trapezium, one turned upside down, fit together into a parallelogram with base (a + b) and the same height. The trapezium is half of it.
teach.method: Area = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height.

alternatives.title: Split into pieces
text: Draw a diagonal: the trapezium becomes two triangles with the same height, bases a and b.
Add their areas: ½ × a × h + ½ × b × h.

families.title: Area and perimeter of an L-shape
explanations: whole-rectangle (procedural): The whole rectangle was found but the cut-out corner was not taken away.
perimeter-for-area (conceptual): The sides were added (the perimeter); area counts the squares inside.
added-cut (procedural): The cut-out was added instead of taken away.
cut-shortens (conceptual): Cutting the corner was thought to shorten the perimeter; the two new edges (11 cm and 2 cm) replace exactly the edges that were removed.
area-for-perimeter (conceptual): The area was found; the perimeter is the distance around the edge.
missed-side (procedural): One of the six sides was missed; go all the way round.

teach.idea: An L-shape is a big rectangle with a small rectangle taken away. Its area is less than the big rectangle's, but its perimeter is the same: the two new edges replace the two that were cut off.
teach.method: Area = big rectangle − cut-out. Perimeter: add all six sides (here it equals 2 × (width + height) of the big rectangle).

alternatives.title: Split into two rectangles
text: Draw one line to split the L into two rectangles.
Find each rectangle's area and add them.

families.title: Area of a rectangular path
explanations: width-once (procedural): The path width was taken off only once; the path is on both sides, so the inner rectangle is 26 m by 16 m.
corners-missed (conceptual): The four strips along the sides were found, but the four corner squares were missed.
outer-only (procedural): The outer rectangle was found but the garden was not taken away.
corners-twice (conceptual): The four strips along the sides were added, so the corner squares were counted twice.
inner-only (procedural): The inner rectangle (the part without the path) was given.

teach.idea: A path around (or inside) a rectangle is the space between two rectangles: the bigger one minus the smaller one.
teach.method: Outside path: (L + 2x)(W + 2x) − LW. Inside path: LW − (L − 2x)(W − 2x). The width is added (or taken off) on both sides.

alternatives.title: Strips and corners
text: Split an outside path into two long strips (L by x), two short strips (W by x) and four corner squares (x by x).
Add them all: do not forget the corners.

families.title: Multiplying decimals
explanations: points-lined-up (procedural): The decimal point was placed as in addition (lined up); in a product, the decimal places of both numbers are added.
point-ignored (procedural): The digits were multiplied but the decimal point was left out.
one-place-off (procedural): The point was moved one place too far; the answer has 2 decimal places.

teach.idea: Tenths times tenths make hundredths (0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01), so the answer has as many decimal places as the two numbers together.
teach.method: Multiply the numbers as if there were no decimal points, count the decimal places in both, and give the answer that many decimal places. Estimate to check (e.g. 1.9 × 3.1 is about 2 × 3 = 6).

alternatives.title: Use fractions
text: Write each decimal as a fraction: 0.7 × 1.3 = 7/10 × 13/10.

families.title: Dividing decimals
explanations: divisor-only-shifted (procedural): The divisor was made a whole number (× 100) but the dividend was not multiplied by the same amount.
point-wrong-way (procedural): The decimal point was moved the wrong way; check with an estimate.
one-place-off (procedural): The decimal point in the answer is one place out; line up the point in the quotient with the dividend's point.

teach.idea: Multiplying both numbers in a division by the same amount does not change the answer (12 ÷ 4 = 120 ÷ 40), so you can make the divisor a whole number first.
teach.method: Move the decimal point in the divisor to make it whole, move the dividend's point the same number of places, then divide as usual, keeping the point in line.

alternatives.title: Check by multiplying
text: Estimate first: 7.2 ÷ 0.8 is like 72 ÷ 8.
Check: the answer × the divisor must give the dividend.

families.title: Multiplying and dividing decimals by 10, 100 and 1000
explanations: wrong-way (conceptual): The point was moved the wrong way; multiplying makes the number bigger, so the point moves right.
places-off (procedural): The point was moved the wrong number of places; 100 has 2 zeros, so move it 2 places.

teach.idea: Multiplying by 10 makes each digit worth ten times as much, so every digit moves one place to the left; dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right.
teach.method: Count the zeros in 10, 100 or 1000 and move the decimal point that many places: right for ×, left for ÷. Fill empty places with zeros.

alternatives.title: A place-value table
text: Write the number in a place-value table (hundreds, tens, ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths).
Slide every digit across one column for each zero; the point stays where it is.

families.title: Multiplying fractions and mixed numbers
explanations: cross-multiplied (procedural): The fractions were cross-multiplied (top × other bottom); to multiply fractions, multiply top by top and bottom by bottom.
added (conceptual): The fractions were added; 'of' and '×' mean multiply.
whole-kept-apart (procedural): Only the fraction part was multiplied and 2 was kept as it was; change the mixed number to an improper fraction first (2 11/12 = 35/12).

teach.idea: a/b × c/d means c/d of a/b: cutting each of the b pieces into d smaller ones makes pieces of size 1/(b × d), and you take a × c of them.
teach.method: Change mixed numbers to improper fractions, multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms, and simplify.

alternatives.title: Area model
text: Draw a square. Shade a/b of it across and c/d of it down.
The part shaded both ways is the product: a × c small rectangles out of b × d.

families.title: Dividing fractions using reciprocals
explanations: no-flip (procedural): The fractions were multiplied without turning the second one upside down; dividing by c/d is multiplying by d/c.
flipped-first (procedural): The first fraction was turned upside down instead of the second; only the divisor is replaced by its reciprocal.
multiplied-by-whole (conceptual): The fraction was multiplied by 8; sharing into 8 equal parts makes each part smaller.

teach.idea: Dividing asks 'how many lots of the divisor fit?'. Dividing by c/d is the same as multiplying by d/c, its reciprocal, because c/d × d/c = 1.
teach.method: Keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, turn the second fraction upside down, then multiply and simplify.

alternatives.title: Same-size pieces
text: Write both fractions with the same denominator: 3/4 ÷ 1/8 = 6/8 ÷ 1/8.
