Now count: how many 1-eighths fit in 6-eighths? 6.

families.title: Adding and subtracting integers
explanations: negatives-make-positive (conceptual): Two negatives were taken to make a positive; that rule is for multiplying. Adding two debts makes a bigger debt.
minus-negative-as-minus (conceptual): Taking away (−11) was done as taking away 11; subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its opposite.
sign-lost (procedural): The size is right but the sign is wrong; check which way you moved on the number line.
sizes-added (conceptual): The sizes were added; with one positive and one negative number, they cancel, so find the difference of the sizes.
difference-of-sizes (procedural): 33 was taken off towards zero; subtracting a positive number moves left on the number line, further below zero.

teach.idea: On a number line, adding a positive number moves right and adding a negative number moves left. Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite.
teach.method: Change any subtraction into adding the opposite. Same signs: add the sizes and keep the sign. Different signs: subtract the sizes and take the sign of the larger size.

alternatives.title: Positive and negative tokens
text: Use + tokens and − tokens; a + and a − together make zero and can be removed.
To take away tokens you do not have, first add zero pairs (+ and −), then remove what you need.

families.title: Integer differences in temperature and height
explanations: ignored-negative (conceptual): −1 was treated as 1; going from −1 up to 0 is 1 steps, then on to 20.
sizes-added (conceptual): The sizes were added; both values are below zero, so the gap is the difference of the sizes.

teach.idea: The change from one value to another is end − start. On a number line it is the distance between the two points, counting through zero.
teach.method: Subtract the start from the end; subtracting a negative start means adding its size.

alternatives.title: Go through zero
text: Count up from the start to 0, then from 0 to the end.
Add the two parts (when both values are below zero, just count the gap).

families.title: Ordering positive and negative integers
explanations: ignore-sign (conceptual): The numbers were ordered by their size without the minus sign. On the number line, −4 is to the left of −3, so −4 is smaller.
negatives-reversed (conceptual): Among the negative numbers, the one with the bigger digit was taken as bigger. −4 is further below zero than −3, so −4 is the smaller number.
decreasing (procedural): The numbers were written largest first; increasing order starts with the smallest.

teach.idea: On a number line, numbers get bigger as you move to the right. Every negative number is left of 0, and the further a negative number is from 0, the smaller it is.
teach.method: Mark the numbers on a number line, then read them from left to right.

alternatives.title: Think of a thermometer
text: −8 °C is colder than −3 °C: it is further below zero.
So start with the coldest (most negative) temperature and go up to the warmest.

families.title: Multiplying by a number near 100 using the distributive property
explanations: wrong-sign-correction (conceptual): 102 is 100 plus 2, so 99 × 2 must be added to 99 × 100.
correction-not-multiplied (procedural): Only 2 was added; every one of the 99 lots gains 2, so it is 99 × 2.
part-left-out (procedural): Only 99 × 100 was found; the 99 × 2 part was left out.

teach.idea: Multiplication spreads over addition and subtraction: k × (100 − 2) = k × 100 − k × 2.
teach.method: Write the number near 100 as 100 plus or minus a little, multiply k by each part, then add or take away.

alternatives.title: Split a rectangle
text: Think of k × 98 as the area of a rectangle k by 98.
It is a k by 100 rectangle with a k by 2 strip cut off: k × 100 − k × 2.

families.title: Removing brackets after a minus sign
explanations: sign-not-changed (conceptual): When brackets after a minus sign are removed, every sign inside changes: 99 − (49 + 10) = 99 − 49 − 10.
last-term-dropped (procedural): The 10 inside the brackets was forgotten after the brackets were removed.

teach.idea: Taking away a bracket takes away everything inside it: taking away (b − c) takes away b but gives c back.
teach.method: Remove the brackets and change the sign of every term inside, then group numbers that are easy to combine.

alternatives.title: Money in and out
text: Spending ₹47 and then getting ₹8 back is the same as spending ₹(47 − 8).

families.title: Writing a number as a product of primes
explanations: composite-left (procedural): The splitting stopped too early: 25 is not prime, so it can still be split into 5 × 5.
one-included (conceptual): 1 was written as a factor. 1 is not a prime number, so it is not part of the list.
repeat-missed (conceptual): Each prime was written only once. A prime must be written as many times as it divides the number.

teach.idea: Every whole number greater than 1 is either prime or can be split into primes in exactly one way (apart from order).
teach.method: Divide by the smallest prime that goes exactly (2, then 3, then 5 …) again and again until 1 is left. The divisors are the prime factors.

alternatives.title: A factor tree
text: Split the number into any two factors, for example 72 = 8 × 9.
Keep splitting every factor that is not prime: 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 and 9 = 3 × 3.
The primes at the ends of the branches are the answer: 2, 2, 2, 3, 3.

families.title: The smallest multiplier that makes a perfect square
explanations: itself (conceptual): 500 × 500 is a perfect square, but it is not the smallest; only the primes without a partner are needed.
largest-prime (procedural): The largest prime factor of 495 was used; the primes without a partner decide the multiplier, not the largest prime.
one-unpaired (procedural): Only one of the primes without a partner was used; every prime without a partner needs one more copy.

teach.idea: In a perfect square every prime factor comes in pairs, because the number is something times itself.
teach.method: Write the number as a product of primes and pair equal primes. Multiply together the primes that have no partner: that is the smallest multiplier.

alternatives.title: Even powers
text: Write the number in index form, for example 180 = 2² × 3² × 5.
A perfect square has only even powers, so multiply by each prime with an odd power once: here by 5.

families.title: A ratio in its simplest form
explanations: not-simplest (procedural): Both numbers were divided by 2, but they still have a common factor; divide by their highest common factor, 6.
order-reversed (conceptual): The ratio was written the other way round; the first quantity named comes first.
units-not-matched (conceptual): The two lengths were compared in different units. Change metres to centimetres first (1 m = 100 cm).

teach.idea: A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind. Dividing both by the same number gives an equal ratio, like an equivalent fraction.
teach.method: Make the units the same, then divide both numbers by their highest common factor.

alternatives.title: Equal groups
text: 18 : 24 means 18 of one thing for every 24 of another.
Make groups of 6: 3 groups and 4 groups. So for every 3 of the first there are 4 of the second: 3 : 4.

families.title: The missing term of an equivalent ratio
explanations: additive (conceptual): The same amount was added to both terms. Equivalent ratios multiply both terms by the same number (here 10).
scale-factor-given (procedural): 10 is how many times bigger the terms became; the missing term is 12 × 10.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (9 × 2) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Equivalent ratios are made by multiplying (or dividing) both terms by the same number, just like equivalent fractions.
teach.method: Find what the known term was multiplied by, then multiply the other term by the same number.

alternatives.title: A ratio table
text: Write the ratio in two rows: 2 | 3.
Keep doubling, tripling … both rows together: 4 | 6, 6 | 9, 8 | 12, until you reach the known number.

families.title: Finding a unit rate
explanations: multiplied (conceptual): The total was multiplied by 11. To find the amount for one, share the total equally: divide by 11.
subtracted (conceptual): 11 was taken away from the total; sharing equally means dividing.
division-slip (recall): A division step slipped. Check by multiplying back: the answer × 11 should give 1089.

teach.idea: A unit rate is the amount for one unit: one kilogram, one hour, one kilometre or one day.
teach.method: Divide the total by the number of units. Check by multiplying back.

alternatives.title: Share it out
text: Imagine the total being shared equally among the units, one by one.
Each unit gets the same amount: that amount is the rate.

families.title: The better buy by unit price
explanations: bigger-pack (conceptual): The bigger pack was taken to be the better value. A bigger pack is not always cheaper per item: compare the price of one soap.
price-difference (procedural): The difference between the two prices per soap was given; the question asks for the price of one soap in the better pack.
lower-total (conceptual): The pack with the lower total price was chosen. The packs hold different numbers of soaps, so compare the price of one soap.

teach.idea: To compare packs of different sizes, compare the same amount from each: the price of one item is the fairest comparison.
teach.method: Divide each pack's price by the number of items, then choose the lower price per item.

alternatives.title: Buy the same number
text: Find a number of soaps both packs can make, for example 12 from packs of 4 and 6.
Work out what 12 soaps cost using each pack, and see which is cheaper.

families.title: Time taken working together
explanations: add-days (conceptual): The days were added. Working together is faster than either alone, so the answer must be less than both.
average-days (conceptual): The average of the two times was found. Two people working together finish sooner than the faster one alone.
rate-not-inverted (procedural): The work done in one day (1/23 + 1/24) was given; the number of days is 1 divided by that.

teach.idea: Rates add: if Arun does 1/6 of the job each day and Bala 1/12, together they do 1/6 + 1/12 = 1/4 each day.
teach.method: Add the work done per day, then divide 1 whole job by that rate.

alternatives.title: Count pieces of a bigger job
text: Pretend the job has 12 pieces (a number both times divide).
In one day Arun does 12 ÷ 6 = 2 pieces and Bala 12 ÷ 12 = 1: together 3 pieces a day, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 days.

families.title: Laws of exponents with one base
explanations: reversed-subtraction (procedural): The powers were subtracted the wrong way round: it is the top power minus the bottom power.
added-exponents (procedural): The powers were added; that is the rule for multiplying, not dividing.
multiplied-exponents (conceptual): The powers were multiplied. aᵐ × aⁿ puts 12 factors and 8 factors together, so the powers add.
added-for-power (conceptual): The powers were added. (aᵐ)ⁿ is aᵐ written 6 times, so the powers multiply.
power-of-power (procedural): The first power was raised to the second; the powers simply multiply.
divided-exponents (conceptual): The powers were divided. Dividing cancels factors, so the powers subtract.

teach.idea: A power counts how many times the base is multiplied. Multiplying joins the factors (add the powers), dividing cancels them (subtract), and a power of a power repeats them (multiply).
teach.method: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. A negative power means a fraction: a⁻² = 1/a².

families.title: The units digit of a large power
explanations: multiplied (conceptual): The units digit 9 was multiplied by 19; a power multiplies 9 by itself 19 times.
last-digit-of-power (procedural): The last digit of the power (0) was used; use the remainder when 60 is divided by the length of the cycle.
remainder-zero (procedural): 60 divides exactly by the length of the cycle, so the answer is the LAST digit of the cycle, not 1.

teach.idea: Only the units digit affects the units digit of a product, and the units digits of powers repeat in a short cycle.
teach.method: Write the units digits of the first few powers until they repeat. Divide the power by the cycle length; the remainder tells the place in the cycle (remainder 0 means the last place).

alternatives.title: A table of units digits
text: Powers of 7: 7, 9, 3, 1, then 7 again: a cycle of 4.
7³⁰: 30 = 4 × 7 + 2, so it is the 2nd in the cycle: 9.

families.title: Zero and negative powers
explanations: negative-as-minus (conceptual): 10⁻⁴ was read as a negative number. A negative power means a fraction: 10⁻⁴ = 1/10⁴.
multiplied (conceptual): 10 was multiplied by −5. A power is repeated multiplication; a negative power is 1 over the positive power.
reciprocal-missed (procedural): The value of the positive power was given; a negative power turns it into 1 over that number.
sign-ignored (procedural): The powers were added as 5 + 2; the second power is −2, so it is 5 − 2.

teach.idea: Each step down in the power divides by the base once: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4.
teach.method: Combine the powers first (add them, keeping the signs), then a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.

alternatives.title: Keep dividing
text: Write the powers of the base in a row and divide by the base each time you go left.
The pattern shows a⁰ = 1 and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, never a negative number.

families.title: Crores and lakhs in millions
explanations: crore-is-million (conceptual): 1 crore was taken as 1 million. 1 million is 10 lakh, so 1 crore (100 lakh) is 10 million.
crore-hundred-million (recall): 1 crore was taken as 100 million; 1 crore is 10 million (and 100 crore is 1 billion).
lakh-is-million (conceptual): 1 lakh was taken as 1 million. 1 lakh is 1,00,000 = one hundred thousand; 10 lakh make a million.

teach.idea: Both systems use the same digits; only the grouping differs. 10 lakh = 1 million, and 1 crore = 10 million.
teach.method: Rewrite the number with international commas (groups of three: 34,000,000) and read the millions.

alternatives.title: Count the zeros
text: 1 lakh has 5 zeros, 1 million has 6, 1 crore has 7.
So 1 crore = 10 million, and 10 lakh = 1 million.

families.title: Multiplying integers
explanations: sign-rule (conceptual): A positive times a negative was made positive. The product of a positive and a negative number is negative.
added (conceptual): The two numbers were added instead of multiplied.
fact-slip (prerequisite): A multiplication fact (12 × 2) is not yet reliable.

teach.idea: Multiplying by a negative number reverses the direction: so a negative times a positive is negative, and a negative times a negative is positive.
teach.method: Multiply the sizes, then decide the sign: same signs give +, different signs give −.

alternatives.title: Follow a pattern
text: Keep going: −3 × (−1) = 3, −3 × (−2) = 6. A negative times a negative is positive.

families.title: Selling price or cost price from a profit or loss per cent
explanations: amount-only (procedural): Only the loss (40% of ₹1,000) was found; the selling price is the cost price minus it.
wrong-direction (conceptual): The loss was added. A profit means selling for more than the cost; a loss means selling for less.
applied-forward (procedural): The loss was applied to the selling price as if it were the cost price. Here the selling price is known and the cost price is the unknown.
percent-of-sp (conceptual): 40% of the selling price was added to it. Profit and loss per cent are of the COST price, so the selling price is 60% of the cost price: divide by 60 and multiply by 100.
percent-as-rupees (conceptual): 40% was used as ₹40; 40% of ₹1,000 means 40 out of every 100 rupees.

teach.idea: Profit or loss per cent compares the profit or loss with the cost price: 20% profit means the selling price is 120% of the cost price.
teach.method: To find the selling price, find p% of the cost price and add it (profit) or take it away (loss). To find the cost price, divide the selling price by (100 ± p) and multiply by 100.

alternatives.title: Think of 100 parts
text: Split the cost price into 100 equal parts.
With a 15% profit the selling price is 115 of those parts; with a 15% loss it is 85 parts.

families.title: Simple interest, amount, rate or time
explanations: no-hundred (conceptual): 13% means 13 out of 100, so divide by 100: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100.
one-year (procedural): Only one year's interest was added; the money is lent for 3 years.
amount-given (procedural): The amount (principal + interest) was given; the question asks for the interest only.
interest-only (procedural): Only the interest was found; the amount is the principal plus the interest.
time-forgotten (procedural): The interest is for 3 years; divide by the time too: R = SI × 100 ÷ (P × T).
one-year-interest (conceptual): One year's interest in rupees was given; the rate compares it with the principal, out of 100.
rate-and-time (conceptual): The interest was divided by the rate; divide it by one year's interest (P × R ÷ 100) to count the years.
year-interest-given (procedural): One year's interest was given; the time is how many years of that interest make the total.

teach.idea: Simple interest is the same every year: R% of the principal, so T years give T times as much. SI = P × R × T ÷ 100.
teach.method: Write SI = P × R × T ÷ 100, put in the three numbers you know, and work out the fourth.

alternatives.title: Year by year
text: Find one year's interest first: R% of P.
Add it once for every year. To find the time, count how many years of interest make the total.

families.title: Discount and GST
explanations: discount-only (procedural): Only the discount was found; the selling price is the marked price minus the discount.
wrong-direction (conceptual): The discount was added; a discount makes the price lower.
tax-only (procedural): Only the GST was found; the price including GST is the price plus the tax.
percent-as-rupees (conceptual): 50% was used as ₹50; 50% of ₹3,000 means 50 rupees for every 100 rupees.

teach.idea: A discount is a per cent of the marked price taken off; GST is a per cent of the price added on.
teach.method: Find the per cent of the price, then subtract it (discount) or add it (GST).

alternatives.title: One multiplication
text: A 20% discount leaves 80% of the price: multiply by 80 and divide by 100.
18% GST makes 118% of the price: multiply by 118 and divide by 100.

families.title: Sharing an amount in a given ratio
explanations: one-part (procedural): The value of one part (₹460 ÷ 23) was given; Ravi gets 9 parts.
shared-equally (conceptual): The money was shared equally. In a ratio the shares are different: count the parts first.
other-share (procedural): Someone else's share was given; check whose part of the ratio is asked for.
ratio-as-fraction (conceptual): The ratio 9 : 1 was read as the fraction 9/1 of the whole. The whole is 10 parts, so Anu gets 9/10 of it.

teach.idea: A ratio a : b splits the whole into a + b equal parts; the first person gets a of them and the second b.
teach.method: Add the terms to find the number of parts, divide the total by it to find one part, then multiply by the person's number of parts.

alternatives.title: A bar model
text: Draw one bar for each person: a boxes, b boxes (and c boxes).
All the boxes are equal; the total divided by the number of boxes is the value of one box.

families.title: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing rational numbers
explanations: add-tops-and-bottoms (conceptual): The tops and the bottoms were added (or subtracted) separately. Write both fractions with the same denominator first.
sign-error (conceptual): The sign is wrong: compare the sizes of the two fractions to see whether the answer is above or below zero.
minus-negative (conceptual): Subtracting −1/6 was done as subtracting 1/6. Taking away a negative number is the same as adding its opposite.
cross-multiplied (procedural): The fractions were cross-multiplied. To multiply fractions, multiply top by top and bottom by bottom.
not-flipped (procedural): The fractions were multiplied without turning the second one upside down. Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.
flipped-first (procedural): The first fraction was turned upside down; it is the second one (the divisor) that is flipped.

teach.idea: Rational numbers follow the same rules as fractions, together with the sign rules for integers.
teach.method: For + and −, write both with a common denominator and combine the tops. For ×, multiply tops and bottoms. For ÷, multiply by the reciprocal of the second. Then fix the sign and simplify.

alternatives.title: Move on the number line
text: Adding a negative fraction moves left; subtracting a negative fraction moves right.
Mark the first fraction and move by the second to see the sign of the answer before working it out.

families.title: Compound interest and depreciation
explanations: simple-interest (conceptual): Simple interest was found. With compound interest, each year's interest is added on and earns interest too.
amount-given (procedural): The amount was given; compound interest is the amount minus the principal.
simple-depreciation (conceptual): 20% of the ORIGINAL value was taken off every year. Each year the loss is 20% of that year's starting value, which keeps getting smaller.
loss-given (procedural): The total loss in value was given; the question asks what the machine is worth.
growth (conceptual): The value was increased; depreciation means the value goes down each year.
full-rate-each-half (procedural): For half-yearly compounding the rate for each half-year is 10%, not 20%, and there are 4 half-years.
compounded-yearly (procedural): The interest was compounded once a year; half-yearly means 4 periods at 10% each.

teach.idea: With compound interest, each period's interest joins the principal, so the next period's interest is bigger. Depreciation works the same way, downwards.
teach.method: Amount = P × (1 + R/100)ⁿ (depreciation: 1 − R/100). Half-yearly: use R/2 for each half-year and 2n half-years. Interest = amount − principal.

alternatives.title: A year-by-year table
text: Year 1: interest on the principal, add it on.
Year 2: interest on the new amount, add it on. Repeat for each year, then subtract the starting principal.

families.title: Cubes and cube roots
explanations: times-three (conceptual): 25³ was worked out as 25 × 3; a cube multiplies 25 by itself three times.
squared (procedural): 25 was multiplied by itself only twice (that is 25²).
near-cube (recall): A cube next to the right one was used; check: −30 × (−30) × (−30) = −27000.
divided-by-three (conceptual): The number was divided by 3; a cube root is the number that, multiplied by itself three times, gives it.
square-root (procedural): The square root was found; a cube root needs three equal factors, not two.
sign-dropped (conceptual): A negative number has a negative cube root, because a negative × negative × negative is negative.

teach.idea: A cube is a number times itself three times; a cube root undoes it. Three negative factors make a negative, so negative numbers have negative cube roots.
teach.method: For a cube root, use the units digit to guess the last digit of the root and the size to guess the tens, then check by cubing. Or use prime factors in groups of three.

alternatives.title: Group prime factors in threes
text: Write the number as a product of primes, e.g. 1728 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 3.
Take one prime from each group of three equal primes: 2 × 2 × 3 = 12.

families.title: The smallest multiplier that makes a perfect cube
explanations: one-each (procedural): Each incomplete group got one more prime; a group of one needs two more to make three.
leftover-given (procedural): The primes left over after taking out the complete groups of three were given; the multiplier is what is MISSING to complete those groups.
square-of-number (conceptual): Multiplying by 2000 × 2000 does make a cube (2000³), but it is not the smallest; only the missing primes are needed.
square-thinking (conceptual): The primes were paired as for a perfect square. A perfect cube needs every prime in groups of three.

teach.idea: In a perfect cube every prime factor comes in groups of three, because the number is something times itself three times.
teach.method: Write the number as a product of primes and group equal primes in threes. Multiply by whatever primes are needed to complete every group.

alternatives.title: Powers that divide by 3
text: Write the number in index form, e.g. 72 = 2³ × 3².
A perfect cube has every power a multiple of 3: 3² needs one more 3, so multiply by 3.

families.title: When doubling overtakes adding
explanations: last-day-behind (procedural): The last day on which Plan A was still ahead (or equal) was given; the question asks for the first day Plan B is ahead.
start-as-day-one (procedural): The start was counted as day 1; here the start is day 0.
power-as-multiplication (conceptual): After n days of doubling the amount is ₹7 × 2ⁿ, not ₹7 × 2 × n: each day multiplies by 2 again.
doubling-as-adding (conceptual): Doubling was treated as adding ₹10 each day. Doubling adds the whole current amount, which itself keeps growing.

teach.idea: Adding grows by the same amount each step (linear); doubling grows by more and more each step (exponential), so doubling always overtakes in the end.
teach.method: Make a table of the two plans day by day: add for one, double for the other, and look for the first day the doubling plan is bigger.

alternatives.title: Folding paper
text: Fold a sheet in half again and again: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 … layers.
Adding one sheet each time gives only 2, 3, 4, 5 …: doubling soon leaves adding far behind.

families.title: A numeral in another base, in base ten
explanations: read-as-ten (conceptual): The digits were read as a base-ten number. In base 9 the places are worth 1, 9, 81, …, not 1, 10, 100.
digit-sum (conceptual): The digits were simply added; each digit must be multiplied by the value of its place first.
places-reversed (procedural): The place values were taken from the left; the rightmost digit is the ones place, then 9s, then 81s.

teach.idea: In base b, each place is worth b times the place to its right: 1, b, b², b³, … just as base ten has 1, 10, 100.
teach.method: Multiply each digit by the value of its place and add the results.

alternatives.title: Multiply and add from the left
text: Start with the first digit. Multiply by the base and add the next digit; repeat to the end.

families.title: A base-ten number in another base
explanations: remainders-top-down (procedural): The remainders were written in the order they were found. The first remainder is the ones digit, so read them from the last one up.
one-division (procedural): Only one division was done: 199 = 22 × 9 + 1, but 22 is 9 or more, so it must be divided by 9 again.
unchanged (conceptual): The base-ten digits were kept. In base 9 only the digits 0 to 8 are used and the places are worth 1, 9, 81, ….

teach.idea: Writing a number in base b means making groups of 1, b, b², … : the remainders after dividing by b are the digits, ones first.
teach.method: Divide by b again and again, writing each remainder. Stop at 0, then read the remainders from the last to the first.

alternatives.title: Take away the biggest places
text: List the place values: for base 3, 1, 3, 9, 27, 81.
Take away as many of the biggest place value as fit; the count is that digit. Repeat with the next place.
